text: CITY OF BUENA VISTA COUNCIL AGENDA REGULAR MEETING OCTOBER 15, 2026 | 6:00 PM Council Chambers – 2039 Sycamore Avenue ADG #1: CALL TO ORDER, PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE, & PRAYER ADG #2: APPROVAL OF THE AGENDA ADG #3: APPROVAL OF MINUTES FROM THE OCTOBER 1, 2026 REGULAR COUNCIL MEETING, PUBLIC HEARING, & EXECUTIVE SESSION ADG #4: RECOGNITION/COMMUNICATION FROM VISITORS Citizens who desire to speak to council regarding items NOT listed on the agenda will be recognized at this time. Please limit your statement to three (3) minutes. ADG #5: REPORTS: 1. Mayor 2. City Manager – Managerial Activities Update 3. City Attorney 4. Council Committees/Members 5. Department Heads A. Tom Roberts, Community Development – Community Garden MOU Update / Upcoming AFID Grant Application 6. Invited Community Organizations B. Jen Carpenter, Main Street Buena Vista ADG #6: PRESENTATIONS TO CITY COUNCIL & THE PUBLIC 1. Kim Shaw, Rockbridge Area Community Services ADG #7: CONSIDER APPOINTMENTS TO BOARDS, COMMISSIONS, AND COMMITTEES None. OLD BUSINESS NONE NEW BUSINESS NONE ADJOURNMENT 1 • UPCOMING MEETINGS • October 19 | 6:00 PM – Cemetery Committee October 26 |4:00 PM – Budget & Finance Committee • November 5 | 6:00 PM – City Council UPCOMING EVENTS • Every Monday | 6:30 PM – Line Dancing @ The American Legion • Every Friday | 3:00 PM – Farmers Market @ Magnolia Square • Every Friday | 6:00 PM – Friday Events @ Straws • October 16 | 7:00 PM – Word Bridge Wright Night @ Leaf & Lore • October 17 | 8:00 AM – Heroes Breakfast @ The American Legion • October 17 | 4:30 PM – BVFD Annual Harvest Dinner • October 21 | 7:00 PM – Book Club @ Leaf & Lore • October 31 | 4:00 PM – Spooktacular • October 31 | 1:00 PM – Halloween Festival @ GMP • October 31 | 6:00 PM – Spooktacular Golf Cart Parade • October 31 | 6:30 PM – Halloween Film Night @ Straws 2 ADG #3 Draft CITY OF BUENA VISTA CITY COUNCIL REGULAR COUNCIL MEETING, PUBLIC HEARING, & EXECUTIVE SESSION October 1, 2026 | 6:00 PM Council Chambers – 2039 Sycamore Avenue The Buena Vista City Council met for a Regular Council Meeting, Public Hearing, and Executive Session on Thursday, October 1, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. Members Present: Mayor Jesse Lineberry Vice-Mayor Danny Staton Amy Gilliam Michelle Poluikis William Kerr Stephanie Noel-Branch Ronald Cash Members Absent: None ADG #1: CALL TO ORDER, PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE, & PRAYER Mayor Lineberry called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m. and Councilmember Kerr delivered the opening prayer. ADG #2: APPROVAL OF THE AGENDA Councilmember Cash moved to approve the agenda, Councilmember Kerr seconded, and the motion carried. ADG #3: BUENA VISTA CITY COUNCIL PUBLIC HEARING Pursuant to Code of Virginia Section 15.2-1800, the Buena Vista City Council will receive public comment on the following matter: First Amendment to Lease, 5.104 acres to Advanced Drainage Systems. This amendment would extend the end date of the lease from 2036 to 2046. • City Attorney Brian Kearney explained that the property currently leased by Advanced Drainage Systems is part of a proposed land exchange between ADS and the City. Under the proposed exchange, the City would acquire the rear portion of the property, while the front portion would be conveyed to The Advancement Foundation. The existing pipes and related materials would be relocated to the rear portion, with the relocation expected to take about six months. He stated that ADS recently renewed its lease for an additional 10 years but requested an extension to ensure suﬃcient time to recoup the substantial investment it anticipates making in the property as part of the relocation. ADS has indicated that it will execute the deed of exchange once the lease extension is in place. The parties have also agreed to the other terms associated with the exchange, including a new lease term of approximately 19 years. Mr. Kearney noted that because the proposed amendment would extend the lease beyond its current term, a public hearing is required before Council may consider the amendment. There being no public comment, Mayor Lineberry adjourned the Public Hearing. ADG #4: APPROVAL OF MINUTES FROM THE SEPTEMBER 17, 2026, REGULAR COUNCIL MEETING & EXECUTIVE SESSION Councilmember Noel-Branch moved to approve the minutes, Vice-Mayor Staton seconded, and the motion carried. ADG #5: RECOGNITION/COMMUNICATION FROM VISITORS – NON-AGENDA ITEMS • Mike Clements, 403 Magnolia Avenue, addressed Council regarding concerns about responsiveness, transparency, and the manner in which issues raised by citizens are addressed. He stated that it was discouraging to see issues remain unresolved and questioned when and how matters would be addressed. He emphasized that an issue that may seem small to one person can be signiﬁcant to another. Mr. Clements encouraged Council to recognize that residents have diﬀerent perspectives and that disagreements should be discussed and worked through together. He stressed that when a citizen contacts an elected oﬃcial with a request or concern, the resident should receive a response, whether by phone, email, or text, and stated that citizens deserve that level of respect and communication. He reminded Council that they were elected by the citizens to serve and encouraged them to consider their responsibilities carefully, including whether they are able to adequately fulﬁll the duties of their oﬃce and whether they are treating residents fairly. Mr. Clements also expressed concern regarding Council attendance and communication among members, asking that members notify the remainder of Council when they are unable to attend a meeting. He noted that citizens are aware of Council schedules and activities and encouraged them to represent the City in a positive manner when attending meetings or events. He concluded by emphasizing that citizens are paying attention to what is happening in the community, stating, “You can fool the fans, but you can’t fool the players,” and urged Council to follow through when residents ask for assistance rather than passing the matter to another Council member. He expressed concern that unresolved issues were contributing to conditions becoming progressively worse and asked Council to take action and address concerns brought forward by residents. • Avery Brinton, 1 University Hill Drive, spoke about her desire to become more involved in the community and use the next several months to serve local residents. She oﬀered to assist with community service needs and shared that she has been considering organizing SVU students to host a free community car wash, providing residents with an opportunity to have their vehicles washed locally rather than traveling to Lexington. Ms. Brinton expressed appreciation for Council’s service to the community and shared that she greatly enjoys living in Buena Vista, describing it as one of the most beautiful places she has ever lived. • Evan Pearson, 1 University Hill Drive, has lived in Buena Vista for about two years. He spoke about his appreciation for the community and his desire to become more involved. He noted that he is originally from the Harper’s Ferry area, and Buena Vista reminds him of home because of its close-knit community and the sense that residents know and support one another. He shared that he has seen his hometown community become increasingly urbanized as new residents have moved into the area, resulting in a loss of the close community connections that once existed. He expressed a desire to contribute to a community where residents remain connected and engaged in local government. Mr. Pearson stated that he and Ms. Brinton are willing to assist with community service projects and help wherever their eﬀorts may be useful. • Mealy Sizer, thanked City Council for the opportunity to work for the City for 23 years, stating that it had been an honor and that she had met many wonderful people during her time with the City. She also expressed concerns regarding the deactivation of her City-issued cell phone while she was returning from vacation and the presence of three police vehicles at the park when she arrived for work the following morning. Mrs. Sizer stated that, at 80 years old and not being a violent person, she did not feel the police presence was necessary and did not appreciate the way it was handled. She concluded by thanking Council and wishing the best for the park and the City. ADG #6: REPORTS: 1. Mayor Mayor Lineberry expressed his excitement for the upcoming fall season and announced several upcoming community events, including Mountain Days, scheduled for October 9-11, and the upcoming Halloween festivities in downtown and at Glen Maury Park. He also announced that the City is planning a family-oriented New Year’s Eve celebration on December 31, 2026, to conclude the nation’s 250th anniversary year. The event is expected to include early activities, cider, hot cocoa, and ﬁreworks. More details to come. 2. City Manager Ms. Onaitis acknowledged Mealey Sizer and expressed appreciation for her years of service to the City. She also addressed the importance of communicating Council member schedules and apologized for any recent oversight, stating that she would ensure this information is included in future reports. She reported on several recent citizen, utility, and media inquiries, including questions related to Cityfunded community organizations and the utility billing grace period. She also recorded a new BV Mini Beat segment and met with SVU leadership and other stakeholders to discuss collaboration, economic development, and the university’s role in the community. She attended Mr. Spencer Suter’s retirement celebration and announced her plans to attend the upcoming Baker’s Box ribbon cutting at Magnolia Square. Regarding regional initiatives, Ms. Onaitis reported that work continues on the regional Department of Social Services facility, including completion of the construction punch list and discussions regarding a future right-of-way. The City is also working with VDOT regarding acceptance of the access road serving the 911 dispatch center and DSS facility. The City is working with Rockbridge County and Lexington on a potential third-party facility maintenance agreement for the DSS building. She also reported that the three localities are working with the Virginia Department of Health to explore the possibility of adding a VDH location at the DSS site. Discussions are underway regarding potential funding and state support. She also plans to meet with the regional Community Services Board to learn more about available programs, services, and grant opportunities. Ms. Onaitis provided an update on Rockbridge Recovery and Hope House, noting that she has been communicating with board members regarding improvements to internal controls so the City can evaluate future disbursements of opioid abatement funds. She also reported discussions with other area administrators regarding the administration and distribution of those funds and noted that the City and other localities are working to complete required opioid abatement reporting. She reported meeting with the Maury Service Authority regarding support for the City’s ongoing consent order eﬀorts and to learn more about the Authority’s future plans. She also reported that she is working with RARO on a potential “Last Chance Before the Frost” tournament at Glen Maury Park in November. Regarding staﬀ and Council eﬀorts, she reported recent meetings with the Public Works Director, Chief of Police, Parks and Rec Director, Finance Director, and other staﬀ. She noted an upcoming meeting with DEQ regarding the City’s consent order. She also reported holding her fourth executive team meeting and attending the Budget & Finance Committee meeting, where topics included RDA, the ﬁnancial system, school expansion eﬀorts, and ﬁnancial policies. She reported that Public Works staﬀ have received additional guidance regarding overtime, call-out duty, timekeeping, and recording hours worked. She also met with the Commissioner of the Revenue and Treasurer regarding business processes and operational challenges. She also provided an update on RDA and utility billing, stating that City staﬀ are compiling a list of business and operational issues with the ﬁnancial system. Once the issues are identiﬁed, she plans to meet with RDA management to address the concerns and determine whether additional legal action may be necessary. She also reported that utility staﬀ are conducting manual meter readings as a backup to the current billing system to help ensure accurate billing while system issues are being addressed. As for process improvements, Ms. Onaitis reported that the City has begun inventorying existing standard operating procedures and identifying areas where procedures are needed. A similar inventory is being conducted for ﬁnance and purchasing policies, with an update expected at a future Budget & Finance Committee meeting. For economic and community development, she announced that the Economic Development Authority’s façade improvement program opened October 7 and will accept applications through November 6. The program provides reimbursement of up to $5,000 for qualifying exterior building improvements. She also reported that the City, Main Street Buena Vista, and economic development staﬀ will begin holding monthly meetings to improve coordination and resource alignment. Mountain Days planning was a primary topic of the most recent meeting. Ms. Onaitis reminded Council that funding for MSBV will be an important consideration during the upcoming budget process because maintaining certiﬁed Main Street status requires a certain level of funding. She also reported that the EDA recently discussed Brownﬁeld applications and that the City and EDA may each submit applications for up to two sites annually. Regarding public safety, she reported that the Police Department participated in a Rockbridge Report media interview related to police technology. She also mentioned that National Night Out had a strong turnout. She discussed plans to strengthen coordination among local ﬁrst responders and develop a City-wide Continuity of Operations Plan (COOP) addressing operations during emergencies or disasters. Ms. Onaitis also reported that funding analyses are continuing to determine how the City can support school needs, particularly in connection with the proposed expansion. She reminded Council that a community conversation regarding the proposed 1% sales tax referendum is scheduled for October 20 at 6:00 p.m. at the Buena Vista Fire Department. The meeting will provide an opportunity for residents to receive factual information and ask questions, with the Superintendent participating. She also noted that staﬀ are developing revenue projections for school funding formulas and the upcoming budget. In addition, she plans to provide Council with a ﬁrst-quarter expenditure report in November showing expenditures in relation to the allocated budget. 3. City Attorney None. 4. Council Committees/Members Mrs. Gilliam reported that the Budget & Finance Committee discussed the City’s committee structure and potential changes to how committees are organized; additional information will be provided as the discussion progresses. Mr. Cash encouraged residents to attend Mountain Days and highlighted children’s activities including a pie-eating contest and a pumpkin seed-spitting contest, as well as the variety of outdoor-themed prizes available for children, including ﬁshing poles, electronic shooting earmuﬀs, a backpack, sleeping bag, tent, and other outdoor-related items. He noted that the event is designed to connect children with the outdoors, local culture, heritage, and Appalachian traditions. 5. Department Heads/Constitutional Officers/Court Clerks None. 6. Invited Community Organizations Jen Carpenter – Main Street Buena Vista Mrs. Carpenter extended three invitations to Council and the community. She encouraged everyone to attend Mountain Days, October 9-11. She also invited Council members to participate in a downtown walking tour on October 14 from 4:00-5:00 p.m. as part of the Governor’s Summit on Rural Prosperity. The tour will begin at the VIA. Lastly, she invited the community to attend Spooktacular in “Boona Vista” and noted that additional information and social media promotions will be coming soon. Code § 2.2-3711(A)(1), to discuss personnel matters including board and commission appointments (Architectural Review Board, and Beacon Theater Board vacancy); § 2.2-3711(A)(3), (8), and (29), to discuss the acquisition or disposition of real property, where discussion in an open meeting would adversely affect the bargaining position or negotiating strategy of the public body, the award of a public contract where discussion in an open session would adversely affect the City’s bargaining position, and to consult with legal counsel regarding specific legal matters (potential acquisition of blighted downtown property, and Virginia American Water). ROLL CALL Mayor Partin Yes Councilor Ellis Yes Councilor Daye Yes Councilor Wheat - Yes Vice Mayor Joyner - Yes Councilor Harris - Yes Motion Passes 6-0 WELCOME TO VISITORS REPORT TO THE CITY MANAGER Vincent Jones, City Manager, provided several updates to City Council. Mr. Jones announced that Council members had received copies of the City’s Fiscal Year 2027 Budget Book, which had been updated from previous versions and was also available on the City’s website. He stated that the City would submit the FY2027 Budget Book to the Government Finance Officers Association (GFOA) for review, with the goal of establishing an annual practice of submitting the budget document for consideration for GFOA recognition. Mr. Jones described this as an important milestone for the city and recognized Deputy City Manager Stacey Jordan for coordinating the Finance team’s efforts in completing the budget book. He also congratulated Ms. Jordan on two professional recognitions, announcing that she had been named one of the Top 10 Visionary Women Leaders to Watch in 2026 and had been selected by Government Business Review as Deputy City Manager of the Year for 2026, with the related publication expected in October. Council further recognized Ms. Jordan for her contributions to the city, including her work to bring the City’s audits current, identify financing opportunities for capital projects that had not been available to the city in more than ten years, explore refinancing opportunities, and work toward the potential restoration of the City’s bond rating. Mr. Jones and Council expressed their appreciation for Ms. Jordan’s expertise in municipal finance and congratulated her on her accomplishments. Fiscal Year August Financials – Stacey Jordan, Deputy City Manager Stacey Jordan, Deputy City Manager, presented the Finance Committee’s August budget-toactual report and highlighted several additions to the City’s financial reporting. Ms. Jordan stated that the City would begin reviewing the Statement of Revenues, Expenditures, and Changes in Fund Balance throughout the fiscal year, beginning with preliminary FY2026 fund balance figures and adding FY2027 revenues and expenditures to provide an updated year-end fund balance projection. The report would also include updates on the City’s General Obligation (GO) bond projects to allow Council to track the status of each project. For August, Ms. Jordan reported that citywide revenues were trending 0.73%, or approximately $103,000, lower in FY2027 compared with FY2026, while expenditures were approximately 0.47%, or $1.3 million, higher. She attributed the revenue decrease to federal funding, interest income, fines, and insurance claims, while increased expenditures were related primarily to services and supplies for CSA and the schools, as well as the 2% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA). Although FY2027 expenditures were trending slightly higher than the previous fiscal year, Ms. Jordan stated that it remained early in the fiscal year and she anticipated the City would remain in a favorable overall position by year-end. Ms. Jordan reported that General Fund revenues for August were trending 1.72%, or approximately $874,000, higher than FY2026, while expenditures were approximately 0.21%, or $575,000, higher. Increased revenues were attributed to Compensation Board funding, HB 599 police aid, federal revenues, local taxes, and cigarette tax collections. Increased expenditures were primarily associated with the 2% COLA. Enterprise Fund revenues were trending 0.36%, or approximately $329,000, higher, while expenditures were 3.7%, or approximately $787,000, lower than FY2026. The revenue increase was attributed to HWR billing, while the decrease in expenditures resulted from reductions in professional services and supplies. For the schools, August revenues were approximately 1.37%, or $477,000, higher, and expenditures were approximately 1.27%, or $305,000, higher than FY2026. Ms. Jordan noted that approximately $500,000 in projected federal Head Start revenue had not yet been received. Ms. Jordan reviewed the City’s preliminary FY2026 ending fund balance and stated that the Finance Department continued to work through adjustments and final transactions associated with the FY2026 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR). She reported that 1,257 invoices totaling $5,263,910 were paid during August. The City had also paid approximately 52% of its debt service, leaving a remaining debt balance of approximately $3.8 million. Regarding the City’s GO bond projects, Ms. Jordan reported that approximately $2.5 million had been spent or encumbered and that project status updates had been provided by City departments. She also included the Queen Street Pump Station in the report, although it was not funded through the GO bonds, because LGIP funds had been allocated to the project. Ms. Jordan stated that while a significant portion of the project funding had not yet been expended, nearly all contracts had been awarded and vendors were in place to move the projects forward. She advised that the City had spending requirements that must be met by the end of November and stated that, following discussions with department heads, she anticipated the City would meet the required guideline. Major expenditures were expected to involve HWR, the Community Center pool, and paving projects. She noted that paving was expected to be completed by October, construction of the new pool was underway, and HWR continued work on the pump station. Ms. Jordan stated that biweekly meetings regarding the FY2026 ACFR would continue and that the City remained on schedule. She also reported that the FY2027 Budget Book had been submitted to the Government Finance Officers Association (GFOA) for consideration for the Distinguished Budget Presentation Award and was currently under review. Once the ACFR was completed, the City also planned to submit the financial report to GFOA for consideration for its financial reporting award. During Council discussion, Ms. Jordan was asked about the approximately $500,000 in anticipated federal Head Start funding and whether changes at the federal level could affect its receipt. She explained that during the City’s legislative meeting with its delegation, officials indicated that if federal funding was not received, the Commonwealth had surplus funding available to assist the schools until additional information became available. She stated that funding was available to allow the program to continue during the current fiscal year. Ms. Jordan was also asked about the timeline for completion of the FY2026 ACFR. She stated that the report was due by December 15, but the City was working toward an earlier submission, potentially in November. She explained that once all required information was provided to the auditor, David Foley, he planned to conduct sampling in October with the goal of completing the report in November, a process expected to take approximately one month. Hopewell Water Renewal update – Vincent Jones, City Manager Vincent Jones, City Manager, provided an update regarding Hopewell Water Renewal (HWR) and the operation of the City’s wastewater treatment facility. Mr. Jones explained that the City operates the facility on behalf of its residents and industrial partners pursuant to the Hopewell Regional Wastewater Treatment Facility Agreement, which establishes how the facility is operated and funded. He stated that the agreement was last updated in 2017 through the Third Supplement. For approximately four months, the City had been engaged in negotiations with its industrial partners regarding a proposed Fourth Supplement to update the agreement and establish operating guidelines intended to serve the interests of both the City and its industrial partners. Mr. Jones reported that the parties had been unable to reach a resolution through negotiations and, based on Council’s direction, legal action might be necessary to resolve the matter. He advised that the City Attorney and outside counsel were prepared to protect the interests of the City and its residents as the matter moved forward. Mr. Jones concluded his report, and there were no additional questions from Council regarding HWR. **Comments from Mayor Partin on Beacon Theatre ** Mayor John B. Partin Jr. provided comments regarding recent public information concerning the Beacon Theatre and explained City Council’s actions and intentions for the facility. Mayor Partin stated that the City began the process the previous year of transitioning the Beacon from a forprofit entity to a nonprofit entity, which he described as the City’s original intent when the Beacon was renovated and the Beacon LLC was formed in 2012. As part of the transition, the City advised the Beacon Theatre Board that its membership would be expanded to provide greater professional diversity, including individuals with business and financial backgrounds. Council appointed ten members to the Board in April, and the Board had met monthly since that time to facilitate the transfer of institutional knowledge from existing members to new members and to take the steps necessary to achieve nonprofit status. City Council allows for public comment, limited to matters on which the Council has the power and authority to act and are not listed on the printed agenda. Participation: Citizens who wish to participate in a meeting’s public comment period may do so by signing up at the podium at the entrance prior to the beginning of the meeting, emailing their comments to Peyton Nibblett, Deputy City Clerk, at pnibblett@martinsvilleva.gov, calling in their comments to 276-403-5196, or mailing comments to the City of Martinsville, attn.: Peyton Nibblett, Martinsville, VA 24114 (a.) Comments, or a request to speak, must be received by noon the day before a Council meeting for consideration by the Council at the meeting. (b.) Any person submitting comments or requesting to speak must identify themselves by name and address, including zip code. (c.) Remarks are to be limited to 3 minutes or less (as read aloud),address a topic of City business, and refrain from making any personal references or accusations of a factually false and/or malicious nature. (d.) Priority for comments is given to City residents, taxpayers, and business owners.(e.) Speakers may not yield time. (f.) Groups of speakers on the same topic must designate a single representative. Comments violating these rules may not be presented at the Council meeting. (g.) Any speaker violating these rules may be removed from the podium or from the Council Chamber. (h.) This policy does not apply to public hearings, at which any citizen of Martinsville may appear and speak on the subject of the public hearing. 9. Comments by Members of City Council 10. title: A special meeting of the Petersburg Planning Commission to review and discuss the proposed Zoning and Subdivision Ordinance Update
text: City of Petersburg Planning Commission Meeting Agenda Monday, October 26, 2026 6:00 PM Petersburg Public Library 1. Call to Order 2. Roll Call 3. Adoption of the Agenda 4. Discussion/Review a. ZONING AND SUBDIVISION ORDINANCE AMENDMENT AND READOPTION: The City’s Zoning Ordinance is proposed to be holistically repealed and replaced with a reorganized and updated Zoning/Subdivision Ordinance. The proposed Ordinance reorganizes articles and standards; contains technical language changes to ease interpretation/application and to follow the most current Code of Virginia regulations; modifies dimensional standards for the City’s primary zoning districts; and changes permitted land uses within zoning districts that include, but are not limited to, deletion and addition of uses and categorization of certain uses into broader terms, and including additional and modified definitions of terms accordingly. The updated ordinance may be adopted with a delayed effective date. Full Draft Ordinance available for viewing at http://www.petersburgva.org/DocumentCenter/View/9088/Draft-Ordinance---1012026?bidId= Individual Articles available for viewing at http://www.petersburg-va.org/688/CurrentProjects 5. Adjournment PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING OCTOBER 26, 2026 Zoning and Subdivision Ordinance Update Background and Overview • City has been working with Berkley Group since spring, 2024 to rewrite and update the City’s Zoning/Subdivision Ordinance • Work included focus groups, outreach events, surveys as well as review of individual draft articles over the court of several work sessions • Planning Commission held public hearing on full draft ordinance on October 1, 2026 • Several public comments received identifying concerns with the draft ordinance; Planning Commission deferred action for additional time to review the document • Special meeting is scheduled to go through individual concerns and discuss potential solutions Lot Sizes •Draft ordinance proposed changes to minimum lot area and width requirements, particularly throughout residential districts • Proposed lot sizes were based on existing lot sizes with the goal of allowing new lots to meet the existing development pattern • Concerns were raised that smaller lot sizes will lead to unwanted density and associated impacts, especially in more suburban subdivisions •Proposed update to consider: ◦ Requirements for lower density residential districts (R-1A, R-1, R-2) will remain unchanged and will match current regulations; newly created lots will still be required to meet the present-day standards ◦ Requirements for higher density residential districts (R-3, R-4, R-5, R-5) will be increased from the current draft, but still differ slightly from current ordinance; for example, a new single-family dwellings lot would need to be at least 40 feet in width and 3,500 square feet in area Existing Nonconforming Lots •Both draft ordinance and existing ordinance include provision that a single-family dwelling can be built on a legal nonconforming lot as long as setback and other code requirements can be met • Concern was raised that draft ordinance did not include current requirement that contiguous nonconforming lots under the same ownership be merged or adjusted to becoming less nonconforming before being developed •Proposed update to consider: ◦ The language from the existing ordinance will be incorporated into the new ordinance and the requirement to merge contiguous lots will be retained Uses in Single-Family Districts •Draft ordinance proposed to allow additional residential uses within most residential districts • The proposal was intended to reflect the goals of the City’s Comprehensive Plan by supporting a variety of housing types and encouraging missing middle housing • Concerns were raised about higher density and proximity to existing singlefamily neighborhoods •Proposed update to consider: ◦ Duplexes will be removed as a proposed use in the R-2, Zoning District; the R-1A, R-1, and R-2 districts will be retained a strictly single-family districts ◦ A wider variety of housing types is still recommended in the R-3 and higherdensity residential districts (e.g. triplexes, quadplexes, and townhomes) Unlisted Uses •Draft ordinance proposes language stating the Zoning Administrator can consider and determine whether a use that is not explicitly listed in the Use Matrix is similar to a listed use • Concern was raised that this gives unlimited authority for the Zoning Administrator to allow undefined uses in the city •Proposed update to consider: • Additional language will be added to clarify the criteria the Zoning Administrator considers when determining whether an unlisted use is similar to an existing use, including traffic and environmental impacts, noise, odor, utility demand, impacts to safety and welfare • The ordinance will also specify that the Zoning Administrator provides their findings in writing and the determination can be appealed Temporary Uses •Draft ordinance proposes the creation of a temporary use permit which would be issued for certain uses that do not occur permanently • Temporary uses are identified within the use matrix • Concern was raised that an individual could request any use temporarily, regardless of whether that use is permitted •Proposed update to consider: • The use matrix will be reorganized to clearly identify which uses can be requested temporarily (e.g. seasonal sales, health care structure, construction trailers) and where those uses are allowed; existing language in the draft ordinance identifies how long temporary uses are permitted and how many times in a calendar year Zoning Permits and Accessory Structures •Draft ordinance proposed a requirement for a zoning permit for accessory structures (sheds, fences, etc.) that were under the size that requires building permit • Goal was to provide review that would ensure setback and design requirements are met • Concerns were raised that a permit requirement would be unenforceable and that permits would be required for small decorative yard features •Proposed update to consider: • Zoning permits will just be used for certain unique uses which are identified in the ordinance (e.g. farmers markets and food trucks) • No additional permitting requirement will be introduced for accessory structures; building permit requirements will remain unchanged Form-Based Design Requirements •Draft ordinance proposes design requirements for new construction to ensure size, scale, and character matches existing development • Concern was raised that specific requirements on materials and method of construction violate State Law provisions on Building Code •Proposed update to consider: ◦ City-wide requirements specific to materials for new construction will be removed; these rules would still apply in Highway Corridor Overlay District as allowed by State Code ◦ Requirements specifically regulating form like height, massing, and scale are within the scope of a local zoning ordinance and will be retained Definition of “Family” • Draft ordinance proposed amending the current definition of family to be modernized and clarified • Existing definition: “One person, or two or more persons related by blood, adoption or marriage living and cooking together as a single housekeeping unit with not more than two boarders; or a number of persons, but not exceeding two living and cooking together as a single housekeeping unit, though not related by blood, adoption or marriage shall be deemed to constitute a family. The term "person" used herein shall not be construed to include lodger{s) or boarder(s).” • Proposed definition: “A person living alone, or any of the following groups living together as a single housekeeping unit: (1) any number of persons related by blood, marriage, adoption, guardianship, or duly-authorized custodial relationship; (2) up to four unrelated people; (3) two unrelated people and any offspring related to either of them by blood, marriage, adoption, guardianship, or custodial relationship; (3) residents of an assisted living facility or group home as allowed by Code of Virginia § 15.2-2291. • Concern was raised that the proposed definition could allow overoccupancy, particularly the language about two unrelated individuals and their offspring • Proposed update for consideration: Staff believe the proposed definition is reasonable, but Item 3 could be removed from the definition meaning a family would be considered 1) persons related by blood, 2) up to four unrelated individuals, or 3) a residential group home which the City is required to treat as a single family unit Manufactured Housing •The draft ordinance reflects the recent mandates from Virginia State Code that manufactured housing be allowed by-right wherever stickbuilt housing is allowed as long as 1) a manufactured unit is placed on an individual lot, 2) constructed so that a certificate of occupancy is issued within 5 years of manufacture date, and 3) converted to and taxed as real property (i.e. being placed on permanent foundation) • Concerns have been raised that manufactured homes will impact character, and density in existing single-family neighborhoods • Proposed update for consideration: No substantive changes are proposed as the City is required to abide by State Law, but language in Article 4 can be clarified to reinforce that manufactured homes are only allowed when they meet the criteria outlined above Proposed Changes for Consideration: 1. Article 3: Clarification on uses/structures requiring Zoning Permit (page 2) 2. Article 4: Updates to minimum area and width requirements in Zoning Districts (pages 3-11) 3. Article 5: Façade requirements in Highway Corridor Overlay District (page 12) 4. Article 6: Clarification on unlisted uses, updates to use matrix to restrict uses in single-family districts (pages 13-18) 5. Article 8: Updates to architectural design requirements for compliance with State Code, corrected typo on parking lot requirements (pages 19-23) 6. Article 9: Addition of restrictions on developing contiguous nonconforming lots under common ownership. (page 24) 7. Article 11: Definitions clarified for family, temporary use, and zoning permit (page 25) 1 Division 7. Zoning Permits. 58 Section 3-7-1. Purpose and Intent. The purpose of a zoning permit is to ensure that all uses, structures, signs, site features, and buildings in the City of Petersburg demonstrate full compliance with the provisions of this Ordinance prior to the commencement of construction or the operation. Section 3-7-2. Applicability. (A) The regulations of this Division shall apply to all: (1) Structures, fences, walls, and signs that do not require a building permit, in accordance with Chapter 22, Buildings and Building Regulations, of the City Code; and (2) Uses speciﬁed as requiring a Zoning Permit in Article 7, Use Performance Standards, of this Ordinance. (i) Structures that do not require a building permit in accordance with Chapter 22, Buildings and Building Regulations of the City Code shall not require a zoning permit provided the structure complies with the regulations of the Zoning District in which the structure is located and all other requirements of this ordinance. (B) No zoning permit shall be issued for any of the above unless it complies with the provisions of this Ordinance, or a SUP, variance, or written order from an appeal has been approved as provided by this Ordinance. Editor’s Note: This is a proposed new division to outline the requirements for zoning permits more clearly. The City introduced the zoning permit process in the summer of 2024; text has been introduced to align with the information required. 58 2 City of Petersburg Zoning & Subdivision Ordinance Update Draft Article 4 – Primary Zoning Districts Division 4. Residential District Standards. Section 4-4-1. R-1A, Single Family Residence District. (A) Establishment and Intent. The R-1A District is established to reﬂect existing suburban residential development, primarily characterized by traditional single family dwellings on estate lots. Non-residential uses should complement the existing residential living patterns and are restricted to those that provide community-oriented amenities, services, and recreation. The R1A District is not intended to be expanded for future development; consolidation with the R-1 district is appropriate. (B) Limitations. title: October 19, 2026 Planning Commission Agenda Packet
text: City of Radford Planning Commission Agenda October 19, 2026 10 Robertson St., Radford, VA 6:00pm. – Regular Meeting Call to order Determination of a quorum Approval of Agenda Approval of Minutes: September 21, 2026 – Regular Meeting CITIZEN COMMENTS ON PUBLIC MATTERS: (Please state your name for the record – Please limit comments to 3 minutes or less) 1. Work Session – Zoning Ordinance Update Staff Report Planning Commission Member Comments Adjournment Future Meetings November 12, 2026 - 5:30-7:30 Open House November 16, 2026 – Open House/Regular Meeting City of Radford, Virginia • 10 Robertson Street • Radford, Virginia 24141 • Phone (540) 731-3603 • Fax (540) 731-3699 • www.radfordva.gov Radford Planning Commission Monday, September 21, 2026 Municipal Building Members Present: Mr. Castleberry Mr. Gropman Dr. Pearce Mr. Watson, Chairperson Absent: Mr. Gillespie Mr. Collier, Vice Chairperson Dr. Rzigalinski Staff/Visitors: Melissa Skelton, City Staff Aphi Fancon, NRVRC Staff Mr. Watson called the meeting to order at 6:10 pm in the Radford City Council Chambers at 10 Robertson Street, Radford Virginia. A quorum was present. Approval of Agenda: Mr. Watson approved the agenda. Approval of Minutes for August 17, 2026: Minutes were recommended for approval as submitted by Mr. Castleberry, seconded by Mr. Gropman. Voting Yes: Mr. Castleberry, Mr. Gropman, Dr. Pearce, Mr. Watson Voting No: None Abstain: PUBLIC COMMENTS – Mr. Scott Lang – objects to the draft ordinance for regulating short term stays. He believes it will have a negative impact on his personal business as well as the city in general. His AirBnB focuses on the niche of people with small children and dogs, which would be negatively impacted by the proposed ordinance. He is here to better understand why it has been brought to the table. He is primarily opposed to the requirement for owner-occupancy, which would limit local residents to having more than one AirBnB. Mr. Gropman commented that the zoning ordinance hasn’t been updated since 2007. Mr. Watson commented that the ordinance needed to cover this new area of concern and is still being completed. SUBJECT: Work Session Zoning Ordinance At the last meeting, numerous comments were provided by commissioners. Ms. Fancon has brought a formal response to those comments in a handout. Handouts were provided as paper copies and will be provided electronically. Ms. Fancon went through the tabular handout and explained each row. Following are the PC member comments: Mr. Watson pointed out that the main use of the term “Family” in the document is as a designator for different types of residential construction. The document will be checked to ensure it’s not used elsewhere, and the terms for housing will be changed accordingly. Ms. Fancon described the new regulations pertaining to manufactured homes. There will be a new addition to the general provisions to comply with these regulations. Additional details are available from Ms. Fancon. Mr. Watson pointed out that the terms “mobile home” and “manufactured housing” are being used interchangeably when there are actual differences. Dr. Pearce pointed out that it would be helpful to see proposed language before reacting or commenting in detail. She stated that she is opposed to additional requirements that would remove a designer’s capacity to optimize a home for solar orientation, passive design, and other site-responsive considerations. Ms. Skelton pointed out that the state regulations are ostensibly designed to allow for affordable housing, but housing built to manufactured housing standards tends to have higher operating costs, resulting in reduced affordability overall. Dr. Pearce agreed but pointed out that other options (e.g., tiny homes that might be built on a mobile chassis) which would meet higher efficiency standards have been precluded elsewhere in the ordinance. Ms. Fancon defined “short term rental” as being occupancy for a limited period in an owner’s primary residence without the building owner present. This is different from bed and breakfast, homestay, and ADUs, which are something else. Discussion ensued about variations of non-owner occupancy in different districts by right vs. SUP. Mr. Watson expressed concern that approving these types of occupancy will quickly get away from us if SUPs are required. He advocated having standards/standardized guidelines that must be met, or the owner would lose the capacity to engage in that type of activity. Participants agreed that there are many variations that can be confusing. Farmers’ markets are not listed in any district as a by-right use. B2, B3, and mixed use were noted as possible places for this to be included directly. Ms. Fancon proposed to further integrate this discussion into the next draft. Public input opportunities were discussed, including two open houses (likely Nov 2 and 12, from 5:30-7:30). Ms. Fancon said that she would prepare posters to be available at the sessions that people could use to become familiar with the document’s content. She stated that the document would be cleaned up prior to any public release. The document will also be available online at the NRV site, where people can review and comment. The member of the public present said that having two weeks with a pdf to review would likely be enough time to make good use of a public input opportunity. It was suggested that most people probably have specific areas of interest within the code and would not review the whole thing. Motion to adjourn: Motion to adjourn was made at 7:25 by Mr. Castleberry, seconded by Mr. Gropman. Voting Yes: Mr. Castleberry, Mr. Gropman, Dr. Pearce, Mr. Watson Voting No: None Abstain: COMMISSION MEMBER COMMENTS Mr. Castleberry – none Mr. Gropman – none Dr. Pearce – none Mr. Watson – none Submitted by: Annie R. Pearce, Secretary Date: September 21, 2026

title: Action Agenda
text: City of Roanoke, Virginia CITY COUNCIL INFORMAL SESSION October 5, 2026 9:00 AM City Council Chamber 215 Church Avenue, SW AGENDA The City of Roanoke is a safe, caring and economically vibrant community in which to live, learn, work, play and prosper. A vibrant urban center with strong neighborhoods set amongst the spectacular beauty of Virginia's Blue Ridge. NOTICE: City Council meetings will be televised live and replayed on RVTV Channel 3 on Thursdays at 7:00 pm, and Saturdays from 10:00 am to 5:00 pm; and video streamed through YouTube Live at youtube.com/RoanokeVa. Council meetings are offered with closed captioning for the deaf or hard of hearing. CALL TO ORDER - ROLL CALL. All present. Welcome ITEMS FOR ACTION: A communication from Mayor Joseph L. Cobb requesting that the Council convene in a Closed Meeting to discuss vacancies on certain authorities, boards, commissions and committees appointed by the Council, pursuant to Section 2.23711 (A)(1), Code of Virginia (1950), as amended. • Architectural Review Board • City Planning Commission • Roanoke Arts Commission • Board of Zoning Appeals • Economic Development Authority • Fair Housing Board • Gun Violence Prevention Commission • Human Services Advisory Board • Roanoke Neighborhood Advocates • Roanoke Public Library Board • Towing Advisory Board (7-0) A communication from the City Attorney requesting that City Council convene in a closed meeting to consult with legal counsel regarding a certain legal matter requiring the provision of legal advice by the City Attorney concerning contract obligations involving a City-owned facility in the Central part of the City of Roanoke, pursuant to Section 2.2-3711 (A)(8), Code of Virginia, (1950), as amended. (7-0) A communication from the City Manager requesting that City Council convene in a closed meeting to discuss or consider the disposition of publicly held real property in the Northwest area of the City where discussion in an open meeting would adversely affect the bargaining position or negotiating strategy of the public body, pursuant to Section 2.2-3711 (A)(3), Code of Virginia, (1950), as amended. (7-0) Items listed on the 2:00 pm City Council docket requiring discussion/clarification and addition/deletions to the 2:00 pm agenda. None. The City Manager shared the following comments: Last week, the Roanoke City Police Department held a Love Where You Live event at Ferncliff Apartments, bringing together officers, City staff, volunteers, and community partners. Our Stormwater team recently completed the City’s annual report documenting our compliance with our stormwater permit. The report is an important communication tool that helps us share the work we’re doing to protect our local waterways, including 10 citywide street-sweeping cycles that removed more than 1,000 tons of sediment, cleaning storm drains, inspecting nearly 29,000 feet of pipe, and reaching more than 38,000 residents through public outreach. text: City of Roanoke, Virginia CITY COUNCIL October 19, 2026 2:00 PM City Council Chamber 215 Church Avenue, SW AGENDA The City of Roanoke is a safe, caring and economically vibrant community in which to live, learn, work, play and prosper. A vibrant urban center with strong neighborhoods set amongst the spectacular beauty of Virginia's Blue Ridge. NOTICE: City Council meetings will be televised live and replayed on RVTV Channel 3 on Thursdays at 7:00 pm, and Saturdays from 10:00 am to 5:00 pm; and video streamed through YouTube Live at youtube.com/RoanokeVa. Council meetings are offered with closed captioning for the deaf or hard of hearing. 1. CALL TO ORDER - ROLL CALL. All present. Moment of Silence in memory of the late Claudia Whitworth, long-time publisher of the Roanoke Tribune who passed away on October 8, 2026; and beloved City employee Jeff White, Codes Compliance Officer, who passed away on October 17, 2026. The Invocation was delivered by The Reverend Alexander MacPhail, Rector, Christ Episcopal Church. The Pledge of Allegiance to the Flag of the United States of America was led by Mayor Joseph L. Cobb. Welcome ANNOUNCEMENTS: 2. PRESENTATIONS AND ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS: A proclamation declaring October 25 - 31, 2026 as National Lead Poisoning Prevention Week. The Mayor advised that going forward, the 2:00 pm meeting would begin with the Council Members providing "shout-outs" or announcing community events recently attended. The Council Members made the following announcements: Council Member Nash “shouted out” the Excel Center located in Melrose Plaza and commented that they hosted a meeting to recruit more adult learners seeking high school diplomas. Council Member Hagen “shouted out” the Bear Theatre production of Death by Design, a murder mystery comedy written by local playwright Stacy Upton. Council Member Sanchez-Jones "shouted out" GO Fest organizers and the Champs Boxing Gym for a successful event this past weekend. Vice-Mayor McGuire "shouted out" the GO Fest organizers, thanked poll workers for their hard work and advised that early voting has begun. Mayor Cobb "shouted out" the Blue Ridge Literacy annual celebration and encouraged everyone to get the booklet produced titled "Writing from the Heart." 3. HEARING OF CITIZENS UPON PUBLIC MATTERS: The City Council sets this time as a priority for citizens to be heard. If deemed appropriate, matters will be referred to the City Manager for response, recommendation or report to the City Council. Kimberly Tulou, appeared before the Council representing PedalSafe ROA with several requests for the Council to reinforce the safe routes to school initiative and the Safety Action Plan previously adopted. 4. Cobb, Chair, Roanoke City Council Personnel Committee, requesting that Council convene in a closed meeting to discuss annual performance evaluations of Council-Appointed Officers, pursuant to Section 2.2-3711 (A)(1), Code of Virginia (1950), as amended. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Concurred in the request. C-3. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Received and filed. REGULAR AGENDA: 5. PUBLIC HEARINGS: None. 6. PETITIONS AND COMMUNICATIONS: Presentation of the Roanoke Cultural Endowment Update. Shaleen Powell, Executive Director, Roanoke Cultural Endowment, Spokesperson. (Sponsored by Mayor Cobb and Council Member Volosin) Received and filed. 7. REPORTS OF CITY OFFICERS AND THE CITY MANAGER: 1. City Manager: BRIEFING: Arts and Culture Plan 2026 - 15 minutes. ITEMS RECOMMENDED FOR ACTION: a. (7-0) COMMENTS OF THE CITY MANAGER. None. PUBLIC MATTERS FOLLOW-UP Carol Corbin, Communications Manager, reported on the following matters from the September 21 and October 5, 2026, Meetings: Bus Rider At the September 21 meeting, a resident inquired about a direct route on the 15 bus to the Valley View Walmart. The resident also reported her concern to the GRTC Board, which operates the Valley Metro bus system. Valley Metro officials are looking into the possibility of future route modifications and will follow up with the resident. In the meantime, Valley Metro confirmed that the resident can take any bus to the transfer station, and get on the 11 bus, for drop off at Walmart. Passengers with a qualifying disability can also contact Valley Metro for more information about paratransit services. Meals Tax A resident spoke at the September 21 meeting with questions about City meals tax revenue and deferred maintenance projects. The August 2026 Monthly Financial Report, along with a breakdown of completed and in-progress City HVAC projects and elevator modernization work, were provided to the resident by the City’s FOIA Officer. Safe Streets for All Also at the September 21 meeting, a representative from a local organization brought concerns about the age of the City’s Street Design Manual. Public Works reports that it is in the process of updating its published manual. However, the department is following design practices that are based primarily on the latest applicable federal and state standards and supplemented by recognized industry guidance such as the National Association of City Transportation Officials. 8. 2. Recommendation It is my recommendation that the board authorizes the Treasurer to issue the tax refund in the amount of $4,897.15 to USCOC of Virginia due to the abatement of the Public Service Tax by the Commissioner of Revenue. 27 28 DATE: October 9, 2026 TO: Cumberland County Board of Supervisors Summer Medina, County Administrator FROM: Jennifer Crews, Assistant County Administrator of Finance & Administration RE: Opioid Settlement Funds Appropriation for Drug Recovery Court Expenditures Background In December 2024, the Board of Supervisors approved a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between the Counties of Cumberland, Buckingham, and Prince Edward and the Central Virginia Recovery Court. The MOU defined the general roles and responsibilities of the counties in their collaborative effort to facilitate and support the Recovery Court while acknowledging each county's budgeting constraints and limitations. The Counties agreed to make good-faith efforts to allocate funds for the Recovery Court, recognizing that such allocations are contingent upon the availability of funds, budgetary constraints, and legislative appropriations. The counties acknowledged that expenditures for the Recovery Court may qualify as appropriate opiate abatement expenses for the purpose of utilizing settlement proceeds received from the Opioid Abatement Authority (OAA). The Counties agreed to fund their percentage of the Recovery Court operations based on the number of slots allocated. Currently, the initial allocation is 2 slots per locality which would require 1/3 funding of the budget from each of the 3 counties. As stated in the MOU, Prince Edward County is the fiscal agent for the Recovery Court. Prince Edward has established and maintained the accounts and disbursed the funds for the Recovery Court for FY ’25, ’26, and ’27. In September, Prince Edward invoiced the County for one-third (1/3) of the Recovery Court’s total operational costs for FY ’25 and FY ’26. The invoices totaled $51,229.06. Recommendation It is my recommendation that the Board approves an appropriation of $51,229.06 for the County’s share of the FY ’25 and FY ’26 costs associated with the Recovery Court. Motion MINUTES OF THE CUMBERLAND COUNTY PLANNING COMMISSION CIP WORKSHOP Cumberland County, Virginia March 24, 2025 PRESENT: Matt Seal, District 3 Steve Donahue, District 2 Hubert Allen, District 4, Vice-Chairman Steve Rosen, District 1, Chairman Harry Donahue, District 5 William Flippen, At-Large ALSO PRESENT: Derek Stamey, County Administrator Stephany S. Johnson, Planning Director, Zoning Administrator, and Planning Commission Secretary ABSENT: Paul Stimpson, Board of Supervisors Liaison to the Commission Kevin Meadows, At-Large CALL TO ORDER AND ROLL CALL The meeting was called to order at 6:30 p.m. A quorum was established, and guests were welcomed. APPROVAL OF AGENDA MOTION: A motion was made by Commissioner Allen and seconded by Commissioner Steve Donahue to approve the agenda as presented. The motion was approved unanimously. CAPITAL IMPROVEMENTS PLAN County Administrator, Derek Stamey, presented an updated Capital Improvement Plan and supporting project-request forms. The purpose of the workshop was to: • Review the status of projects from the prior year. • Examine current capital requests. PC Minutes 20250324 1 Page 1 of 12 • Establish general priorities. • Identify projects that could be deferred. • Discuss grant and partnership opportunities. • Consider lower-cost alternatives. STATUS OF PRIOR-YEAR PROJECTS Extension Office Repairs Structural concerns had been identified in a basement wall at the Extension Office. An on-call engineering firm developed a repair that avoided major excavation and reconstruction. The work was being funded with American Rescue Plan Act funds and was expected to cost less than $10,000, with no additional county appropriation requested. Route 60 Sewer-Line Repair A sewer line between the Shell station and tire shop on Route 60 had become deformed, causing water to collect inside the pipe. Although sewage continued to flow, administration described the project as a necessary repair rather than an optional improvement. The proposed work would likely require: • Excavation approximately 15 feet deep. • Temporary lane restrictions or closure. • Engineered construction plans. • Coordination with the Virginia Department of Transportation. • Possible modification of nearby commercial entrances. • Funding from the county’s fund balance. Alternative trenchless repair methods had been considered but were determined to be unsuitable because of the pipe’s material and condition. Commissioners suggested examining protective casing and other engineering options where practical. Parks and Recreation Improvements Approximately $100,000 in solar-project funding had been designated for park renovations. PC Minutes 20250324 2 Page 2 of 12 About half of the funding had been used for improvements at the ball fields near Routes 13 and 60, including: • New dugouts. • New fencing. • A new concession-stand roof. • Restroom renovations. County employees completed much of the work internally, substantially reducing project costs. The county also received approximately $36,000 in grant funding for improvements at the Luther P. Jackson complex, including doors, electrical work, and signage. Solar funds were expected to provide the required local match. School Drainage Improvements A drainage problem near the school cafetorium had been addressed without a major capital expenditure. Roof drains were redirected so stormwater discharged onto the ground rather than overwhelming an undersized drain and backing water into the building. Staff had not observed adverse effects from the revised drainage arrangement. Range Road Fiber The county worked with Firefly to locate a fiber facility on county property near the Public Works and Animal Control facilities. In exchange, fiber service was extended to Range Road, producing an estimated savings of approximately $200,000. Public-Safety Radio System The county had ordered components for its new emergency communications system. The project required a tower behind the sheriff’s office. The county would be responsible for the foundation, while the Virginia State Police would install the tower and provide substantial technical and project assistance. The State Police partnership was expected to provide: • Discounted Motorola equipment. • Tower installation. PC Minutes 20250324 3 Page 3 of 12 • Dispatch-system work. • Vehicle-radio installation. • Project management. • Reduced or eliminated ongoing operating costs. Administration estimated that a county-led project could have cost approximately $5 million. The partnership was expected to save between $3 million and $4 million. Completion was anticipated during late summer or early fall. Vehicle Replacement Program Requests included replacement vehicles for the Sheriff’s Office and county departments. Administration recommended continuing to consider used vehicles from localities with strong fleet-management programs. Cumberland had previously purchased former police vehicles from Hanover County for approximately $5,000 to $6,000 each with about 80,000 miles. Discussion distinguished between: • Emergency and law-enforcement vehicles requiring greater reliability. • Administrative and maintenance vehicles that could reasonably be purchased used. • Vehicles used in less demanding assignments, such as school-resource duties. Commissioners discussed vehicle warranties, repair histories, maintenance costs, fleet records, and the relative quality of newer vehicle models. The proposed replacement policy would allow discretion rather than require automatic replacement at a particular age or mileage. Replacement decisions would consider nonroutine repair expenses in relation to acquisition cost. Routine maintenance, tires, brakes, and accident-related repairs would not count toward the replacement threshold. The Commission also discussed whether school buses should be driven home by individual drivers or whether shared vehicles could reduce bus mileage. Administration agreed to ask school staff about current practices. Vehicle leasing and lease-purchase arrangements had been examined but were not considered advantageous for a locality with a relatively small fleet. PC Minutes 20250324 4 Page 4 of 12 Fencing and Site Security The plan included approximately $50,000 for additional fencing near the Public Works shop, Animal Control facility, communications tower, and shell building. Commissioners suggested that: • A future tenant of the shell building might contribute toward fencing. • Improvements should be coordinated with other planned work in the area. • Outside or creative funding should be used where possible. Administration classified the fencing as a priority that should be pursued through shared or alternative funding rather than relying entirely on county funds. Transfer-Station Paving The pavement at the Randolph Transfer Station was described as severely deteriorated, with deep potholes and an inadequate base. Repeated patching had not provided a lasting solution. A proper repair would require: • Removing the existing pavement. • Installing a compacted stone base. • Applying heavy-duty asphalt. • Reconstructing the entrance from apron to apron. Administration estimated that Randolph might be paved for approximately $30,000. Remaining funds from a proposed $50,000 allocation could address part of the Hamilton Transfer Station. Paving at Hamilton could be delayed until after work associated with a potential solar-project electrical easement to avoid damaging new pavement. Concrete was discussed as a longer-lasting option but was estimated to cost substantially more than asphalt. Library Roof Administration recommended moving the library roof to a later year. The roof should remain in the long-term Capital Improvement Plan, but it was not considered an immediate replacement need. Luther P. Jackson HVAC Systems PC Minutes 20250324 5 Page 5 of 12 Approximately nine or ten HVAC units at the Luther P. Jackson complex were installed around 2009 and had reached or exceeded their estimated 15-year service life. The units serve areas including: • The gymnasium. • Social Services. • The clothes closet. • Bear Creek Academy. Commissioners discussed: • Replacing all units at once versus staggering replacement. • The risk of multiple failures during extreme weather. • Commercial versus residential-grade equipment. • Mini-split systems. • Future roof work. • Locating equipment on the roof. • Maintenance accessibility. • Developing in-house HVAC capabilities. Administration indicated that a phased replacement schedule could be considered. Commissioners also suggested coordinating HVAC work with proposed roof construction where feasible. Animal Control Improvements The proposed Animal Control project included an adoption room and additional space intended to improve animal placement and reduce euthanasia. Administration reported that: • Transfer opportunities to other shelters had declined. • Shelters throughout Virginia and the country were experiencing overcrowding. • Cumberland’s shelter had maintained an approximately 94 percent save rate. • Staff actively promoted animals through social media, public events, and rescue partnerships. The county was seeking funding through: • Envigo settlement proceeds. PC Minutes 20250324 6 Page 6 of 12 • Corporate and foundation grants. • Fundraising events. • Donations. • Sponsorships and naming rights. • Potential fee adjustments. The county had unsuccessfully applied for a $50,000 T-Mobile grant and was considering Dominion Foundation and other opportunities. Commissioners suggested: • An outdoor adoption area. • Adoption parades and public events. • Donation stations. • Sponsorship walls. • Partnerships with schools. • Online giving programs. • Higher surrender or adoption fees where appropriate. • Expanded marketing and community engagement. Administration classified the project as a medium priority and recommended pursuing outside funding rather than relying solely on county revenue. Public Works Facility Several Public Works buildings were described as deteriorated, with rotting siding, leaking roofs, limited climate control, and scattered storage. The initial concept involved consolidating operations into a new facility estimated at approximately $500,000. Commissioners questioned whether the full project was necessary and discussed alternatives such as: • Repairing selected existing buildings. • Demolishing only the structures in the poorest condition. • Reusing existing concrete pads. • Purchasing prefabricated metal buildings. • Creating a combination shop and covered-equipment-storage structure. PC Minutes 20250324 7 Page 7 of 12 • Insulating and conditioning only the portion used for repairs and staff. • Coordinating the project with the school bus facility. Administration agreed that the project needed additional study and that a more affordable alternative should be developed. Pump-Station Generators The county had portable generators and transfer switches but lacked permanent generators at several pump stations. During an extended outage, staff would have to move portable equipment from station to station and manually pump down each facility. Administration expressed concern about staff safety, road access during severe weather, and the risk of a sewage overflow. Permanent generators at priority locations would: • Start automatically. • Reduce emergency response time. • Protect the sewer system. • Reduce the need to move portable equipment during storms. Potential funding sources included grants and Envigo settlement funds connected to waterquality protection. Commissioners questioned preliminary cost estimates and requested verification of generator capacity, installation requirements, and pricing. The possibility of increasing utility rates was discussed. Administration stated that the greater financial need was increasing the number of system customers rather than significantly raising rates. Information Technology The county requested approximately $140,000 to replace aging network switches and related information-technology equipment. Administration and commissioners agreed that information technology was a high priority because unreliable systems affected communications, telephone service, employee productivity, and routine county operations. PC Minutes 20250324 8 Page 8 of 12 The consensus was that the equipment needed to be replaced rather than treated as an optional improvement. Fire and Emergency Medical Services Capital requests included emergency-services equipment and an ambulance. Commissioners discussed: • Prioritizing ambulance replacement. • Seeking state grants that could cover approximately 70 percent of the cost. • Repurposing existing generators or equipment where possible. • Seeking corporate support from Colonial Pipeline. • Exploring used specialized vehicles from larger localities. • Coordinating foam-response equipment with Colonial Pipeline and regional partners. The ambulance was generally identified as a high priority, particularly if substantial grant funding could be secured. School Capital Requests School requests discussed during the workshop included: • An accessible playground. • Restroom and concession facilities at the football field. • Athletic-field lighting. • An elementary-school roof replacement. • A school transportation or bus facility. Most school requests were identified by school staff as low priority, except for the elementaryschool roof. Elementary-School Roof The pitched portion of the elementary-school roof dated to approximately 1996 and was identified as a high-priority replacement project. Commissioners emphasized protecting the county’s investment in the school and avoiding damage from further roof deterioration. PC Minutes 20250324 9 Page 9 of 12 Athletic-Field Lighting The request was approximately $400,000 per year for two years, or $800,000 total. The proposed work appeared to include lighting at baseball or multipurpose fields and potentially upgrades to older equipment. Commissioners discussed whether LED fixtures could reduce operating costs. School Bus Facility The Commission discussed whether a school transportation facility and county Public Works shop could be combined or coordinated to avoid duplicating buildings and equipment. No final design recommendation was made. Other Capital and Economic-Development Projects Some projects were described as beneficial but not urgent. Administration recommended avoiding county commitments to low-priority amenities unless grant, corporate, or partner funding became available. Commissioners encouraged staff to pursue: • Corporate grants. • Foundation support. • Donated equipment. • Partnerships with neighboring localities. • Sponsorships. • Economies of scale by bidding related projects together. • Repurposing usable county equipment. • Design alternatives that reduce long-term costs. The Commission discussed the advantages and disadvantages of traditional design-bid-build procurement and alternative construction methods. Members emphasized the importance of qualified contractors, cost controls, public engagement, and avoiding excessive change orders. Priority Discussion Commissioners identified a general group of high-priority projects rather than adopting a strict numerical ranking. PC Minutes 20250324 10 Page 10 of 12 Projects receiving the strongest support included: • Ambulance replacement, particularly with grant assistance. • Elementary-school roof replacement. • Route 60 sewer-line repair. • Information-technology switch replacement. • Essential law-enforcement vehicles. • Selected HVAC replacements. • Transfer-station paving. The sewer-line repair was already moving forward and therefore did not require further priority ranking. The animal-control project remained important but was expected to depend primarily on grant, settlement, or fundraising proceeds. Administration explained that identifying a group of priority projects would allow staff to pursue appropriate grants and corporate opportunities as they became available. No formal recommendation adopting the full Capital Improvement Plan was made during the workshop. Future Capital Improvement Process Commissioners requested that future Capital Improvement Plan workshops be scheduled earlier in the annual process. Members recommended meeting with administrators and department representatives when requests were first submitted, allowing the Commission to: • Review proposals before the list was finalized. • Remove low-priority or impractical requests earlier. • Request supporting information. • Suggest alternatives. • Identify funding opportunities sooner. Administration agreed to begin the process earlier in future years. The motion was approved unanimously. Adjourn – Motion Page 1 of 1 CUMBERLAND COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS PUBLIC HEARING The Cumberland County Board of Supervisors will meet on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, at 6:00 p.m., or as soon thereafter as may be heard, in the Cumberland Middle/High School Cafetorium, 16 School Road, Cumberland, Virginia 23040, to conduct a public hearing pursuant to Virginia Code Section 15.2-2204, which such hearing may be continued or adjourned, as required under applicable law, and to consider the following items and take actions in furtherance thereof: Conditional Use Permit #26-03 – Dominion Energy Virginia’s Cumberland Energy Center: A conditional use permit request by Dominion Energy Virginia to construct and operate the Cumberland Energy Center, a dual-fuel combined-cycle power station, and associated interconnection, transmission and other facilities as allowed under Sec. 74133(25) of the County zoning ordinance, off Duncan Store Road, in the north-western area of the County, bordering the James River and Buckingham County, on eight parcels of land described as Tax Map numbers 10-A-12 (portion), 10-A-13, 10-A-64, 14-A-2, 14-A-3, 14A-18, 14-A-18A, and 14-A-19). All parcels are zoned A-2, Agricultural. As indicated in the Comprehensive Plan, no parcels are located within a growth area or Village Center. The request is in Election District 1. The proposed development application, proposed conditions to the conditional use permit, and all supporting materials are available for public review on the County's website at: https://www.cumberlandcounty.virginia.gov/343/Cumberland-Energy-Center-Project Materials are also available for public review at the office of the Cumberland County Planning Department, County Administration Building, 1 Courthouse Circle, Cumberland, Virginia, between 8:30 am and 4:30 pm of each business day. The public is invited to attend this hearing, at which persons affected may appear and present their views. Questions or comments may be directed to the Planning & Zoning Department at (804) 492-3520. Persons with disabilities are urged to contact the County Administrator’s Office at (804) 492-3625 at least five (5) days before the meeting to arrange for any necessary accommodations.
