Duncan & Sons, Inc., Fremar, LLC, Barry & Donna Tyson Rafiraza Jaffary, for Virginia Electric and Power Company, dba Dominion Energy, Virginia Conditional Use Permit and Substantial Accord Determination request by Dominion Energy Virginia to construct and operate the Cumberland Energy Center, a dual-fuel combined-cycle power station, and associated interconnection, transmission and other facilities as allowed under Sec. 74-133(25) of the County zoning ordinance. The proposed facility would be located off Duncan Store Road in the northwestern portion of the County, near the James River and the Buckingham County line, on portions of Tax Map Parcels 10A-12, 10-A-13, 10-A-64, 14-A-2, 14-A-3, 14-A-18, 14-A-18A, and 14-A-19. 1 A-2, Agricultural A-2, Agricultural with CUP 8 parcels totaling approximately 972.58 acres (see attached Conceptual site plan dated June 16, 2026 and updated July 30, 2026) Agricultural, Residential Not located in an area designated for growth None Revised 10/17/2026 1 Surrounding Area Information: Direction North/East South West Adjacent Existing Uses Ag/Forestal/Limited Residential Ag/Forestal/Commercial Ag/Forestal/ Limited Residential Adjacent Zoning Adjacent Comp. Plan Area (2023) A-2 Agricultural A-2 Agricultural A-2 Agricultural Background Information and Summary of Request: The Applicant is proposing to develop and operate a public utility generating plant, specifically a dualfueled combined cycle power station, in the northern part of the County bordering the James River and Buckingham County. The project property is comprised of 9 parcels of land that include some unimproved tracts, previously timbered tracts, as well as tracts with existing improvements including residential dwellings and accessory structures. Surrounding properties are primarily forested or agricultural, some with single-family residential homes. The Colonial Pipeline Tank Farm is located south of the project property. While the Conditional Use Permit request is for a total of 972.58 acres, the applicant provides that the area built after construction will be limited to 140 acres plus an additional 55 acres to connect the power lines to the transmission lines, for a total of just under 200 acres. The project, as requested, will include: • Natural gas fuel yards (storage and loading) • Fuel oil Yard (storage and loading) • Chilled water processing and storage area • Water treatment building, Raw water treatment building, and water storage tanks • Administration building, Maintenance building and Warehouse building • Power Island with o Two combined cycle power trains (300-foot tall stacks) o Air cooled condenser (130-foot tall) o HRSG Drum (105-feet) o Steam Turbine Building (120-foot) • Collector yard, Generation Tie Transmission Lines, and 500KV Switchyard Natural gas will be delivered to the project site via pipeline by Columbia Gas of Virginia. Backup fuel will be delivered to the site via truck. Backup fuel will only be used during times when natural gas is not available. Power produced onsite will be collected in the collector yard and delivered via the proposed onsite switchyard that will interconnect with existing overhead transmission lines that traverse the project property, and will carry the energy generated by the project to the transmission grid. Dominion is requesting a condition to modify the height limitation for the A-2 zoning district. Current regulation restricts structures exceeding 60 feet in height; however, the Zoning Ordinance section 74702 provides that the Board of Supervisors may modify the applicable regulations as part of the Conditional Use Permit process. The Applicant is requesting the modification to allow for the structure height to be no more than 300 feet for the four exhaust stacks and up to 199 feet for certain other buildings 2 and stacks on the project property. The final height of the structures is to be determined at the final site plan submission. The County retained the services of Gentry Locke to assist the County in reviewing the project as a whole. While the application itself was deemed to have met the requirements of the Code for completeness on July 7, 2026, staff and legal counsel continued to design comprehensive conditions to provide to the Commission and Board of Supervisors for consideration. ITEMS TO NOTE Lighting All lighting shall not constitute a nuisance and shall not produce glare or spillover onto adjacent properties. Fixtures will be DarkSky compliant. Height Buildings and structures associated with the project can be built up to 199 feet above ground level, and emission stacks can be built up to 300 feet above ground level. Noise Noise levels will be 75 dBA or less at all external property lines and 65 dBA at any dwelling on any parcel adjacent to the project property in existence at the time of conditional use permit approval. Buffers In addition to buffers required by DEQ and VDOT, and except for areas required for entrance roads, the facility shall have a buffer and setback of not less than 100 feet, except as noted on the Master Plan. Traffic and Road Improvements The Applicant will repair any damage to the construction traffic route attributable to the Project during development and construction. Permanent project entrance ways and parking areas will have asphalt surface or better. Emergency Services The Applicant proposes to provide training classes to both paid and volunteer first responders. However, there was no consensus on how a specific condition relating to the impact this project would have on Emergency Services staffing and equipment. Therefore, staff and legal counsel have proposed condition 8.f.ii. Emergency Services. Dominion Energy, Virginia, and Cumberland County are still evaluating and designing water service infrastructure for the Cumberland Energy Center. If the project is approved, the current plan is for Dominion Energy to build, own and operate dedicated water and wastewater infrastructure exclusively for the project, while Cumberland County will provide contractual rights to water supply and will assist with system routing. Dominion Energy, Virginia’s infrastructure will not be the responsibility of Cumberland County taxpayers. At this time, Cumberland County has not decided whether to develop any additional infrastructure that would be used by the County for public water service. Any decision to participate in the water system would be subject to a future County decision-making process. Revised 10/17/2026 3 Consistency with the 2023 Comprehensive Plan: Because the proposed public utility generating plant is a public utility facility, Virginia Code § 15.22232 requires the Planning Commission to review the general location, character, and extent of the Project and determine whether it is substantially in accord with the Cumberland County Comprehensive Plan. Several portions of the Cumberland County Comprehensive Plan are relevant to the Planning Commission's review of the proposed public utility generating plant and associated substantial accord determination. The Plan identifies four central themes: Village Centers, Preserve Cumberland, Creating Opportunity, and Fostering Stewardship, which together provide the framework through which the County evaluates land use, infrastructure, economic development, and other planning decisions. (Plan Overview and Central Themes, pp. 13-21). The proposed Project is located within an area identified on the Future Land Use Map as Agricultural/Rural Residential. The Comprehensive Plan describes these areas as places intended to preserve rural character, support agricultural and forestry activities, conserve natural resources, and limit sprawling residential development. The Plan further notes the importance of protecting agricultural lands, maintaining the County's rural landscape, and preserving the agricultural economy that contributes to Cumberland County's character and identity. (Agricultural/Rural Residential; Goal 5: Preserve Rural Character & Economies, pp. 34-38, 64). The Comprehensive Plan also contains a number of policies related to economic development, employment opportunities, infrastructure, and utilities. The Creating Opportunity section includes goals related to expanding economic opportunities, attracting businesses, supporting employment growth, and encouraging investment in the County. The Plan specifically discusses industrial areas, economic development opportunities, infrastructure investment, and the importance of creating opportunities for residents while maintaining Cumberland's rural character. (Goal 8: Create Diverse Economic Opportunities; Industrial Areas, pp. 42-47, 60, 64). Relevant policies are also found in the Fostering Stewardship section of the Plan. Goal 15, Supportive Utilities, discusses utility infrastructure, future utility needs, and the importance of ensuring adequate utility service to support the County's long-term needs. The Plan identifies supportive utilities, infrastructure planning, and identification of future utility needs as important considerations for the County moving forward. The Public Facilities Master Plan also includes discussion of utility infrastructure, public utilities, and future utility planning. (Goal 15: Supportive Utilities, p. 58; Public Facilities Master Plan, pp. 16-17 of the Utilities section). The sections discussed above contain many of the Comprehensive Plan policies that relate to the location, character, and extent of the proposed facility. To assist the Planning Commission with its discussion, staff has included draft resolutions for consideration that would support either a finding that the Project is substantially in accord with the Comprehensive Plan or a finding that the Project is not substantially in accord with the Comprehensive Plan. The draft resolutions reference various policies and goals contained within the Comprehensive Plan and are provided as a resource to assist the Planning Commission during its discussion and deliberation of the Application. The Planning Commission did find the project substantially in accord with the 2023 Comprehensive Plan and adopted Resolution 2026-01A at their August 31, 2026 Public Hearing. 4 Consistency with the Zoning Ordinance: Sec. 74-133. – allows for specific uses in the A-2, Agricultural Zoning District with a Conditional Use Permit; Subsection 25 permits public utility generating plants, public utility boosters or relay stations, transformer substations and other facilities in the A-2 Zoning District with a Conditional Use Permit. Sec. 74-701 – recognizes that there are certain uses which, because of their unique characteristics, cannot be properly classified in any particular district without consideration, in each case, of the impact of those uses upon neighboring land and of the public need for the particular use at the particular location. The Conditions as proposed and recommended by staff meet the requirements of the Zoning Ordinance. Public Notification: The applicant held the following community meetings: April 23, 2026, 5:30 PM Cartersville Ruritan Club 2168 Cartersville Road, Cartersville, VA 23027 May 28, 2026, 5:30 PM Cartersville Volunteer Fire Department 1600 Cartersville Road, Cartersville, VA 23027 June 8, 2026, 5:30 PM Cartersville Volunteer Fire Department 1600 Cartersville Road, Cartersville, VA 23027 July 21, 2026, 5:30 PM Cumberland Middle School Gym 16 School Road, Cumberland, VA 23040 The Planning Commission, Board of Supervisors, and County staff were invited to attend site visits to tour the Brunswick Power Station, Greensville Power Station, and the Bear Garden Power Station. The Board held a workshop with the Applicant on October 6, 2026. The Planning Commission held its public hearing on this application on Monday, August 31, 2026, where they sent CUP 26-03 to the Board of Supervisors with a recommendation of approval. Adjoining property owners were sent a notice for this public hearing via first-class mail on October 5, 2026. Staff also provided notice of this public hearing to the County Administrators and Zoning Administrators of Buckingham and Fluvanna Counties as required by Code of Virginia § 15.2-2204.C on October 5, 2026. Staff posted the public hearing notice on the Public Hearings webpage of the County website and the three bulletin boards located in the administration building on October 5, 2026. Notice was published in The Farmville Herald on October 7, 2026, October 9, 2026, October 14, 2026, and October 16, 2026. Staff Recommended Conditions: Revised 10/17/2026 5 Should the Board wish to recommend approval of the proposal, staff recommends the following conditions: Pursuant to the Cumberland County Zoning Ordinance (the “Ordinance”), a Conditional Use Permit (the “CUP”) was granted by the Cumberland County Board of Supervisors (the “County”) to Virginia Electric and Power Company (d/b/a Dominion Energy Virginia) (“Dominion” or the “Applicant”) on October 20, 2026, to construct a Public Utility Generating Plant and associated interconnection, transmission and other facilities as allowed under Sec. 74-133(25) of the Ordinance (the “Project”) on Tax Map Parcels 10-A-12 (portion west of White Road), 10-A-13, 10-A-64, 14-A-2, 14-A-3, 14-A-18, 14-A-18-A, and 14-A-19 (collectively the “Property”), totaling approximately 972.58 acres as shown on the Preliminary Site Plan submitted with the Application for the CUP (the “Application”). The following CUP conditions (the “Conditions”) shall apply to the Project. To the extent the Conditions are inconsistent with or more specific than the Ordinance, the Conditions shall control. The CUP and associated conditions shall run with the land and not be affected by a change in ownership of the Applicant or the Project or any change in the Ordinance. 1. Scope of the CUP. The Project authorized by this CUP will produce electrical power through a combined cycle combustion turbine and steam turbine generating system, using natural gas and/or backup ultra-low sulfur heating oil, and does not involve the use of burning coal or nuclear reaction. The use of ultra-low sulfur heating oil is permitted for use as a backup fuel only. Backup fuel will only be used during periods of natural gas curtailment or interruption, during equipment startup or testing, or as required for system reliability. The Project will be developed in general conformity with the plan for development attached hereto as Exhibit 1 (the “Preliminary Site Plan”), entitled “Combined Cycle Study Cumberland County Site Plan”, dated June 16, 2026, revised July 30, 2026. 2. Design: a. Lighting. Lighting shall not constitute a nuisance and shall not produce glare or spillover onto adjacent properties. All lighting will be limited to the minimum necessary for security purposes, and fixtures will be DarkSky compliant to prevent glare or nuisance to the public. During construction of the Project, any temporary construction lighting shall be positioned downward, inward, and shielded to eliminate glare to adjacent properties. Any on-site lighting provided for the operational phase of each facility shall be shielded away from adjacent properties and shall be positioned downward to minimize light spillage onto adjacent properties. Emergency and/ or safety lighting shall be exempt from this condition. b. Height. Pursuant to Sec. 74-702 (a)(14), the Board of Supervisors waives Sec. 74-138 of the Cumberland County Code and authorizes buildings and structures associated with the Project (including towers constructed for electrical lines) to be constructed up to 199 feet in height above ground level and emission stacks up to 300 feet above ground level. Those features shall be located generally in those areas as depicted on the Preliminary Site Plan. c. Setbacks and Buffering. The Setbacks and Buffers applicable to the Project shall generally conform to those depicted on the Preliminary Site Plan, but in any case, shall comply with the following minimum standards: i. There shall be a minimum of a one hundred (100) foot setback from the fencing around the Project to any public rights of way and any adjacent property line. 6 ii. text: CLERK'S BOARD SUMMARY REPORT OF ACTIONS OF THE FAIRFAX COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS TUESDAY October 13, 2026 This does not represent a verbatim transcript of the Board Meeting and is subject to minor change. For the most upto-date version, check the website https://www.fairfaxcounty.gov/boardofsupervisors/board-meeting-summaries. This document will be made available in an alternative format upon request. Please call 703-324-3151 (VOICE), 711 (TTY). 19-26 SA:sa At a regular meeting of the Board of Supervisors of Fairfax County, Virginia, held in the Board Auditorium of the Government Center at Fairfax, Virginia, on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, at 9:37 a.m., there were present: • Chairman Jeffrey C. McKay, presiding • Supervisor Walter Alcorn, Hunter Mill District • Supervisor James N. Bierman, Jr., Dranesville District • Supervisor Patrick S. Herrity, Springfield District • Supervisor Andres F. Jimenez, Mason District • Supervisor Rodney Lusk, Franconia District • Supervisor Dalia Palchik, Providence District • Supervisor Rachna Sizemore Heizer, Braddock District • Supervisor Kathy L. Smith, Sully District • Supervisor Daniel G. Storck, Mount Vernon District Others present during the meeting were Bryan J. Hill, County Executive; Elizabeth Teare, County Attorney; Jill G. Cooper, Clerk for the Board of Supervisors; Dottie Steele, Chief Deputy Clerk for the Board of Supervisors; Jacob Caporaletti, Management Analyst; Ekua Brew-Ewool and Sameera Awan, Deputy Clerks, and JeeWon Davis, Administrative Assistant, Department of Clerk Services. Board Summary -2- October 13, 2026 BOARD MATTER 1. MOMENT OF SILENCE (9:37 a.m.) The Board asked everyone to keep in thoughts the family, friends, and/or colleagues of: • Michael Kirby, who died recently. He was a longtime Northern Virginia resident and resided in the Mason District; he recently retired as liaison for the National Endowment of the Arts; was a former legislative staffer to Congressman Jim Moran of Virginia, as well as Bob Matsui and Glenn Anderson, both of California; and was former chair of the Fairfax County Democratic Committee, in addition to the various other roles he played in politics, particularly in Fairfax County • Members of the Fairfax County Fire and Rescue Department’s Urban Search and Rescue Team, Virginia Task Force 1, for their international deployments and efforts following the earthquakes in Venezuela earlier this year; also, the 10-member support team currently deployed in Panama following a recent earthquake, where they have been conducting reconnaissance and structural assessments (NOTE: Later in the meeting the Board recognized Members of Virginia Task Force 1 for their efforts. See Clerk’s Summary Item #2.) • Thomas Gum, who died recently after being struck by a vehicle near the intersection of Old Keene Mill Road and Backlick Road in Springfield. He was a dedicated volunteer at Provision Church, where he helped connect individuals experiencing housing difficulties with community resources and support; and will be remembered for his commitment to helping others despite his own personal challenges. A memorial service is scheduled for October 19, 2026, at 5 p.m. in the open field adjacent to the Springfield Garage • Irene Smith, who died recently, at the age of 102. She was a longtime Franconia District resident who lived in the Clermont Woods community for over 50 years. A nurse by profession, she was also a dedicated member of the Clermont Woods Civic Association, where she regularly attended meetings and remained actively involved in her community Board Summary -3- October 13, 2026 AGENDA ITEMS 2. RESOLUTION TO RECOGNIZE MEMBERS OF VIRGINIA TASK FORCE 1 (USA-01) (9:44 a.m.) (NOTE: Earlier in the meeting, the Board recognized Virginia Task Force 1 during the moment of silence. See Clerk’s Summary Item #1.) Chairman McKay relinquished the Chair to Vice-Chairman Smith and moved approval of the Resolution to recognize Virginia Task Force 1 (USA-01) for its search and rescue deployment to Venezuela following the devastating earthquake in summer 2026. The motion was multiply seconded and carried by unanimous vote. Vice-Chairman Smith returned the gavel to Chairman McKay. 3. RESOLUTION TO RECOGNIZE GIN DANCE COMPANY (10:06 a.m.) Supervisor Alcorn, jointly with Chairman McKay, moved approval of the Resolution to recognize Gin Dance Company for its artistic and cultural contributions to Fairfax County. The motion was multiply seconded and carried by unanimous vote. 4. PROCLAMATION DESIGNATING OCTOBER 2026 AS “PEDESTRIAN SAFETY MONTH” IN FAIRFAX COUNTY (10:18 a.m.) Chairman McKay relinquished the Chair to Vice-Chairman Smith and moved approval of the Proclamation designating October 2026 as “Pedestrian Safety Month” in Fairfax County. The motion was multiply seconded and carried by unanimous vote. Vice-Chairman Smith returned the gavel to Chairman McKay. 5. PROCLAMATION DESIGNATING OCTOBER 2026 AS “DOMESTIC VIOLENCE AWARENESS MONTH” IN FAIRFAX COUNTY (10:47 a.m.) Supervisor Palchik, jointly with Chairman McKay, moved approval of the Proclamation designating October 2026 as “Domestic Violence Awareness Month” in Fairfax County. Chairman McKay seconded the motion and it carried by unanimous vote. 6. PROCLAMATION DESIGNATING OCTOBER 2026 AS “COMMUNITY PLANNING MONTH” IN FAIRFAX COUNTY (11:05 a.m.) Supervisor Smith, jointly with Chairman McKay, moved approval of the Proclamation designating October 2026 as “Community Planning Month” in Board Summary -4- October 13, 2026 Fairfax County. Chairman McKay seconded the motion and it carried by unanimous vote. 7. PRESENTATION OF THE VOLUNTEER FIRE COMMISSION AWARDS AND ANNUAL REPORT (11:22 a.m.) Shawn Stokes, Chief of the Dunn Loring Volunteer Fire Department, and Chair of the Volunteer Fire Commission, presented the 2025 annual report. Tracey Reed, Assistant Fire Chief, Fire and Rescue Department (FRD), announced the recipients of the Volunteer Fire and Service Awards, while Chairman McKay, Mr. Stokes, and John Butler, Fire Chief, FRD, presented to the following individuals: • Volunteer Firefighter – Sebastian Herbolsheimer, Vienna Volunteer Fire Department • Operational Officer – Adam Serle, Vienna Volunteer Fire Department (Was not present to receive award) • Volunteer Emergency Medical Services (EMS) Provider – Maggie Baxter, Bailey’s Crossroads Volunteer Fire Department • Ivy Volunteer Basic Life Support Provider – Ivy Ayala, Springfield Volunteer Fire Department • Volunteer Advanced Life Support Provider – Brett Lorenz, Bailey’s Crossroads Volunteer Fire Department • EMS Rookie – Alex Lam, McLean Volunteer Fire Department (Was not present to receive award) • Volunteer Firefighter Rookie – Christian Georgi, Burke Volunteer Fire Department • Volunteer Administrative Officer McLean Volunteer Fire Department • Volunteer Administrative Member – Jonathan Leidenheimer, Vienna Volunteer Fire Department • Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) Member – Julie Thomas, CERT Support • Canteen/Auxiliary Member – Richard Prien – Patricia Moynihan, Board Summary -5- October 13, 2026 • Fire Chief’s Award – Aly Lubov, Dunn Loring Volunteer Fire Department • Special Recognition – Hannah Davis, Fire and Rescue Academy • Special Recognition – EMS Training Division, Fairfax County Fire and Rescue Department • VFC Chairman’s Award – Jerry Strider, Bailey’s Crossroads Volunteer Fire Department (Was not present to receive award) DMS:dms ADDITIONAL BOARD MATTERS 8. RESOLUTION OF RECOGNITION REQUEST FOR YVONNE DEMORY (11:43 a.m.) Chairman McKay relinquished the Chair to Vice-Chairman Smith and asked unanimous consent that the Board direct staff to prepare a Resolution of Recognition for Yvonne Demory in recognition of her 20 years of service on the Fairfax County Board of Equalization and for her leadership as Chair. PROCLAMATION REQUEST TO DESIGNATE OCTOBER 24, 2026, AS “WORLD POLIO DAY” IN FAIRFAX COUNTY (11:43 a.m.) Jointly with Supervisor Bierman, Chairman McKay asked unanimous consent that the Board direct staff to prepare a Proclamation designating October 24, 2026, as “World Polio Day” in the County. PROCLAMATION REQUEST TO DESIGNATE OCTOBER 2026 AS “HINDU HERITAGE MONTH” IN FAIRFAX COUNTY (11:43 a.m.) Jointly with Supervisor Sizemore Heizer, Chairman McKay asked unanimous consent that the Board direct staff to prepare a Proclamation designating October 2026 as “Hindu Heritage Month” in the County. Without objection, it was so ordered. Board Summary 12. -6- October 13, 2026 PROCLAMATION REQUEST TO DESIGNATE NOVEMBER 8, 2026, AS “DIWALI” IN FAIRFAX COUNTY (11:43 a.m.) Jointly with Supervisor Sizemore Heizer, Chairman McKay asked unanimous consent that the Board direct staff to prepare a Proclamation designating November 8, 2026, as “Diwali” in the County. Without objection, it was so ordered. 13. PROCLAMATION REQUEST TO DESIGNATE OCTOBER 2026 AS “FILIPINO AMERICAN HERITAGE MONTH” IN FAIRFAX COUNTY (11:43 a.m.) Chairman McKay asked unanimous consent that the Board direct staff to prepare a Proclamation designating October 2026 as “Filipino American Heritage Month” in the County. Without objection, it was so ordered. 14. PROCLAMATION REQUEST TO DESIGNATE NOVEMBER 2026 AS “NATIONAL ADOPT A SENIOR PET MONTH” IN FAIRFAX COUNTY (11:43 a.m.) Jointly with Supervisor Lusk, Chairman McKay asked unanimous consent that the Board direct staff to prepare a Proclamation designating November 2026 as “National Adopt a Senior Pet Month” in the County. Without objection, it was so ordered. 15. PROCLAMATION REQUEST TO DESIGNATE NOVEMBER 15 – 21, 2026, AS “HUNGER AND HOMELESSNESS AWARENESS WEEK” IN FAIRFAX COUNTY (11:43 a.m.) Chairman McKay asked unanimous consent that the Board direct staff to prepare a Proclamation designating November 15 – 21, 2026, as “Hunger and Homelessness Awareness Week” in the County. Without objection, it was so ordered. 16. ORDINANCE ESTABLISHING A LOCAL RETAIL CANNABIS TAX (11:44 a.m.) Chairman McKay stated that the Virginia General Assembly adopted the final biennial budget on June 29, 2026, and included language authorizing the establishment of an adult use recreational cannabis retail marketplace for Virginia (Item 4-14) in Enactment Clause 5, with sales beginning July 1, 2027, (Code of Virginia Code- Subtitle II. Cannabis Control Act). These provisions include: 1. New local authority to tax retail cannabis sales Board Summary -7- October 13, 2026 2. Expansion of local ordinance authority to prohibit the consumption, possession, or offering of cannabis in any public place or on public school property 3. Authority for localities to adopt ordinances regulating the hours of operation for cannabis retailers The Cannabis Control Authority will develop regulations for licensing of cultivators, processors, and retailers and other regulated activities during the second half of 2026, with licenses issued in early 2027 and retail sales beginning July 1, 2027. During that time, local governments will be considering how they will exercise their new authority, especially regarding land use and taxing. Localities are required to levy a local tax rate by ordinance on cannabis retail sales, which rate may be set between 1 - 3.5 percent. This tax is in addition to the State sales and use tax on the same product and the State marijuana tax. The State will start with a rate of six percent for the marijuana tax until July 1, 2029, and a rate of eight percent after July 1, 2029. The State marijuana tax rate is in addition to any tax imposed under the Virginia Retail Sales and Use Tax Act. In addition to this tax ordinance, the Department of Planning and Development will be separately crafting a Zoning Ordinance amendment to incorporate necessary local regulations. Therefore, Chairman McKay asked unanimous consent that the Board direct the: • Director of Tax Administration to present an ordinance setting the local tax rate on retail cannabis sales at 3.5 percent and to bring the ordinance before the Board for consideration in the Spring of 2027, in time for the Board to adopt the ordinance after a public hearing no later than May 1, 2027 • County Executive and the Department of Management and Budget to include estimated revenues from this source in the County Executive’s Fiscal Year 2028 Advertised Budget Plan Without objection, it was so ordered. Following a brief discussion, with input from Tracy Strunk, Director, Department of Planning and Development, regarding zoning and State law provisions/regulations, Vice-Chairman Smith returned the gavel to Chairman McKay. Board Summary 17. -8- October 13, 2026 REQUEST FOR AN EXPEDITED PUBLIC HEARING FOR SPECIAL EXCEPTION APPLICATION SE-2026-SU-00012, LOVE HAND HOME HEALTH INC. (SULLY DISTRICT) (11:49 a.m.) Supervisor Smith stated that Love Hand Home Health Inc. has filed a Special Exception Application on the property identified as Tax Map Parcel 34-4((13))02. The applicant is seeking a special exception to permit an adult day care center in an existing commercial building. The adult day care center would provide services for up to 125 participants by combining two existing suites on the ground floor of the existing building. Slight modifications are proposed to the existing surface parking lot at the front of the building to create an outdoor recreation area for the day care participants. No change to the gross floor area of the existing building is proposed. The pending application is scheduled for a Planning Commission public hearing on November 4, 2026. To be heard prior to the end of the year, the applicant is asking for an expedited Board public hearing to be scheduled. Therefore, Supervisor Smith moved that the Board direct the Director of Planning and Development to schedule Special Exception Application SE-2026-SU-00012 for a public hearing before the Board on November 17, 2026. The applicant understands that the scheduling of a Board public hearing date in no way relieves it of the requirement to comply with applicable standards of the Zoning Ordinance. In addition, the authorization does not dictate that the pending application will be approved, nor does it prejudice staff’s review. This motion should not be construed as a favorable recommendation by the Board of the pending application at this time. Chairman McKay seconded the motion and it carried by unanimous vote. 18. PROCLAMATION REQUEST FOR ANIL AND ANUPAMA SHARMA (11:50 a.m.) Supervisor Sizemore Heizer stated that George Mason University (GMU) recently announced the renaming of the Center for Innovation and Entrepreneurship at its Costello College of Business in honor of Northern Virginia entrepreneur Anil Sharma and his wife, Anupama Sharma. The newly named Anil and Anupama Sharma Center for Innovation and Entrepreneurship reflects their extraordinary generosity and their commitment to shaping the future of education, innovation, and opportunity in our region. Anil and Anupama Sharma came to the United States 30-years ago as first-generation immigrants with little more than ambition and a willingness to take risks. Guided by those values, Anil Sharma founded 22nd Century Technologies, now one of the largest privately held government contracting firms in the nation. This year, the Sharmas made a major philanthropic gift to GMU as part of its “Mason Now: Power the Possible” one-billion-dollar comprehensive campaign. In recognition of their generosity and longstanding engagement with the University, Board Summary -9- October 13, 2026 GMU renamed the Center for Innovation and Entrepreneurship in their honor. Their investment strengthens the mission of the region’s flagship public University and expands GMU’s role as a catalyst for entrepreneurship and innovation. Their contribution will significantly expand opportunities for students, alumni, faculty, and local four innovators, helping to build a stronger regional entrepreneurial network. This work is especially vital as the County continues to diversify its economic base, intentionally growing an economy less dependent on the federal government and more driven by homegrown innovation, industry, and talent. Their investment directly supports this vision, empowering GMU to prepare the next generation of leaders who will shape the county’s economic future. The Sharmas’ immigration story continues to inspire their philanthropy. When they arrived in the United States, Anil Sharma faced the same challenges many new immigrants in the County still encounter today: limited networks, limited resources, and the need to build opportunity from the ground up. Mr. Sharma credits his success with the freedom to learn, to adapt, and to take risks, which are opportunities he now seeks to extend to others. Through the newly named Center, the Sharmas hope to instill these same values in the students it serves, ensuring that future generations have the tools and confidence to succeed. Therefore, jointly with Chairman McKay and Supervisor Bierman, Supervisor Sizemore Heizer moved that the Board direct staff to prepare a Proclamation for Anil and Anupama Sharma, in recognition of their foundational investment in GMU, commitment to strengthening innovation and entrepreneurial opportunity, and their vital role in supporting the County’s economy, to be presented in the Board Room. Chairman McKay seconded the motion and it carried by unanimous vote. 19. The report was entitled “Evaluating the Restaurant Permitting Process” and reviewed the timeliness, efficiency, and overall experience of the permitting process for restaurants opening in the County. The report observed some lengthy permitting timelines for restaurants opening in the County and identified several key concerns from restaurant owners. To address these issues, the Auditor to the Board included three recommendations aimed at making the permitting process easier to navigate, strengthening coordination and consistency across County agencies, and reducing avoidable delays and uncertainty. Ultimately, addressing these recommendations will help restaurants open more easily and quicker in the County. The Audit Committee concurred with all recommendations. The report can be found at the following Committee meeting link below and was distributed to the Board Summary -10- October 13, 2026 Board electronically: https://www.fairfaxcounty.gov/boardofsupervisors/boardsupervisors-audit-committee-meeting-oct-6-2026. Smith Fairfax County Engagement with VA Executive Order 22 (Data Centers) October 27, 2026 On September 18, 2026, Governor Spanberger issued Executive Order 22, launching the Virginia Data Center Accountability Framework focused on community engagement, environmental protection, energy affordability, clean energy, and workforce development. The Executive Order strengthens transparency by requiring public disclosure of material information about proposed data center projects, including incentives, resource demands, and potential community impacts. It also directs state agencies to develop new standards, guidance, and tools, such as model community engagement and impact-evaluation practices, for use in data center oversight. The Executive Order strengthens the Commonwealth’s role in regulating key components of data center operations that Fairfax County cannot control, including energy infrastructure, air quality, and water-related impacts. As the Commonwealth develops its policies, the County should remain engaged to ensure local concerns and experiences inform the process. Fairfax County has already taken significant steps to manage and better understand the impacts of data center development. In 2024, the County adopted targeted Zoning Ordinance amendments to clarify where data centers are allowed and what size they can be, require pre and post construction noise studies, visual screening, and certain building design standards. Complementary updates to the Comprehensive Plan in 2025 provide guidance on data center siting, addressed compatibility with surrounding uses, and incorporated considerations related to air quality, energy sources, and water usage. Together, these efforts have strengthened the County’s development framework for data centers, positioning Fairfax County to engage constructively with the state’s evolving policies on data center development. As our partners at the Commonwealth work to implement the Governor’s Data Center Accountability Framework, I want to ensure that we as a County continue to be proactive in our pursuit of responsible data center development. As such, I move that the Board direct the County Executive to address the following topics: 3 • Engagement with the Commonwealth on the ongoing efforts associated with Executive Order 22. As the economic engine of the Commonwealth, it is important for Fairfax County to be fully engaged in the state’s work to develop new standards, transparency tools, and community-focused policies for data center development. Participation in these discussions will ensure that the County’s needs, challenges, and experiences are represented as decisions are made that will directly affect our residents, infrastructure, and long-term planning. • Evaluate Community Benefits Plans (CBPs) as a best practice for encouraging developers to address local impacts and provide measurable community benefits, including workforce opportunities and infrastructure improvements. • Consider whether further improvements can be made to the County’s existing information-sharing processes for data center projects. The County makes information about data center projects available to residents as part of the public-facing zoning and site plan development processes. This allows residents, staff, and decision makers to access critical details about these projects, including projected community impacts. The County does not enter into Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs) that constrain information sharing in the context of these data center zoning and/or site plan approval processes. • Identify opportunities for coordination with state agencies and utility providers on energy affordability, infrastructure demands, air quality, water use, and other impacts beyond the County’s direct authority. I further move that the County Executive report findings and recommended next steps to the Board at a committee meeting within 120 days. 2 4 Rachna Sizemore Heizer Braddock District Supervisor Kings Park Library 9002 Burke Lake Road Burke, VA 22015 703-425-9300 Braddock@fairfaxcounty.gov www.fairfaxcounty.gov/braddock Board Matter Supervisor Rachna Sizemore Heizer Publicity Request – Best of Braddock Awards and Reception Background: Mr. Chairman, for more than thirty years the Braddock District Supervisor has held a ceremony to honor the residents and organizations in our district who have committed their time and resources to make our community a better place to live, work, and play. I’m excited to host the next Best of Braddock Awards Ceremony and Reception on Tuesday, November 10 at 6:30 p.m., and I invite my colleagues and the broader community to join us! The evening will start with a reception, followed by the awards ceremony to recognize and celebrate our active and dedicated community members. We will be celebrating an especially impressive slate of people and organizations this year, including our Best of Braddock awardees, the winners of the 2026 Battle of the Bands, and the winners of our first ever intergenerational art competition. Motion: Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I move without objection, that the Office of Public Affairs promote this event to the community through the County’s communications channels. 5 County of Fairfax, Virginia To protect and enrich the quality of life for the people, neighborhoods and diverse communities of Fairfax County To, Board Matter Hunter Mill District Supervisor Walter Alcorn October 27, 2026 Hunter Mill District Coats for Kids Drive Background: As winter approaches, there are many children who need warm winter coats. To help our youngest residents stay warm, my office is sponsoring a children’s coat drive in partnership with Heritage Fellowship Church in Reston. We are focusing our coat drive on children since our little ones outgrow their winter jackets so quickly, and there’s always a need for more. I invite our community to donate new or gently used, clean winter coats for kids. Coats and jackets in all children’s sizes are needed from newborns to teens, but there’s also a high demand for coats for elementary and middle school children. Donations may be made from now through Saturday, January 9, and they may be dropped off anytime day or night in the collection bin at the North County Governmental Center, 1801 Cameron Glen Drive, Reston. Or donations may be brought to Heritage Fellowship Church, 2501 Fox Mill Drive, Reston, on Saturdays between 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. from November through Jan. 9. While in the past residents have generously donated other winter clothing, such as sweaters, hats, scarves and gloves, we cannot accept these items due to space limitations. Working with Heritage Fellowship Church and others, the coats that are collected will be donated to schools, Head Start programs, community and teen centers, local shelters, nonprofits, faith groups and other community organizations. Last year, we distributed more than 1,000 coats, demonstrating the great need for this coat drive. I encourage our community to give the gift of warmth again this year! For questions or more information, please contact Lisa Singer in my office by email at lisa.singer@fairfaxcounty.gov or call 703-478-0283, TTY 711. Walter L. As the Board may be aware, he resigned his position after I appointed him as the Hunter Mill District representative on the Planning Commission. Under RCC’s governing procedures, the Board of Supervisors makes appointments to fill vacant seats that occur in between the center’s community selection process for its board called the Preference Poll. Alcorn, Supervisor Hunter Mill District Fairfax County Board of Supervisors 1801 Cameron Glen Drive, Reston, VA 20190 703-478-0283 8 HunterMill@fairfaxcounty.gov County of Fairfax, Virginia To protect and enrich the quality of life for the people, neighborhoods and diverse communities of Fairfax County To, Board Matter Hunter Mill District Supervisor Walter Alcorn October 27, 2026 Recognizing Reston Chorale’s 60th Anniversary Background: The Reston Chorale is celebrating its 60th anniversary this year. For those who’ve never heard this beloved Reston institution perform, the Reston Chorale is a mixed-voice, auditioned chorus with a broad repertoire that spans classic rock to Broadway to great choral masterworks both old and new. Founded in the fall of 1966, the Chorale remains a vibrant voice to Robert E. Simon, Jr.’s legacy. The vocal group was established two years after Reston’s founding. Simon, a lifelong pianist and choral musician himself, recruited James Christian Pfohl to create the chorale as part of the multi-faceted Reston Music Center — which included a summer music camp, a children’s choir and a chamber orchestra. In October 1966, Pfohl invited singers to join the choir he was forming, and 40 musicians accepted his invitation. With these members, the Chorale debuted at its first performance billed as “Christmas in a New Town” on December 18. The ensemble, which included Bob Simon, performed from a tree-shaped platform on Lake Anne’s Washington Plaza, along with other musical groups that day. The PBS TV-station WETA also filmed the concert, airing it on Christmas Eve. Six decades later, the Chorale continues to delight audiences, and it has performed at distinguished venues, including the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, Wolf Trap, George Mason University's Center for the Arts, and the Rachel M. Schlesinger Concert Hall and Arts Center. To launch its 60th season, the Chorale will present Threads of Joy on Saturday, December 5, a festive concert of sacred and secular holiday music. Later that month, the Chorale will offer its always popular, annual Messiah singalong, and the group’s season continues into the spring with additional concerts that will include the world premieres of two choral works commissioned by the group. Jimenez October 27th, 2026 Recognition of Jean Rackowski and Mary Lee DeSpirito for their Volunteer Service to ACCA Mr. Chairman, today it is my honor to recognize the service of two outstanding volunteers in the Mason District Community: Jean Rackowski and Mary Lee DeSpirito. As my colleagues may know, The Annandale Christian Community for Action, or “ACCA”, has spent decades helping individuals and families throughout our community meet essential needs. This includes their outstanding pre-school program but also access to food and furniture and other support. The organization's impact would not be possible without the dedicated volunteers who give their time, energy, and leadership to help their neighbors. Jean and Mary Lee are two such volunteers who have made extraordinary contributions to ACCA and the residents it serves. Jean Rackowski began volunteering with ACCA's food pantry in 1992 and served as chair of the program from 1994 through 2019. For 25 years, she has provided hands-on leadership to help ensure local families had reliable access to food and compassionate assistance. Although Jean had originally planned to retire in 2019, the COVID-19 pandemic changed those plans, and she continued serving as pantry operations manager through a particularly challenging period. That decision is just one of many indications of her dedication to people the organization serves. As she prepares to step down from role of Chair on November 12, Jean will continue supporting the food pantry as a buyer and helping the incoming Andres F. Jimenez Mason District Supervisor 6507 Columbia Pike Annandale, Virginia 22003 Phone: 703-256-7717 11 volunteer manager through the transition. Her more than three decades of service reflect an extraordinary commitment to the well-being of our neighbors. Mary Lee DeSpirito has served ACCA for more than 35 years, taking on numerous leadership roles and consistently responding to the needs of local families. Among her most significant contributions has been her leadership of ACCA's furniture program, which has delivered emergency furniture to families in need and helped them furnish their homes with dignity. As ACCA transitions this work to a partnership model, Mary Lee's leadership remains an important part of the program's legacy. She also continues to lead ACCA's annual Individual Giving Campaign and has worked with Fairfax County boards and community organizations addressing shelter, furniture, and food insecurity. Both Jean and Mary Lee have demonstrated what it means to serve a community with compassion, generosity, and dedication. Their sixty years of combined volunteer service have helped strengthen ACCA's programs and improve the lives of countless individuals and families throughout Fairfax County. Their contributions deserve recognition and appreciation from the Board of Supervisors. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I ask that the Board direct staff to prepare two separate resolutions to be presented as separate out-of-board room recognitions – one recognizing Jean Rackowski and another recognizing Mary Lee DeSpirito -- for their exceptional volunteer leadership and longstanding service to ACCA and the Fairfax County community. TIMING: Board action is requested at this time so UOSA may establish trust, execute participation documents, and begin formal funding of long-term OPEB obligations. BACKGROUND: The UOSA was created under the Virginia Water and Waste Authorities Act. It operates a regional water reclamation facility serving Fairfax County, Prince William County, the City of Manassas, and the City of Manassas Park. Members of the UOSA Board of Directors are appointed by these jurisdictions, including Fairfax County. UOSA currently provides retiree health insurance benefits to eligible retired employees. The cost of providing these benefits is reported as OPEB in accordance with GASB Statement No. 74. Establishing a qualifying trust will allow UOSA to begin funding these obligations over time and reduce its net OPEB liability. The UOSA Board of Directors has adopted a resolution to establish an OPEB trust and has expressed its intent to join the VACo/VML Pooled OPEB Trust, originally established in 2008 through the joint exercise of powers by Fairfax County and Henrico County. Participation will allow UOSA to invest OPEB assets through a professionally managed pooled structure designed for Virginia local governments. 14 Board Agenda Item October 13, 2026 Under Section 15.2-1544 of the Code of Virginia, a political subdivision, such as UOSA, whose governing body is appointed in whole or in part by another locality must receive authorization from that locality to establish and fund such a trust. Because Fairfax County appoints members to the UOSA Board, Fairfax County’s authorization is required before UOSA can proceed. EQUITY IMPACT: Authorizing UOSA to establish and participate in an OPEB trust supports equitable and fiscally responsible long-term funding of retiree healthcare benefits. Stable OPEB funding promotes intergenerational fairness and strengthens the financial resilience of regional public service entities. FISCAL IMPACT: This action does not create any fiscal obligation for Fairfax County. UOSA will independently fund the trust and all related participation costs. and WHEREAS, members of the UOSA Board of Directors are appointed by participating jurisdictions, including Fairfax County, Prince William County, the City of Manassas, and the City of Manassas Park; and WHEREAS, UOSA provides retiree health insurance benefits to eligible retired employees and desires to establish an Other Post-Employment Benefits (“OPEB”) trust consistent with Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB) Statement No. 74, for the purpose of funding and providing retirement benefits, including health insurance, to UOSA retirees; and WHEREAS, the UOSA Board of Directors has adopted its own resolution expressing UOSA’s intent to establish an OPEB trust and to participate in the VACo/VML Pooled OPEB Trust, which was originally established in 2008 through the joint exercise of powers by the Counties of Fairfax and Henrico; and WHEREAS, Section 15.2-1544 of the Code of Virginia, 1950, as amended, provides that the governing body of a local government that appoints in whole or in part the governing body of another political subdivision may authorize that political subdivision to establish an OPEB trust; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the Board of Supervisors of Fairfax County hereby authorizes the Upper Occoquan Service Authority to establish and fund an Other Post Employment Benefits Trust pursuant to the provisions of the Governmental Accounting Standards Board Statement 74; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that UOSA is hereby authorized to participate in the VACo/VML Pooled OPEB Trust and to execute all documents necessary to effect such participation; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that this authorization is granted pursuant to Section 15.2-1544 of the Code of Virginia, and a certified copy of this resolution shall be forwarded to the Upper Occoquan Service Authority. Given this year of our Nation’s 250th Anniversary, by the Fairfax County History Commission. 9 Attachment 1 Executive Summary Executive Summary July 2025—June 2026 4 Major Initiatives 250th Commemoration 5 Strengthening Ties with Fairfax County Park Authority 6 Outreach Historic Courthouse and Historic Records Center 7 William H. Randall Estates Historic District 7 7 Section 106 10 Threatened Sites Sustained Efforts Advocacy 14 2026 History Conference 15 Awards 17 Oral History 18 Inventory of Historic Sites 18 Historic Markers 19 Resident Curator Program 21 Budget Report 22 Membership Meet Our Members 23 Advisory Members 23 Front Cover (from top moving left to right): Fairfax Resolves booklets, Dunn Loring Elementary School Historic plaque, Commissioner Michelle Arcari Rose; Commissioners Subhi Mehdi and Brian Heintz presenting History Commission Award, unveiling of the James Goins historical marker, History Conference speaker Richard Bell; Interactive exhibit at Fairfax County History Conference; Commissioner Anne Stuntz at the Legato Schoolhouse; Supervisor Dalia Palchik and Commissioner Sue Kovach Shuman with a drawing of the Historic Fairfax County Courthouse. 3 10 Attachment 1 Executive Summary The Fairfax County History Commission is pleased to present its FY 2026 annual report, which aligns with the county’s strategic plan, particularly the key drivers of equity and inclusive engagement. The Commission positively impacts Fairfax County residents through activities for lifelong education and learning, cultural and recreational opportunities, and effective and efficient government. We thank the Board of Supervisors for the opportunity to preserve and promote the history of our county. Highlights of our achievements during this reporting period include: • • • • • • • • • • • Leading and supporting the commemoration of the nation’s semiquincentennial through our partnership with and membership in the Fairfax County 250th Commission. Organizing and presenting our record-breaking 2026 Fairfax County History Conference. Creating and launching the video series Revolutionary Voices: The Fairfax Story. Reprinting the popular revolutionary document, the Fairfax Resolves. Rewarding outstanding historical research and writing in our community. Advocating for the preservation and protection of Dunn Loring Elementary School, the Bowman Distillery, Laurel Hill House and other properties on our Threatened Sites List. Expanding our coverage of African American history by advancing markers for First Baptist Church of Merrifield and Spring Bank Colored School. The Commission acknowledges and thanks staff from the Department of Planning and Development, the Architectural Review Board, the Park Authority, the Virginia Room, and Channel 16 for their contributions and support. We look forward to another productive year in FY 2027! Subhi Mehdi Chair, Fairfax County History Commission 4 11 Attachment 1 Major Initiatives 250th Commemoration History Commission display at History Conference. Conference. In FY 2026, the History Commission prioritized county and regional efforts to observe and commemorate the semiquincentennial of the American Revolution, the Revolutionary War, and the Independence of the United States of America. The resources of the History Commission supported the efforts of the Fairfax County 250th Commission and partner organizations in executing activities and events commemorating the past, present and future of America across the nine supervisory districts of Fairfax County. Four history commissioners serve directly on the Fairfax 250 Commission. Two commissioners, Gretchen Bulova and Tammy Mannarino, served as officers during this fiscal year, leading the creation, enhancement and amplification of hundreds of activities and events. Both regularly speak on behalf of Fairfax 250 to arts, military and community organizations. Commissioners Mannarino and Bulova led the publication of two booklets interpreting and reprinting foundational documents written by Fairfax County residents in the Revolutionary period: The Fairfax Resolves and The Virginia Declaration of Rights. They supported a third booklet published by Fairfax 250, Honoring the Fairfax County, Virginia Patriots of the Revolution. Commissioners Subhi Mehdi (Dranesville) and Jen Macpherson (Franconia) represented their Supervisory Districts on the body, assisting in planning and public outreach. Additionally, other commissioners supported 250th efforts within Fairfax County through their related activities and networks outside the History Commission. Commissioners Anne Stuntz and Holly Irwin, for example, shared opportunities for cross-promotion of community efforts in their work with Vienna 250 and Falls Church 250, respectively. Similarly, in her role at the Fairfax County Park Authority, Commissioner Cheryl-Ann Repetti supported Fairfax 250 by providing outreach and historical content for exhibits. The History Commission printed and distributed more than 1000 copies of The Fairfax Resolves. Commissioner Sue Kovach Shuman led two efforts that provided depth to the county’s marking of this important period: the 2026 History Conference and the Oral History project, Revolutionary Voices: The Fairfax Story, both of which are detailed later in this report. All history commissioners supported 250th events through their advocacy of an amazing array of historical sites in Fairfax County. Their support of the 2026 5 12 Attachment 1 Major Initiatives Conference made it the largest and most interactive to date. Finally, History Commission Advisory Member Mary Lipsey represented the Springfield District on the Fairfax 250 Commission, providing educational expertise and experience to appreciative audiences. Strengthening Ties with Fairfax County Park Authority The Fairfax County History Commission (FCHC) and the Fairfax County Park Authority (FCPA) both execute core functions in support of Fairfax County’s history and heritage resources. They are both committed to their roles -- which sometimes overlap. Notably, the FCPA stewards more than 40 sites on the History Commission’s Inventory of Historic Sites. The FCPA routinely attends FCHC’s Inventory Committee meetings and the FCHC tracks FCPA’s Resident Curator program. The History Commission’s Advocacy Committee often makes use of outreach opportunities provided by FCPA events. This year’s celebration of America’s 250th saw additional collaborations between the FCHC and the FCPA on public education. Having experienced the benefits of this close collaboration and recognizing their common function as county cultural resource stewards, the commission observed that overall coordination and cooperation between the two entities could be improved. In a bid to enhance strategic communication, the History Commission appointed Commissioner Todi Carnes as a formal liaison to the FCPA. Commissioner Carnes worked previously with FCPA Friends groups as an advocate for parks. The commission hopes to develop processes and programs that will facilitate a more synergistic relationship between the FCHC and the FCPA, leading to better support for the county’s history and heritage resources. Toward this end, FCPA Archaeology and Collections Branch staff at Fairfax Commissioner Carnes has met with County History Conference. key Park Authority personnel, attended Park Authority Board meetings, and has been observing interactions between the two organizations. Increased engagement is planned in FY 2027. Consistent with one of the Commission’s purposes stipulated in the Board of Supervisors 2019 authorizing resolution, Commissioner Carnes will also explore how the creation of trusts and endowments might be implemented to secure financing in support of FCPA-owned historic structures and properties. 6 13 Attachment 1 Outreach Historic Courthouse and Historic Records Center On December 18, 2025, The Fairfax County Historic Courthouse and Circuit Courts Historic Records Center experienced a catastrophic HVAC System failure. Operations at the Historic Courthouse were suspended and historic documents were relocated to the Main Courthouse, Merrifield (Prosperity Avenue) and a Springfield warehouse. The History Commission wrote a letter to the Board of Supervisors on January 15, requesting that the County prioritize the historic building restoration while the staff and tenants have been evacuated instead of adhering to the judicial center master plan timetable approved in 2021. The Commission also urged that the irreplaceable historic records being temporarily rehoused be safely stored. It is unfortunate that the timing of this failure encumbered research efforts and canceled events that would have enhanced the County’s commemoration of the nation’s 250 th anniversary. William H. Department of Planning & Community Development A meeting of the Franklin County Planning Commission was held on Tuesday, September 8, 2026 in the Board Room located at the Franklin County Government Center. THOSE PRESENT: Victor Evans – Chair, Union Hall District Ron Jefferson – Vice Chair, Gills Creek District David Pendleton – Blackwater District David Clements – Rocky Mount District C.W. Doss – Blue Ridge District Addison Hancock – Snow Creek District Matthew Peters – Boone District OTHERS PRESENT: Lisa Cooper – Planning Director Chris Dadak – County Attorney Jenn Richardson – Clerk Tina Franklin – Planner II THOSE ABSENT: NONE Chairman Evans called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m. Mr. Evans asked if the Planning Commission had any comments or changes to the August 11, 2026 minutes. There were no changes requested. The minutes were approved as written. Mr. Evans introduced the next item on the agenda: APPLICATION for SPECIAL USE PERMIT – Application of Chad Burnopp, Applicant, and David & Sandra Burnopp, Owners, requesting a special use permit, on an approximate .49 acres of property zoned A-1, Agricultural District. The parcels are located at 762 Redwood Road in the Union Hall Election District of Franklin County and further identified by real estate records as Tax Map/Parcels #0540015900 and #0540016302. The purpose of this special-use permit request is to allow for sales, service and repair of automobiles, trucks, recreational vehicles, motorcycles in Department of Planning & Community Development existing building(s). This property has a future land use designation of Rural Area – County. (SPEC-26-5 #0540015900 and #0540016302). Ms. Tina Franklin presented the staff report. She stated that the property has a single-family dwelling and two (2) detached garage structures, with frontage along Redwood Road and is surrounded by A-1, Agricultural Zoning. She stated that this area consists of residential dwellings, farmland, and wooded properties. Ms. Franklin stated that the proposed automotive repair shop is conducted in the detached garage behind the home that is placed diagonally on the property and is accessed from Redwood Road (Route 705) as shown on the conceptual plan. Ms. Franklin stated that there is a wood privacy fence between the subject property and 780 Redwood Road on the left side of the subject property along with a tree line towards the front of the property line and a wood privacy fence between the subject property and 712 Redwood Road on the right side of the subject property. Ms. Franklin stated that the county received a complaint regarding the applicant conducting automotive repair in the detached garage(s). Ms. Franklin stated that staff had not received any phone calls about the application. Ms. Franklin displayed four (4) GIS maps of the property. Ms. Franklin stated the property has frontage and will be accessed on Redwood Road. She stated that the surrounding area is single-family dwellings on both sides of the subject property, and the rest of the area is vacant farmland and wooded lots. She stated that this small business would not generate much more traffic than the single-family dwelling does on a daily basis. Ms. Franklin stated that the business averages three (3) customers per day to about fifteen (15) per week and 60-65 per month. She stated that the noise generated by this business would be minimal because the service and repair are accomplished inside of the garage, which 2 Department of Planning & Community Development would help reduce the noise of the shop. Ms. Franklin stated that the landscape screening and privacy fence would protect the aesthetics of the surrounding area. Ms. Franklin stated that the staff conclude that the use will not be a substantial detriment to adjacent properties, change the character of the zoning district, and will be in harmony with the purpose and intent of this chapter, and with the uses permitted by-right in the A-1, Agricultural zoning district. Ms. Franklin stated that staff recommended that the Planning Commission recommend approval of the special use permit with the following five (5) conditions: 1. The proposed use shall be developed in substantial conformance to the conceptual plan titled “Burnopp, 762 Redwood Road, Tax Map #’s 0540015900 and 0540016302, prepared by applicant. 2. The applicant/owners shall vacate the property line between the two (2) parcel id #’s 0540015900 and 0540016302 by plat or deed of vacation approved by the Planning Department. 3. The landscaping and privacy fence along the southern property line between subject property and 780 Redwood Road and the privacy fence along the northern property line between the subject property and 712 Redwood Road shall be maintained. 4. The applicant must adhere to all VDOT regulations regarding the entrance to the property for the use to allow for service and repair of automobiles, trucks, recreational vehicles, motorcycles. 5. No vehicles being serviced shall be parked in front of the single-family dwelling. Ms. Franklin asked if the Planning Commission had any questions for her. The Planning Commission had no questions for Ms. Franklin. Ms. Franklin stated that the applicant had provided her with four (4) signatures from adjoining property owners in support of the use to be submitted for the record. (See attachment.) Chairman Evans invited the applicant up to the podium to present. Mr. Burnopp did not have anything additional to add. 3 Department of Planning & Community Development Mr. Evans stated that the business has been in operation for a while. Mr. Burnopp affirmed the statement. Mr. Evans asked if the applicant understood and accepted the conditions. Mr. Burnopp stated yes. Mr. Jefferson asked the applicant about the hours of operation. Mr. Burnopp stated 8am – 5pm Monday through Friday. Mr. Evans stated that the Planning Commission had an opportunity to do a site visit. He stated that they were impressed by what Mr. Burnopp was offering the community. Mr. Evans stated that Condition 5 stated that ‘no vehicles being serviced shall be parked in front of the single-family dwelling.” He stated that the conceptual plan had some customer vehicles in front. Mr. Burnopp stated that the van parked in the front was his personal van. Mr. Evans stated that the Planning Commission wanted to make it clear that given the location, all customer vehicles would be behind the dwelling. Mr. Burnopp agreed. Mr. Evans stated that the Planning Commission would like to add a stipulation that the fencing be at least five (5) feet high. Mr. Burnopp agreed to this stipulation. Mr. Hancock asked the applicant what is done with the used oil. Mr. Burnopp stated that he puts used oil in a large barrel at the back of property and that it is picked up by a man that has a waste oil heater. Mr. Evans opened the opportunity for citizen comment. There were no citizens who signed up to comment on the application. Mr. Evans asked the audience if there was anyone who wished to comment on the application. Seeing none and hearing none, Mr. Evans closed the opportunity for citizen comment. The Planning Commission began their deliberations. Mr. Evans stated that he applauds the fact that the applicant has an in-demand skill and that he is providing a service to his neighbors in the community. Mr. Jefferson stated that he would like to would like to make a condition on the hours of operations to be 9am to 6pm Monday through Friday. He stated that the 4 Department of Planning & Community Development permit would stay with the property regardless of who owns it in the future. Mr. Jefferson stated that he would like there to be a Condition 6 of hours of operation, Monday through Friday 8am to 6pm. Mr. Peters stated that the Planning Commission received a letter of support from the adjoining property owners, and that they would be the ones most affected by the hours of operation. Mr. Peters stated that he does not feel comfortable limiting the applicant’s ability to make income. Mr. Evans stated that with the condition suggested by Mr. Jefferson would be giving the applicant an extra hour. Mr. Peters stated that he does not feel comfortable adding that restriction. Mr. Jefferson stated that the conditions would go with the property and he wants to ensure that future owners would not have hours of operation that exceed a certain time. Mr. Peters asked about the sound ordinance. Ms. Cooper stated that the noise ordinance does not regulate Mr. Burnopp’s type of business. Mr. Evans stated that the noise ordinance regulates amplified sounds only. Mr. Peters stated that he is uncomfortable adding a sixth (6th) condition. Mr. Pendleton made a motion to approve the application with the added Condition 6 of hours of operation, Monday through Friday 8am to 6pm. Mr. Clements seconded the motion. Mr. Peters asked if there was a reason why Saturday wasn’t added in the hours of operation. Mr. Peters stated that he is not comfortable limiting the hours of operations. He asked if having a condition of hours of operation was normal when someone in an A-1 applied for a special use permit for a garage. Ms. Cooper stated that they try to encourage businesses close to single-family dwellings to have hours of operation. Mr. Evans asked Mr. Pendleton if he would amend his motion and add Saturday as a day of operation. Mr. Pendleton agreed. Ms. Richardson stated that the motion is to approve with six (6) conditions. She stated maintaining a five (5) foot fence was added to Condition 3 and hours of 5 Department of Planning & Community Development operation being Monday through Saturday from 8am to 6pm would be added as Condition 6. A roll call vote was conducted. The motion to approve the special use permit with the 5 conditions recommended by staff, the addition to Condition 3, and the added Condition 6 was approved; 7-0-0-0 voting was as follows: AYES: Peters, Pendleton, Doss, Clements, Hancock, Jefferson, Evans NAYS: None ABSENT: None ABSTAIN: None Chairman Evans announced that the Board of Supervisors would hear this case on October 20, 2026. Chairman Evans opened the podium for open citizen comment. There were not citizens that wished to speak; therefore, Chairman Evans closed the opportunity. Chairman Evans began the discussion on the Zoning Ordinance update. He stated that there were three (3) items on the agenda: review staff’s annotation of articles and decide if their method of annotation was acceptable, assign citizen comments to Planning Commission members, and review the results of the August 20 Board of Supervisor Work Session. Mr. Evans stated that staff had provided the Planning Commission with hard copies of the way they foresaw annotating the proposed Zoning Ordinance so that the Planning Commission understood what was required by the Code of Virginia, what was carried over from the current Zoning Ordinance, and what was staff input. Ms. Cooper stated that staff had finished annotating Articles 1 and 2. She stated that the articles had been emailed to the Planning Commission the previous Friday. She stated that if any Planning Commission member wanted hard copies of the articles at the dais to email Ms. Richardson. Ms. Cooper stated that the first three (3) articles are difficult because a lot of the contents come from the Code of Virginia. Ms. Cooper explained the legend for the annotated articles: red is for new or staff changes, blue is for Code of Virginia, green is what is in the current ordinance, pink 6 Department of Planning & Community Development is what is currently being work on, and citizen comment will be highlighted in orange. Ms. Cooper stated that instead of having another color, the default assumption should be that staff was satisfied with an article unless otherwise stated. She stated that staff was satisfied with Articles 1 and 2, except for the section that is still being worked on that is outlined in pink. Ms. Cooper stated that she wanted ‘as amended’ whenever code 15.2-2280 is mentioned. Mr. Dadak stated that ‘et seq.’ meant in sequence. Ms. Cooper stated that staff added ‘working waterfront area’ to section 1-1-3 because it was part of the state code. She stated that when we got to Article 4, there would be strike-throughs and suggestions from staff. She stated that Articles 1, 2, and 3 deal with the state code technicalities. She stated that Article 3 explained what the Planning Commission, Board of Zoning Appeals, and Zoning Administrator do, and how permitting is done. Mr. Peters asked if the Planning Commission will know what changes were added by The Berkley Group. Ms. Cooper stated that she would not distinguish between staff and The Berkley Group because staff hold daily discussions on possible changes based on citizen comments and Planning Commission comments. Ms. Cooper stated that anything the staff did not want would be indicated by a strikethrough. Mr. Evans stated that there was a fair amount of coordination between staff and The Berkley Group as to what to have in the Zoning Ordinance. There was a discussion regarding the color legend. Mr. Evans stated that if it is in black font, it existed in the current ordinance, and if it is in red font, it did not exist in the current ordinance. Mr. Evans stated that the format was good. Mr. Evans stated that if the text is not annotated, that was an addition based on best practice. Ms. Cooper agreed. 7 Department of Planning & Community Development Mr. Hancock asked if the citizen comment highlighted in orange was something that the staff felt was worthy of being added but not required by law. Ms. Cooper stated that the citizen thought that it was unfair that the United States or the Commonwealth of Viriginia or the County of Franklin should not have to be subject to the provisions contained within. She stated that the citizen would like to see that removed. Ms. Cooper stated that she presumed that the Planning Commission would like her to do some type of presentation when discussing the articles. Mr. Evans stated that the Planning Commission needed to let Ms. Richardson know how they would like to receive the reviewed articles. He stated that the intention was that as staff completed the review of the articles, the Planning Commission would receive them two (2) weeks prior to the work session. He stated that the public would also be able to review the documents. Mr. Jefferson asked about the yellow highlighting. Ms. Cooper stated that the yellow highlighting is for the insertion of dates and articles. She stated that the highlights and footnotes would not exist in the final ordinance. Mr. Evans stated that it would be helpful to add yellow to the color legend. Ms. Cooper stated that the crosswalk is helpful. She stated that across the top, it has the previous zoning ordinance and then divisions. She stated that 25-1: The Authority Enactment stated where in the draft Zoning Ordinance and the sections that it was in. She stated that she wanted the Planning Commission to have the crosswalk in case they could not find something in the current ordinance; the crosswalk will indicate where it could be found in the draft ordinance. Mr. Evans stated that the citizen comments had been divided amongst the Planning Commission. He stated that each Planning Commission member should review the comments and organize accordingly to ensure that the comments are addressed during the work sessions. Ms. Cooper stated that The Berkley Group organized citizen comments and the spreadsheet was provided at the May 13th meeting. She stated that Ms. Richardson 8 Department of Planning & Community Development had created a spreadsheet for citizen comments received after the May 13th meeting. Mr. Evans reviewed the results of the August 20th Board of Supervisors Work Session. He stated that things had been shifted and that the Zoning Ordinance Work Sessions would go out to September 1, 2027. He stated that in September or October 2027, the Planning Commission would be prepared to hold the public hearing and make a final action as to what would be proposed for the Board of Supervisors adoption. Mr. Evans stated that the Board of Supervisors wanted updates at the end of every work session. He stated that the Board of Supervisors left it up to the Planning Commission when joint work sessions were … among the Board of Supervisors that they would like to move ahead with addressing data centers specifically. He stated that the Board of Supervisors liked the idea of convening a panel to discuss the pros and cons of a data center so that … that staff is in the process of looking at other localities' ordinances related to data centers. He stated that in the proposed zoning ordinance, there were approximately four (4) pages of standards on data centers. Mr. Evans stated that … Peters asked if it was worth discussing amending the Zoning Ordinance to allow data centers by special use permit instead of by right. Ms. Cooper stated that the Planning Commission wouldn't just want to amend it for a special use permit. … by the County Attorney with the Board of Supervisors about the idea of establishing data center standards and conditions countywide as county code. He stated that creating land use standards for data centers in a non-zoned area would not … Evans stated that whatever the Planning Commission did regarding data centers, it would only apply to the zoned areas. Mr. Hancock stated that it is a great consideration that a subject matter expert is going to be an important part of the … the County's authority to accept voluntary proffers, in writing for the issuance of a zoning map amendment.
