Code § 2.2-4382, the King and Queen County Board of Supervisors (the “Board”) hereby adopts the following procedures to be used in the procurement of Construction Management (“CM”) projects in King and Queen County (the “County”) over which the Board has authority. These Procedures are effective as of October 14, 2025. The procedures to be used in selecting a CM and awarding a contract are as follows: 1. The County shall comply with all requirements set forth in the Va. Code, including, but perhaps not limited to, those requirements set forth in Va. Code § 2.2-4382. 2. Construction Management may be utilized on projects in the County, provided that (i) the project is a complex project and (ii) the procurement method for the project is approved by the local governing body. 3. The Board shall adopt a resolution on a per project basis setting forth the Board’s (i) approval for using the CM method, and (ii) determination that the project is a complex project. 4. A copy of all Resolutions adopted pursuant to these Procedures shall be maintained in the procurement file. 5. Prior to publishing the Request for Qualification, the County will have in its employ or under its control or will retain as necessary a Virginia-licensed engineer or architect with the professional competence to advise the County regarding use of construction management for a specified construction project. The Virginialicensed engineer or architect will assist the County with preparation of Request for Proposal (RFP), and evaluation of proposals received in response to the RFP. 6. Public notice of the Request for Qualifications shall be posted on the Commonwealth of Virginia central electronic procurement website, known as eVA, or the County’s website, or both, at least 30 days prior to the date set for receipt of qualification proposals. 5 7. The CM contract shall be entered into no later than the completion of the schematic phase of design, unless prohibited by authorization of funding restrictions. 8. Prior CM experience or previous experience with the County shall not be considered as a prerequisite or factor considered for prequalification of a contract. The County may consider the experience of each contractor on comparable construction management or design-build projects. 9. All CM contracts to which the County is a party, except CM contracts involving infrastructure projects, shall require that (i) no more than 10 percent of the construction work, as measured by the cost of the work, be performed by the construction manager with its own forces, and (ii) the remaining 90 percent of the construction work, as measured by the cost of the work, be performed by subcontractors of the construction manager, which the construction manager shall procure by publicly advertised, competitive sealed bidding to the maximum extent practicable. For any work not procured by publicly advertised competitive sealed bidding, the CM shall provide documentation detailing the reasons that was not done and such documentation shall be placed in the procurement file. 10. Price is a critical basis for award of the CM contract. 11. When appropriate, the County will post or confirm the posting on the Commonwealth of Virginia central electronic procurement website, known as eVA, or the County’s website, or both, when and where the general contractor plans to advertise bid packages for subcontracting opportunities. 12. A two-step competitive negotiation process must be used in the procurement of a CM contract consistent with Chapter 43.1 and the Construction Management Procedures As Adopted by the Secretary of Administration (effective December 17, 2024) for state public bodies. 13. text: BERKLEY GROUP FINANCIAL CONSULTING PROPOSAL We received a financial assessment from the Berkley Group regarding our operations, interdepartmental workflows, and policies. There is room for improvement in workflows between offices software systems to make our balancing procedures more efficient and timely. Based on our discussions and interviews with Berkley Group, we could define workflows and transition to Berkley Group for our financial consulting and audit preparation. They are proposing, and staff is requesting, to perform this work monthly. Lunenburg does not have the funds to hire a full-time finance director, nor is there a need for full-time. The County Administrator and Treasurer’s office handle all budget and finance for the County, and the School Board takes care of their budget and finance, but a part-time staffing would bridge the gap between the two entities and streamline balancing procedures. For the FY27 year, this would mean additional expenditure added to the budget for approximately half of the year. However, in FY28, the County would no longer contract with ClearPoint Consultants, and the budget could be held to the prior year’s amounts. Also, Berkley Group can accommodate inperson fieldwork, which would reduce local staff workload for audit preliminary fieldwork and monthly closing reconciliations, as necessary. The goal of this transition would be better transparency, continuity of operations (especially in the case of transition/turnovers/absences), and additional capacity for financial activities. Please see the attached work order from Berkley Group for consideration. Main Street in the Town of Madison, Virginia. The meeting was called to order by Chairman Zachary Whitman at 7:00 PM. The chairman called for the room to recite the Pledge of Allegiance and followed with a moment of silence. Determine Presence of a Quorum & Microphone Reminder Chairman Whitman determined there was a quorum. As a quorum was established the following members were present, Chairman Zachary Whitman, Commissioners Clay Jackson, Jim Smith, Steve Carpenter, Nathan Cowan, and Wayne Dyer. Also, present was Allen Nicholls, Zoning Administrator, Hannon Wright, County Attorney, and Jonathon Weakley, County Administrator. Board of Supervisor members present were, Chairman Carty Yowell, Vice-Chairman Jim Jewett, Supervisors Jud Buchanan, Nancy Sharman, and Mike Snider. Vice-Chairman Pete Elliott and Commissioner Anne Gore were absent. Adoption of Agenda Jackson moved to adopt the agenda as presented, seconded by Dyer. Aye: Whitman, Jackson, Smith, Carpenter, Cowan, and Dyer; Nay: (0); Abstain: (0); Absent: Elliott and Gore. The motion passed. General Public Comment The Chairman opened the floor to public comment. Mike Sharman – Novum area resident – expressed concerns regarding proposed Virginia constitutional amendments expected to appear on the upcoming ballot, specifically addressing reproductive rights, marriage, and restoration of voting and other political Page 1 of 6 rights for convicted felons. Mr. Sharman urged consideration of the long-term implications of constitutional amendments compared with the election of individual candidates. Hearing nothing further, the floor was closed. New Business Adoption of Minutes – August 19, 2026 Cowan moved to approve the minutes as presented, seconded by Carpenter. Aye: Whitman, Smith, Carpenter, and Cowan; Nay: (0); Abstain: Jackson and Dyer; Absent: Elliott and Gore. The motion passed. Public Hearings (Case No. ZOA-05-26-01) Sign Ordinance Amendment The Board of Supervisors has directed the Planning Commission to consider amendments to Madison County Code of Ordinances, Appendix 1, Article 12-1-2(16), Article 12-6-14, Article 12-6-15, and Article 12-6-16, and possibly repealing Madison County Code of Ordinances, Appendix 1, Article 12-6-15. These are sign ordinances related to temporary signs, particularly on County-owned property. Smith – expressed opposition to the proposed sign ordinance amendments, citing First Amendment concerns regarding the prohibition of political signage on County property during early voting. While acknowledging that the proposed language is content-neutral, the Commissioner questioned whether the prohibition is narrowly tailored to serve a significant governmental interest and whether it leaves adequate alternative means of communication. He noted the limited and potentially costly alternatives available for reaching early voters given the cost of direct mailings, and the lack of a physical newspaper, and expressed concern that the restriction could significantly limit political communication with that audience. He did state that he would be in support of Supervisor Jewett’s amendment text, with the correction of the allowable size for temporary signs. Wright – stated there is no First Amendment infringement and advised that the proposed prohibition is intended to be content neutral and applies only to temporary signs on County property, not other forms of expression. He further noted the County's interest in controlling clutter and managing its property, while acknowledging that other approaches, such as designated sign areas, could also be considered. The Chairman opened the floor to public comment. Brian Mitchell – Brightwood resident, secretary of the Madison County Electoral Board speaking on behalf of the Electoral Board, expressed concern that the proposed sixsquare-foot limitation for temporary signs would apply countywide, potentially affecting larger campaign and other temporary signs, and would conflict with the existing 40square-foot maximum in Section 12-2. In his personal capacity, Mr. Mitchell recommended retaining the proposed content-neutral definition of temporary sign while removing specific size limitations from the new text and relying on Section 12-2 to regulate Page 2 of 6 maximum sign area. Discussion of possible ADUs in the A-1 and C-1 districts will continue separately, with the next Planning Commission workshop scheduled for October 21. Sign ordinance. Work continues on the proposed repeal and replacement of Article 12. The replacement draft organizes standards by use and district and focuses on sign size, height, and placement. Further Planning Commission review is scheduled for the October 21 workshop. Home occupations and rural services. The Planning Commission subcommittee chaired by Anne Gore is developing the proposed ordinance. This initiative remains part of the Commission's ordinance work program. Active Rezoning Applications 1 Pending Rezoning Applications 0 Ordinance Amendments 3 Pending Special Use Permit Application 1 Administrative Review Staff continues to review subdivisions and site plans and assist owners, surveyors, attorneys, and real estate professionals with development questions. Recent work has included private-road access, agricultural uses, residential development options, and conditions for replacement dwellings. Page 1 of 2 Return to Agenda Subdivision rights and private roads. Staff reviewed subdivision potential for properties served by existing private roads. These reviews address the number of parcels already served, recorded access rights, and limitations on additional lots. Available acreage alone does not establish subdivision eligibility where private-road limitations apply. Family subdivision provisions do not provide a means to circumvent those limitations. Agricultural and commercial uses. Staff prepared a zoning determination for a proposed lavender farm and associated dining, alcohol service, and event uses. The review distinguishes permitted agricultural activities and a qualifying farm market from the proposed hospitality activities, which were not permitted as presented. The property also does not meet the acreage requirement for a wedding or event venue. Staff responded to requests for zoning verification letters and information concerning permitted business uses. Residential development inquiries. Staff evaluated preliminary concepts for residential rental development. The analysis addresses dwelling classifications, density, and public utility requirements. Guidance remains preliminary pending review of a specific site and development proposal. Staff emphasized that anticipated sewer availability is limited in both timing and service area and cannot be assumed for a prospective acquisition. Replacement dwelling conditions. Staff prepared permit conditions and accompanying correspondence for replacement dwelling construction. Where a property does not qualify for two dwellings, these conditions require removal of the existing dwelling in connection with issuance of the certificate of occupancy for the new home. Preliminary Development Review Committee. The October 6 meeting was cancelled because there were no applications or cases requiring committee review. Active Subdivision Applications 7 Active Site Plan Applications 6 Board of Zoning Appeals The Board of Zoning Appeals currently has no cases scheduled for consideration. The BZA continues to address administrative matters. The Board is close to adopting formal bylaws, as it currently operates without adopted bylaws. Appeal Applications 0 Variance Applications 0 Other Departmental Activities Staff continues to coordinate with the Building Department, County Administration, County Attorney, and reviewing agencies on development proposals and ordinance initiatives. Routine assistance includes interpreting permitted uses, reviewing access and parcel configurations, and explaining application procedures before applicants commit to a project. Professional development includes coursework toward the Certified Planning Commissioner program and review of planning commission practices in neighboring jurisdictions. End of Minutes: Attest: Zachary Whitman, Chairman of Planning Commission Date: Allen Nicholls, Secretary of Planning Commission Date: Planning Commission Meeting Minutes Page 4 of 4 ___ Madison County, Virginia – Planning Commission Date: October 21, 2026 Agenda Item: Karl and Gwen Bracqbien has applied to rezone a 12.5-acre parcel identified as Parcel X, a portion of Madison County Tax Map 50-55 on John Tucker Road, from Agricultural (A1) to Residential, Limited (R-1). The purpose of the rezoning is to allow the future development of approximately five to six detached single-family homes. Prepared and presented by: Allen Nicholls, Planning and Zoning Administrator ___ Application for Rezoning Case Number: RZ-09-26-01 Application Information Project Name: Bracqbien Rezoning Applicant: Karl and Gwen Bracqbien (property owner) Property Location: Portion of Tax Map 50-55 (final Tax Map number TBD) Total Parcel Acreage: 12.5 Acreage Proposed for Rezoning: 12.5 Zoning district: Agricultural (A-1) Proposed Zoning: Residential, Limited (R-1) Overview of Request The applicants propose to rezone an approximately 12.5-acre parcel on John Tucker Road from Agricultural (A-1) to Residential, Limited (R-1). The applicants’ stated intent is to subdivide the property into five or six residential lots of approximately two to 2.5 acres each and construct detached single-family homes. The proposed homes would be traditional, stick-built, single-story residences averaging approximately 1,200 square feet, with the possibility of attached one-car garages. The applicants Page 1 of 6 have stated that the homes would be retained under common ownership and operated as longterm rental housing rather than sold as individual speculative homes or used as short-term rentals. The submitted conceptual plan illustrates both five-lot and six-lot development options. Under either option, three lots would be located along John Tucker Road. The remaining lots would be accessed through an existing 50-foot access easement along the eastern side of the property. No formal subdivision plat or site development plan is under review at this time. The current request is limited to a zoning map amendment. The submitted conceptual plan illustrates the applicants’ current intentions but does not establish the final lot configuration, entrance locations, drainfield locations, building locations, or development yield. Any future subdivision would be subject to the Madison County Subdivision Ordinance, Virginia Department of Health approval, Virginia Department of Transportation requirements, privateroad standards, applicable road-maintenance agreement requirements, and all other applicable regulations. The applicants’ stated intention to retain the homes as long-term rentals is also not, by itself, a restriction imposed by the requested R-1 zoning. Unless incorporated into an enforceable voluntary proffer or other legally acceptable restriction, the ownership and rental status of the future homes could change without an additional rezoning. Site and Surrounding Area The subject property is identified as Parcel X on a division survey dated June 4, 2026. The survey depicts Parcel X as containing 12.500 acres and being separated from a larger parent tract formerly identified as Tax Map 50-55. The subject property fronts John Tucker Road, identified on the survey as State Route 614 with a 40-foot right-of-way. The parcel has substantial frontage along John Tucker Road and also adjoins an existing 50-foot access easement recorded in Plat Book 41, Page 14. The property is identified by the applicants as vacant or in agricultural use and appears to consist primarily of open land with wooded areas along portions of its perimeter. The surrounding area is rural in appearance but contains an established pattern of single-family residential development. Nearby properties include agricultural parcels, individual residences, and the Sheffield Way residential subdivision. Residential, Limited (R-1) zoning and residential lots of a size generally comparable to those proposed are present in the surrounding area. The subject property is not served by public water or public sewer. Each future lot would therefore require an approved individual well and septic system, including adequate area for both a primary and reserve drainfield. The availability of suitable well and septic locations has not Page 2 of 6 been established through the rezoning application and would be evaluated through the applicable Health Department and subdivision review processes. The conceptual plans show three proposed lots with access oriented toward John Tucker Road. Under the six-lot option, three additional lots would be served through the existing access easement. Under the five-lot option, two additional lots would use that access. Final entrance locations and configurations would be subject to VDOT and County approval. Procedural History & Public Notice Preliminary Development Review Committee A pre-application meeting was held at the July 7, 2026, meeting of the Preliminary Development Review Committee. Planning and Zoning Administrator Allen Nicholls recused himself from the Committee’s consideration of the case due to a close working relationship with the applicant. During this meeting, comments were made by stakeholders that included the following: VDOT: Matthew Mashhadi advised that, if the private-road entrance serves three parcels, the entrance would need to be constructed to VDOT low-volume commercial entrance standards. Final entrance design and permitting would be addressed during the subdivision and development process.. VDH: Emily Bourdon advised that the applicant would need to demonstrate adequate space for both a primary drainfield and a reserve drainfield for each proposed lot. Individual well and septic approvals would be required before development. Madison County Building Official: Jamie Wilks noted that the applicant is a County employee and stated that Mr. Wilks would personally handle the applicable official inspections and approvals to avoid the applicant’s involvement in the review of his own project. The Preliminary Development Review Committee recommended that the applicant submit a formal rezoning application for consideration by the Planning Commission. Planning Commission The rezoning application was received on August 20, 2026. First workshop scheduled for September 16, 2026. Advertising Advertising will occur in the Piedmont Journal prior to the anticipated November public hearing. Neighbor letters will be mailed prior to the anticipated November public hearing. Summary of Public Comment Page 3 of 6 At the time of this report, the Planning and Zoning Office has received no public comments regarding this case. Existing Zoning Context Key Provisions Provision Minimum Lot Area Minimum Frontage Front Setback Side Yard Rear Yard Height Limit Subdivision Limitations Agricultural (A-1) 3.0 Acres 250 Feet 50 feet (or 100 feet from centerline if ROW < 50 feet) 25 Feet 50 Feet 35 Feet No more than four lots (including residue) within any ten-year period Residential, Limited (R-1) 1.5 Acres w/o public water/sewer 150 Feet 35 feet (or 60 feet from centerline if ROW < 50 feet) 15 Feet 35 Feet 35 Feet w/conditional increases Up to 15 with private well and septic. No limit w/public water/sewer. Links to relevant ordinances: Agricultural (A-1) Zoning Ordinance Residential, Limited (R-1) Zoning Ordinance Analysis: Comprehensive Plan Alignment Madison County’s 2025 Comprehensive Plan emphasizes the preservation of agricultural lands and rural character, the protection of environmentally sensitive areas, and the orderly concentration of residential growth in and near the Town of Madison and established villages. The Plan also recognizes the need for additional housing opportunities, including housing for the local workforce and residents at different stages of life. The proposed rezoning would convert the entire 12.5-acre subject property from A-1 to R-1. The subject parcel is identified in the application as vacant and in agricultural use. Conversion of the parcel to residential use would represent a loss of agriculturally zoned land, but the relatively small acreage and the established residential pattern nearby reduce the potential conflict with the Plan’s broader agricultural-preservation objectives. The proposed density is greater than would ordinarily be expected under A-1 zoning, but it remains low in residential terms. The applicants’ five- and six-lot concepts would result in average lot sizes of approximately two to 2.5 acres. text: Agenda Board of Supervisors Tuesday, October 27, 2026, at 6:00 PM Administration Building Auditorium 414 North Main Street, Madison, Virginia 22727 Call to Order, Pledge of Allegiance & Moment of Silence Determine Presence of a Quorum/Adoption of Agenda Public Comment Consent Agenda 1. Building Auditorium, 414 N. Main Street MEETING #42 — October 13 At a regular meeting of the Board of Supervisors on Tuesday, October 13 at 4:00 PM in the Admin. Building Auditorium: PRESENT: Carty Yowell, Chairman James Jewett, Vice-Chairman Jud Buchanan, Member Mike Snider, Member Nancy Sharman, Member Hannon Wright, County Attorney Jonathon Weakley, County Administrator Brian Gordon, Deputy County Administrator Kimberly Turner, Deputy Clerk ABSENT: None. CALL TO ORDER, PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE & MOMENT OF SILENCE Chairman Yowell called the Board to order. The Pledge of Allegiance was recited, followed by a moment of silence. DETERMINE PRESENCE OF A QUORUM/ADOPTION OF AGENDA Chairman Yowell reported that all members were present and a quorum was established. No changes to the agenda were offered by staff or members. Supervisor Snider made a motion to adopt the agenda as presented, seconded by Vice-Chairman Jewett. Aye: Yowell, Jewett, Buchanan, Snider, Sharman. Nay: (0) Abstain: (0) Absent: (0). PUBLIC COMMENT Chairman Yowell opened the first public comment period. Annette Hyde: Annette Hyde, Radiant resident and chair of the Madison County Democratic Committee, thanked the Board for adopting a temporary sign policy for early voting on September 22 and urged the Board to adopt a clear, fair, and enforceable sign ordinance before the June 2027 primary election. She described concerns about campaign signs at the Administration Building, including signs she said exceeded the temporary policy, and stated that she asked Chairman Yowell and the County Administrator to have the additional signs removed. She said the signs were removed the following Monday. No other member of the public spoke. Chairman Yowell closed the public comment period and stated that another public comment period would be held at the end of the meeting. Return to Agenda CONSTITUTIONAL OFFICERS, COUNTY DEPARTMENTS, COMMITTEES & ORGANIZATIONS 1. Monthly Reports Chairman Yowell invited department heads and agency representatives to identify themselves and provide highlights or updates to their written reports. Economic Development and Tourism Economic Development & Tourism Director, Tracey Gardner, reported that she attended the regional commission’s annual awards dinner, where Lynn Graves received the governmental award, and that Secretary of Agriculture and Forestry, Katie Frazier, was the keynote speaker. The Economic Development & Tourism Director planned to attend the Governor’s Summit on Rural Prosperity and said she would provide updated travel and tourism website statistics at the next meeting. In response to a question, she said the Jack Shop Civil War Trail sign near the landfill had been replaced after being damaged and would remain at its existing location. Emergency Medical Services EMS Chief, Gavin Helme, reported 232 calls for the month and an average response time of 8 minutes, 33 seconds. Orange County sent two ambulances in response to one mutual-aid request; Madison County ultimately needed one. EMS recorded twenty-seven instances when no units were available (NUA), totaling approximately 16 hours and 58 minutes. EMS Chief Helme said the department was fully staffed and had accepted a new medic from Stafford County who was expected to begin in November. Animal Shelter Animal Shelter Manager, Annette Dodson, reported that United Painting had begun sanding the kennel surfaces and expected to paint them during the remainder of the week. At the Apple Harvest Festival, the shelter had adopted four dogs and held three raffles. Tad’s Pinball Challenge raised $1,150 for the shelter, and Alltech Systems donated an additional $500. The Animal Shelter Manager thanked C.E. Baker Holland for donating gravel and the Facilities & Maintenance Manager for spreading gravel and wood chips at the shelter, which improved visitor parking and moved county vehicles to the side of the building. Information Technology Information Technology (IT) Director, Alan Berry, reported that the county phone system had operated without voicemail or call-quality issues for about a month. The county had received 17 FOIA requests since the system went live approximately one month earlier; the IT Director did not have the Sheriff’s Office count. New projectors were installed and tested. The September anti-phishing campaign reached about half of users and had an average score of 92 percent. The IT Director was drafting a breach procedure protocol, a continuity of operations plan, and a three-year cybersecurity plan. He said planning for the cybersecurity work depended in part on Tyler Technologies’ unresolved direction for the county’s Munis system. Most county endpoints were purchased in FY2020; the IT Director estimated that forty would be at end of life by the end of FY2027. He said the first half of the FY2027 replacement plan covered approximately seven or eight machines, while firewalls, switches, and access points were current. In response to Return to Agenda a question, the IT Director said cloud hosting was preferred and that he was reviewing newer building inspection applications that might require an additional module. Human Resources Human Resources Manager, Tillie Strothers, reported that six employees received flu shots at the October 7 clinic held with the Orange County Pharmacy. Open enrollment for New York Life whole-life insurance was scheduled to begin October 27 and continue for about a month. Staff were working on employee evaluation forms. Animal Control Chief Animal Control Officer, Greg Cave, reported that calls for service had increased slightly while emergency calls had decreased. He clarified that an employee’s departure for the Navy could occur in two to six months. The Chief Animal Control Officer described the team’s rescue of Miley, a 14-year-old dog found weak beside a creek after being missing for more than a week; the team brought her up a steep embankment, and she was reunited with her owner. The Chief Animal Control Officer also reported that Jessica Kidd, Animal Control Officer, completed training through NACA and Humane World for Animals and attended equine safety training at Hope’s Legacy. In response to questions, the Chief Animal Control Officer explained that staff contact owners from a dog-tag lists to give them an opportunity to purchase county tags, which are separate from rabies tags and are now lifetime tags priced at $10. School Board School Board member, Mitch Dickey, reported that the School Board had a draft artificial intelligence policy and was exploring ways to raise funds to replace the field house. He invited the public to a school tour scheduled for 9:00 a.m. the upcoming Saturday so residents could see the schools. Parks and Recreation Parks and Recreation Manager, Jerry Carpenter, announced upcoming events at Hoover Ridge Park: a Friday evening event, “Music in the Park” with a food truck, and a Halloween Fest on Saturday, October 17, with children’s hayrides, other activities, and a free movie. He also announced “Haunted Woods” event for the following Saturday and invited volunteers to participate. Finance Finance Director, Jennifer Warren, reported that the finance dashboard had been updated through period three for most county operations; final School Board and Department of Social Services figures were still being collected. She expected to update those figures by the end of the week and noted that downloadable PDF reports were available from the dashboard. The FY2026 audit was scheduled for November 9 through November 20, with remote work during the first week and onsite work during the second week. CONSENT AGENDA 2. Approve Minutes: 09/08/2026, 09/22/2026, & 10/07/2026 3. Supplemental Appropriation #9 - CARP Fund - Facilities Mower Return to Agenda At the Chair’s direction, the October 7 minutes were considered separately because Supervisor Buchanan had been absent from that meeting. Vice-Chairman Jewett made a motion to approve the September 8 and September 22, 2026, minutes, seconded by Supervisor Sharman. Aye: Yowell, Jewett, Buchanan, Snider, Sharman. Nay: (0) Abstain: (0) Absent: (0). The Finance Director explained that the facilities mower was due for replacement after approximately ten years of service and that repair costs were too high. She recommended moving funds from the facilities capital roofing category to equipment rather than using contingency or fund balance. The County Administrator said the mower was a 2011 model with more than 1,800 hours. Chairman Yowell said the roofing allocation was not tied to a specific roof and supported the transfer. Supervisor Snider made a motion to approve Supplemental Appropriation #9, seconded by ViceChairman Jewett. Aye: Yowell, Jewett, Buchanan, Snider, Sharman. Nay: (0) Abstain: (0) Absent: (0). Supervisor Sharman made a motion to approve October 7, 2026, minutes, seconded by ViceChairman Jewett. Aye: Yowell, Jewett, Snider, Sharman. Nay: (0) Abstain: Buchanan. Absent: (0). SPECIAL APPEARANCES 4. Proposed Purchase Policy Amendments – Finance Director & Accounting Specialist Accounting Specialist, Mikayla Johnson, and Finance Director, Jennifer Warren, presented proposed revisions to the county purchasing policy following a review of the Virginia Public Procurement Act and current county policy. They identified the principal changes as increasing the small-purchase threshold from $2,500 to $5,000 and adding construction thresholds permitted by state law: up to $300,000 for non-transportation construction and $25,000 for transportation construction. The Finance Director said surrounding counties had adopted smallpurchase thresholds of $5,000 to $10,000. The Accounting Specialist said the small-purchase threshold would apply countywide to purchases requiring competition and described the county’s quote-tabulation and value-justification process. It was mentioned that the County Attorney has reviewed the proposed policy. Supervisor Buchanan made a motion to adopt the proposed purchasing policy amendments, seconded by Vice-Chairman Jewett. Aye: Yowell, Jewett, Buchanan, Snider, Sharman. Nay: (0) Abstain: (0) Absent: (0). PUBLIC HEARING None. OLD BUSINESS 5. Hoover Ridge Land Lease – County Administrator Return to Agenda The County Administrator reported that the county received two proposals in response to its September 8 request for proposals for approximately thirty-eight acres at Hoover Ridge that had been farmed under a lease ending in November. The proposals offered different approaches: one traditional crop lease and one involving conservation and planting. The County Administrator recommended that the Board defer selection to its second October meeting or appoint a small evaluation committee. The Board indicated that Chairman Yowell and Vice-Chairman Jewett would join the County Administrator in reviewing the proposals. The County Administrator said staff would coordinate their availability and return with a recommendation. 6. Brownfields Grants Request – County Administrator a. Resolution #2026-19 The County Administrator presented a revised resolution authorizing a brownfields grant application for one property, the farmhouse at 242 Madison Mills Lane, with a maximum request of $50,000. He said the estimated amount was $23,333.50, but the resolution would allow the applicant to seek up to the grant maximum. Any local match would be provided privately by the applicant, Ms. Miller, and the county would serve as the grant conduit. The County Attorney confirmed that the revised resolution limited the application to one property and allowed the applicant to seek the maximum amount available from the Department of Environmental Quality. He said funds would not be paid until the department approved of the application. *** RESOLUTION # 2026-19 BE IT RESOLVED, that Madison County wishes to apply for a Virginia Brownfields Restoration and Economic Redevelopment Assistance Fund (VBAF) Site Assessment and Planning Grant established pursuant to § 10.1-1237 of the Code of Virginia, for funds for site assessment of potential environmental problems at real property located at 214 and 242 Madison Mills Lane so that these privately owned properties can be effectively restored for new economic development prospects. WHEREAS, the two above named parcels are contiguous and owned by the same owners (currently David and Elizabeth Perdue) and previously had underground petroleum tanks on one property and an underground heating oil tank on the other, and the full details of their removal and residual impacts are unknown. There is also a structure built in the 1940s that may have lead paint and asbestos. WHEREAS, Diane Miller is hoping to purchase these two parcels and has applied for, and recently been granted, a Special Use Permit to operate a proposed private school that will offer cooking classes. In addition, her business proposal includes using the existing building as a general store. The economic development of these two parcels will benefit the County. WHEREAS, the Perdues and Diane Miller have expressed interest in the County applying for this VBAF grant for 242 Madison Mills Lane to reimburse Ms. Miller for the sums she is likely to expend for a Phase II environmental site assessment (estimated at $16,700) as well as an Return to Agenda Engineering Consulting Service Reliance Letter (estimated $500), and an asbestos and lead survey (estimated $6,133.50). The total for these services is estimated to be $23,333.50. WHEREAS, up to and including $50,000 in grant money is available through VBAF for site assessment and planning, and local matching funds are required by the VBAF Program. It is the County’s understanding and intention to apply for a grant and that Ms. Miller’s qualifying expenditures will serve as the local match funds satisfactory to the Virginia Resource Authority and Virginia Economic Develop Partnership, the entities that administer the VBAF Program. WHEREAS, it is the intention of the Board of Supervisors that Madison County will not expend any County money for this grant application, the various assessments, administering the grant, and/or serving as fiscal agent, but understands staff time will be required in this endeavor. NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the County Administrator is hereby authorized to sign and submit appropriate documents for the application for 242 Madison Mills Lane not exceeding $50,000 in qualifying VBAF Site Assessment and Planning Grant funds for the benefit of the Perdues and Ms. Miller and for the general benefit to the County of economic development of these two parcels. *** Supervisor Sharman made a motion to approve Resolution #2026-19 and authorized the County Attorney and County Administration to work with Ms. Miller to file the grant application, seconded by Supervisor Buchanan. Aye: Yowell, Jewett, Buchanan, Snider, Sharman. Nay: (0) Abstain: (0) Absent: (0). 7. Firefly VATI 2022 & 2024 Updates – County Administrator The County Administrator reviewed the county’s Virginia Telecommunications Initiative (VATI) broadband projects for 2022 and 2024, including areas covered, estimated passings, local-match commitments, and expenditures. He reported that the projects were expected to cover approximately 5,000 passings, with an assumed 60 percent take rate, or about 3,000 connections. The VATI 2022 project was substantially complete, with a few connections remaining; VATI 2024 was expected to close by the end of the calendar year, with approximately $43,122 remaining for invoices. After reconciling prior ARPA commitments and project costs, $222,264 remained available. The Board discussed whether to return the balance to the county’s fund balance or reallocate it. Vice-Chairman Jewett made a motion to direct the County Administrator to transfer the remaining broadband funds, $222,264, to the county’s fund balance, seconded by Supervisor Snider. Community Paramedicine 90 Day Review & RHTP Grant – Tiffany Rannebarger Captain of Community Paramedicine, Tiffany Rannebarger, presented a 90-day review of the community paramedicine program. She reported thirty-nine patient referrals, twenty-nine inperson visits, and twenty-four referrals to partner resources. She said an electronic referral form in the EMS reporting system, and a public QR code had helped streamline referrals. The program was using a risk-stratification score to prioritize visits and aimed to contact referred patients within 24 to 48 hours when circumstances allowed. Captain Rannebarger described the program’s work with social services, Encompass Community Supports, Hospice of the Piedmont, and other partners to address needs outside the program’s scope, including food, transportation, medication, and home-safety needs. She also reported installing five fall-alert devices and eight smoke alarms and purchasing six additional fall-alert devices. Mountain View donated $5,000 toward additional fall-alert devices. Captain Rannebarger described a complex patient case in which EMS and partner agencies coordinated follow-up care, medication access, food delivery, and household equipment. She said the program was also developing a regional mobile integrated health and community paramedicine work group and a workforce plan. She identified transportation, food access, and delays in Medicaid screening as continuing barriers. The Board asked about the program’s partners, outcomes, and methods for measuring changes in emergency calls and patient outcomes. Captain Rannebarger said the program was tracking before-and-after call patterns and longer follow-up periods to assess impact. Captain Rannebarger reported that the county had submitted a $261,454.67 Rural Health Transformation Program grant application before the October 6 deadline. Questions and discussion by Board members BOS Packet Page 3 BOARD OF SUPERVISORS REGULAR MEETING MINUTES September 1 , 2026 AT A MEETING OF THE MIDDLESEX COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS HELD ON TUESDAY, SEPTEMBER 1, 2026, IN THE BOARD ROOM OF THE HISTORIC COURTHOUSE, SALUDA, VIRGINIA: Present: Wayne H. Jessie, Sr., Jamaica District Don R. Harris, Saluda District Reginald A. Williams, Sr., Harmony Village District William A. Harris, Hartfield District Randy Crittenden, Pinetop District Kevin Gentry, County Administrator Heather W. Lewis, County Attorney Britney Bradley, Executive Assistant/Deputy Clerk CALL TO ORDER Chairman Don Harris called the meeting to order at 3:00 p.m. ROLL CALL Mrs. Bradley took attendance with the following roll call: Supervisor Williams Present. Supervisor Bill Harris Present; Supervisor Crittenden Present; Supervisor Jessie Present; and Chairman Don Harris Present. There was a quorum. Supervisor Williams led the group in prayer; Mrs. Bradley led in the Pledge of Allegiance. CONSENT AGENDA The Consent Agenda included approval of the September 1, 2026, meeting agenda; minutes from August 4, 2026, Regular Meeting; disbursements dated August 5, 2026, through September 1, 2026, 108765-108960 $745,411.51 and payroll dated August 14, 2026, $736,772.71. Supervisor Crittenden made a motion to approve the consent agenda, which was seconded by Supervisor Jessie. The following roll call carried the motion: Supervisor Bill Harris Aye; Supervisor Crittenden Aye; Supervisor Jessie Aye; Supervisor Williams Aye, and Chairman Don Harris Aye. PUBLIC COMMENT Chairman Don Harris opened the public comments period at 3:03 p.m. Mr. Keith Ruse, Lovers Lane, Deltaville, addressed the Board regarding the state dock on Jackson Creek in Deltaville. Mr. Ruse stated that his family owns and operates Deltaville Boatyard and that the state dock is important to commercial watermen for loading and unloading gear. He also stated that the dock is used for community events, including the Deltaville 5K and the Jackson Creek Cruise. Mr. Ruse stated that the dock requires regular maintenance and asked that the County and the state work toward maintaining the dock so that it can continue serving the community. Back to Agenda 1 BOS Packet Page 4 BOARD OF SUPERVISORS REGULAR MEETING MINUTES September 1 , 2026 Ms. Nancy Moore, Lovers Lane, Deltaville, also addressed the Board regarding the state dock. Ms. Moore stated that residents met with VDOT in October 2025 regarding the deterioration of the dock and were told that the dock was funded and scheduled for resurfacing. She stated that she later learned additional piling repairs may be needed before resurfacing could occur. Ms. Moore requested that, if VDOT wants Middlesex County to take control of the dock, the County consider requiring a legal agreement that VDOT complete the repairs previously discussed before any transfer occurs. Chairman Don Harris closed the public comment period at 3:09 p.m. CONSTITUTIONAL OFFICERS TREASURER: Report Only. COMMISSIONER OF REVENUE: Report Only. AGENCY AND STAFF REPORTS REASSESSMENT: Mr. Jason Cowan, with Cowan Services, LLC, addressed the Board regarding the 2027 became effective January 1, 2022, and that the reassessment will bring assessments back to current market value. He explained that this was a progress and market update, including what the residential market has done since the last reassessment, how the market was measured, and where the County stands today. Mr. Cowan stated that Cowan Services reviewed two independent measures: the Federal Housing Finance Agency House Price Index and a local MLS analysis completed by Cowan Services. He stated that the local sales analysis included 2,090 closed sales from January 2012 through August 2026 and 65 active and pending listings. The analysis showed that the market has increased roughly one-third since the current assessments took effect. Mr. Cowan reported that the FHFA index showed an increase of 38.0% in the 230xx ZIP code grouping and 36.4% in the 231xx ZIP code grouping from the fourth quarter of 2021 through the second quarter of 2026. He also reported that the local MLS market index showed a 29.9% increase for non-waterfront properties and a 32.6% increase for waterfront properties since January 1, 2022. Mr. Cowan reviewed current market conditions, including a median sale price of $429,900 during the last 12 months, 131 closed sales in the last 12 months, a median time of 82 days from listing to closing, and approximately six months of housing supply on the market. He stated that prices are still rising, but more slowly than in 2021 and 2022, and that the market is more balanced than it was three years ago. Back to Agenda 2 BOS Packet Page 5 BOARD OF SUPERVISORS REGULAR MEETING MINUTES September 1 , 2026 Mr. Cowan explained that the typical current assessment is approximately 64 cents for every $1.00 in market value, or approximately 36% below market value. He stated that this would require an approximate 57% increase to bring the typical assessment up to market value. He emphasized that a reassessment does not raise taxes by itself but redistributes the tax burden based on current market value, and that the Board of Supervisors sets the tax rate. Mr. Cowan stated that data collection is mostly complete, sales analysis is complete, valuation is underway, and review and quality control are upcoming. He stated that assessment notices are expected to be mailed to property owners in late November 2026, with informal review beginning in early December 2026. Property owners will be able to review their records, request a review, submit evidence, request a callback, or schedule an appointment. Mr. Cowan also reviewed the Board of Equalization process. He stated that the Board of Equalization is an independent citizen board appointed by the Circuit Court, separate from the assessor and the Board of Supervisors. The Board of Equalization may hear appeals from property owners who remain unsatisfied after informal review and may raise, lower, or affirm individual assessments. The Board discussed the reassessment process, possible impacts on taxpayers, the importance of clear communication with property owners, and the tax rate equalization process. No action was taken. VDOT: Report Only. SCHOOLS: Dr. Tracy Seitz addressed the Board regarding the one percent sales and use tax referendum for school capital projects and the proposed modernization of Middlesex High School. She stated that, after the Board approved the resolution to place the referendum on the November ballot, the school division began working to provide factual information to the community regarding the referendum and the high school project. Dr. Seitz stated that the proposed tax would not apply to food purchased for human consumption, essential personal hygiene products, or prescription medications. She stated that revenue from the tax could only be used for school construction and major renovation, and could not be used for salaries, textbooks, computers, or other school operating expenses. She also stated that the funds would be controlled by the Board of Supervisors and that, if approved, the tax would expire in July 2046. Dr. Seitz stated that the school division is providing information to the public and that a community meeting regarding the referendum and Middlesex High School modernization project is scheduled for September 15, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. at Middlesex High School. She stated that the meeting would include an overview of the information and an opportunity for community members to tour areas of the high school related to the proposed renovation and modernization project. Back to Agenda 3 BOS Packet Page 6 BOARD OF SUPERVISORS REGULAR MEETING MINUTES September 1 , 2026 Dr. Seitz also updated the Board regarding recent heavy rainfall and water issues at the high school gym. The Board discussed coordinating with the County Engineer and school staff to review the high school storm-drain system and determine whether the system should be camera-inspected for obstructions or damage. Dr. Dana Burnette also addressed the Board regarding the one percent sales and use tax referendum and the high school modernization project. Dr. Burnette spoke in support of the referendum as a potential funding source for school facility needs and stated that the referendum is not simply a vote about taxes, but about how Middlesex County could help pay for a school facility needed by the community for years to come. EDA MARKETING: Report Only. SOCIAL SERVICES: Report Only. NOISE ORDINANCE UPDATE: Ms. Dawn Moore addressed the Board regarding the Noise Ordinance Committee. Ms. Moore stated that the committee had completed three meetings and was making steady progress toward recommendations for the Board. She stated that one member, Wandra Thornton, had stepped down due to unforeseen circumstances. Ms. Moore stated that the committee unanimously decided not to elect a chairperson because members felt the committee was working well with Mr. Walker facilitating the meetings. She stated that the committee generally agrees that Middlesex County should have a limited noise ordinance focused on identifiable noise issues, while protecting ordinary rural and community activities. Ms. Moore stated that the committee believes the ordinance should be clear, understandable, and enforceable, and should avoid vague or subjective standards. She stated that the 2004 ordinance is being used as the starting point, but unclear or legally unenforceable provisions will need to be replaced. She also stated that the committee agreed to recommend one countywide noise standard, rather than separate standards by district or zoning area. Ms. Moore stated that warnings should remain an important enforcement tool and that the ordinance should focus on specific noise sources and conditions. She further stated that issues can be considered. Remaining work includes warnings and penalties, repeat violations, quiet hours, measurement or observation methods, and standards for specific noise sources. The committee hopes to complete its recommendations by October 2026, with staff preparing a revised ordinance for Board consideration in November or December. RCE BUILDING PROJECT: Mr. Chip England, County Engineer, addressed the Board regarding the RCE Building Back to Agenda 4 BOS Packet Page 7 BOARD OF SUPERVISORS REGULAR MEETING MINUTES September 1 , 2026 condition assessment completed by Raymond Global, Inc. Mr. England stated that the report included rough order of magnitude cost estimates for several options, including renovation, replacement, and demolition. The assessment identified several major building concerns, including roof failure, windows and doors beyond their useful life, stair-step cracking in masonry walls, mechanical, plumbing, and electrical systems beyond their useful life, restroom accessibility issues, and the need for additional hazardous-material and exterioraccessibility evaluation. Mr. England reviewed the general cost ranges for the available options. Renovation was estimated at approximately $2.3 million to $2.8 million, while replacement with a similar facility was estimated at approximately $3.1 million to $3.6 million. The Board discussed the condition of the building, the importance of addressing the roof to prevent further deterioration, possible future uses of the building, funding limitations, and whether the County should move toward renovation, roof replacement, or further planning. The Board also discussed the appearance of the building from the highway, including concerns regarding a three-phase power pole, and the need for community input and conceptual design work. Mr. England stated that the next steps could include developing draft scoping and obtaining a pre-proposal from Raymond Global for workshops or charrettes with community members and leaders to help determine the future use and design direction for the building. PAVEMENT IMPROVEMENTS: Mr. England addressed the Board regarding pavement improvements near the Courthouse Building. He stated that staff prepared and advertised an Invitation for Bids on July 22, 2026, to repave areas primarily around the Courthouse Building. Mr. England stated that bids were opened on August 13, 2026, and that six responsive bids were received. Mr. England stated that staff recommended awarding the contract to ProSeal in the amount of $161,931.25. He explained that the base bid areas around the main Courthouse Building were the priority areas, and that several smaller pavement areas would also be addressed while the contractor was mobilized. He stated that the contractor was expected to begin later in the month and would have 45 working days from notice to proceed to complete the work. Supervisor Williams asked whether the asphalt would be completely replaced or milled and replaced. Mr. England stated that approximately three inches of asphalt would be milled and replaced. Supervisor Williams made a motion to award the pavement improvements contract to ProSeal in the amount of $161,931.25, which was seconded by Supervisor Jessie. The motion was carried by the following roll call: Supervisor Jessie Aye; Supervisor Williams Aye; Supervisor Bill Harris Aye; Supervisor Crittenden Aye; and Chairman Don Harris Aye. The Board took a brief recess. REGULAR AGENDA ITEMS Back to Agenda 5 BOS Packet Page 8 BOARD OF SUPERVISORS REGULAR MEETING MINUTES September 1 , 2026 The Foundry: Ms. Beth Justice and Mr. Skip King addressed the Board regarding The Foundry Middlesex; a nonprofit Christian after-school program located in Topping. Ms. Justice stated that the program focuses on tutoring, life skills, character development, creativity, music, teamwork, leadership, and healthy choices. She stated that the program is growing and is looking for a larger facility with a kitchen and additional space for activities. Ms. Justice stated that The Foundry currently operates in an approximately 3,000square-foot building but would like to expand programming and provide additional opportunities for students, including basic cooking skills, music, outdoor activities, tutoring, and family events. She stated that the Free Shade Community Center had been discussed as a possible location because it has a kitchen, stage, and outdoor space. Mr. King thanked Mr. Johnny Fleet for his support and spoke about the positive impact The Foundry has had on local students. He stated that the program currently serves approximately 21 children and provides a safe and supportive environment. He also discussed the tutoring and mentoring efforts of the program and invited Board members to visit The Foundry. The Board discussed possible County-owned facilities and recreational areas that may be suitable for the program, including available outdoor recreation space. Mr. Gentry stated that staff could review options and determine what changes or improvements may be needed. The Board also discussed the current use of the Free Shade Community Center, including the free health clinic and other rentals. DOUGLASS, COLINTY ATTORNEY Chairman Collins calls the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Supervisor Ingram provides the invocation. Chairman Collins leads everyone in the Pledge of Allegiance. Approval of the Agenda: Supervisor Roark moves to approve the agenda. A second is provided by Vice Chairman Toth. Following a voice vote, the motion carries as follows: Ayes: Nays: Collins. Toth,Ingram, Roark. Green-Ausust None BES/Grace N Guidance Daycare: LaTonya Thompson and Danyal McCray of Grace N Guidance Child Care (GNG LLC) present a proposal to open a licensed childcare facility in the former Burkeville Elementary School building for children ages six weeks through grade 4. There is a shortage of dependable childcare, and the Burkeville location would be suitable for employees of nearby state facilities. Staff notes several suitable classrooms and possible playground space has been identified, and the County's insurance would cover children on site. The Board discussed the need for a Department of Education inspection and school transportation coordination. DSS Director Shannon Reed supported the proposal, citing documented need and expense. The Board notes other possible future uses for the Burkeville school building but directed staff to complete a preliminary inspection and improvement list. The Board expresses support for the applicants. Historic District: Catherine Douglass reports that Nottoway County has an existing historic overlay district which she is currently updating. It will be presented to the Planning Commission at its September meeting for their review. The Nottoway Historical Association is holding a Department of Historic Resources application for completion. Supervisor Ingram raised the issue of identifying and protecting historic graveyards, slave cemeteries, and culturally significant sites throughout the County. The consensus of the Board is to proceed with Ms. Douglass updating the Ordinance through the Planning Commission process. Then it will be presented to the Board for their review. 1 c-1 September 10,2026 Setback Vy'aiver: At their last meeting, Gregg Zody presented the Planning Commission a proposed Zoning Ordinance text amendment regarding setback waivers by the Board. The Planning Commission tabled the discussion and will consider it again in September. Given the discussion, }r4rr. Zody intends to revise the wording to limit the Board's setback waiver authority as cell towers, water towers, and County to public projects that require a2232 Review -such private The Planning Commission is an advisory projects-rather than applications. capital board, and the Board of Supervisors is under court order for a courthouse. The setbacks are particularly time-sensitive given the pending courthouse construction. GASB Statement No. 103: Finance Director Jennifer Carter presents GASB Statement No. 103 which mandates that the Board establish a threshold for disclosing significant budget-toactual variances in the County's annual financial statements. She recommends a threshold of $200,000, balancing transparency with practicality. The Board raised no objections to the recommended figure. Ms. Carter noted that formal adoption is required, so these matters will be advertised and placed on the agenda for a future meeting. She also informs the Board there will be public hearings at its special meeting. These are simple formalities for known expenses: budget amendments that require appropriation as well as the public safety radio project grant which exceeded the one-percent statutory threshold for a public hearing. Social Services Bonus: Chairman Collins opened discussion on a proposed ordinance to authorize bonuses for state-related employees. Finance Director Carter presents the figures for consideration. For most state-related offices, the local match can be covered by that department's budget, creating no financial impact to the County. DSS Director Shannon Reed has received an extension on the State deadline of October 6 for the Board to reconsider its previous denial. Whether to grant the bonus to all County employees or only those with State reimbursements was undecided. Supervisor Roark moves to advertise for an Ordinance to pay a one-time bonus. A second is provided by Vice Chairman Toth. Following a voice vote, the motion carries as follows: Ayes: Nays: Collins, Toth,Ingram, Roark. Green-Ausust None The Board fuither agreed to hold a special meeting on September 30, 2026, at 7:00 p.m. in lieu of the October 8th work session, when it will conduct these public hearings. Residential Lot Size in Agriculture and Conservation: Vice Chairman Toth raised the topic of reducing the minimum residential lot size requirement in Agriculture and Conservation zoning districts, currently set at five acres, suggesting a reduction to two or three acres. He notes that the five-acre requirement often results in large tracts of unusable residual land when a parcel is subdivided. Discussion brought out things for consideration, such as protections on residual 2 c-1 September 10,2026 agricultural land, limitations related to family subdivision rules, well and septic capacity, and consistency with the County's Comprehensive Plan goal of maintaining Nottoway's rural character. The Board defened the item to a future work session as further discussion is needed. Board & Community Committee Assignments: Chairman Collins advised that the departure of Supervisor Norton left vacancies on the boards for Piedmont Senior Resources and Crossroads. Supervisor Norton served on the Finance Committee, but that will not meet again until after the new year, and Board committee appointments will be made at the January organizational meeting. Supervisor Green-August is willing to serve on these two community boards, and the Board is agreeable. Formal appointment is forthcoming. EMS/Firefighter: Supervisor Roark raised concerns about efficiency, cost, and tensions between the County's two EMS agencies. He said the County's immediate goal should remain consistent staffing of three 2417 ambulances and cautioned against placing ambulances at all three fire stations. Emergency Services Director Buddy Hyde clarified that a fourth ambulance was previously discussed as a peak-hour unit, not a full-time 24ll unit. The pending expiration of the FASTC contract for Nottoway Rescue was discussed as was competition between the two agencies for personnel. The Board agreed to schedule a work session with both EMS agencies and the fire chiefs to discuss the County's EMS sttucture and long-term direction. Convenience Centers: Supervisor Roark mentions missed site visits to see Buckingham County's automated convenience center system. These will be rescheduled. Administrator Bowen notes that an automated system would require separate entrance and exit lanes. Discussion focused on a phased plan: install an automated unmanned convenience center at the Route 723 site first, as it is the County's busiest, and potentially close lower-traffic manned sites Investigation ofcosts and further consideration is needed before the next budget cycle. Mandatory Country of Origin Labeling for Beef: Vice Chairman Toth presents background on the federal policy allowing importation of foreign beef without mandatory country of origin labeling (MCOOL) and notes that Congress is scheduled to vote soon to decide on reinstatement of labeling. He expressed concern about the impact on both consumers and American cattle producers. He proposed the Board formally contact its congressional representatives asking for their support for mandatory labeling. Vice Chairman Toth makes a motion to authorize the County to draft and send a letter to the County's three Congressional representatives asking for their support for mandatory country of origin labeling (COOL) for beef. A second was provided by Supervisor Roark. Following a voice vote, the motion carries as follows: Ayes: Nays: Collins, Toth,Ingram, Roark. Green-August None Saint Paul's Technical Center: Administrator Bowen reports that discussions are ongoing regarding a potential Saint Paul's Technical Center in Lawrenceville. This would be in partnership with the Newport News Shipbuilding to provide workforce training in skilled trades J c-1 September 10,2026 such as welding. The concept would allow local students to remain in the area, receive technical training, and be hired directly by the shipyard upon completion. The Russell Middle School building in Lawrenceville is being considered for renovation as the facility site, though Brunswick County's School Board has not yet transferred the property. Bowen noted that Nottoway County schools have received inquiries from students interested in the program. At this stage, no financial commitment has been requested-only an indication of partnership interest. The Board expressed support for continuing discussions. Also noted was a meeting with Dr. Quentin Jones of Southside Virginia Community College discussing dual enrollment opportunities and aproposed "Promise" program that would cover community college costs for eligible high school students. Comments from the Board: Vice Chairman Toth clarifies his issue with MCOOL is the right of American consumers to know the origin of the beef products they consume. Supervisor Ingram expressed enthusiasm for the Grace N Guidance childcare proposal, noted personal conflict with providing a bonus to some but not others, and emphasized the need for a constructive work session with Fire and EMS. Supervisor Green-August expressed support for the Grace N Guidance proposal, the location maximizing help to citizens near the Burkeville food pantry. She also supports the need for a joint EMS/fire work session. She expressed enthusiasm for the Saint Paul's Technical Center partnership given her experience assisting students who are seeking welding training. BACKGROUND/REQUEST: Hershell Knott Jr. has requested a Pump and Haul Permit for property located off Battlecreek Road, Stanley, VA, and further identified by tax map number 69-A-86. The property contains approximately 0.36 acres and contains an existing dwelling that was partially destroyed by a house fire approximately 20 years ago. According to Jeff Mason with the Page County Health Department, the Health Department conducted a site evaluation of the property to determine whether a suitable area was available for installation of an onsite sewage disposal system to serve the dwelling. Based on the site evaluation, the required minimum setback of 100 feet from the existing well located on the adjacent property at 1119 Battlecreek Road, together with the location of the existing cistern on the subject property, substantially limits the area available for an onsite sewage disposal system. Additionally, the northern portion of the property contains a drainage way that is subject to receiving surface water runoff. Based on these site conditions, the Page County Health Department has determined that there is no suitable area on the property for installation of either a conventional or alternative onsite sewage disposal system. As a result, Mr. Knott is requesting authorization to pursue a Pump and Haul Permit for the property. The proposed system will utilize a 2,000-gallon sewage holding tank equipped with an alarm feature. Under the Virginia Department of Health regulations governing alternative sewage systems, issuance of a special pump-and-haul permit requires concurrence from the applicable local governing body. The Virginia Department of Health is responsible for issuance of the permit and for determining compliance with the applicable state requirements. STAFF COMMENTS: A copy of the proposed monitoring contract is attached for review by the Board. The Board will need to make a decision on the following items mentioned in the contract: Duration of Contract- The Board will need to decide on what the duration of the permit will be. The last one the Board approved in 2018 was approved for five years. “No longer than ___ years from date, with no automatic right of renewal. Should property ownership be sold or transferred to someone other than the above listed, this permit shall be considered void.” System Pumping Frequency- The Board will need to decide on how often the system must be pumped. The Health Department would require “as needed”. “Pumping of the system is required every ___ days from the time the system is operational, or more frequently, if necessary.” System Monitoring- The Board will need to decide on how often the system will need to be monitored. Staff would recommend the pumping frequency and monitoring have the same time frame. “The system will be monitored by the sewage handler every ___ days. A monitoring report will be submitted by the sewage handler to the Page County Health Department within 24 hours of monitoring on forms provided by the Page County Health Department or as that department may otherwise direct.” MOTION(S): I move that the Page County Board of Supervisors concur with the issuance of a Pump and Haul Permit for Mr. Knott’s property subject to the applicant submitting the required “Pump and Haul of Sewage Monitoring Contract” and a copy of the contract with the sewage disposal handler to Page County and any other requirements deemed necessary prior to issuance of the permit by the Page County Health Department. OR I move that the Page County Board of Supervisors decline to concur with the issuance of the requested Pump and Haul Permit for Mr. Knott’s property. OR I move an alternative motion.
