PRESENT: ABSENT: SECRETARY: STAFF: COUNTY ATTORNEY: OTHERS: TOM BEEBE, ADAM SANDRIDGE, ANTHONY SUBRIZI, JAY MELVIN DAVID WHITMORE CHRIS SLAYDON JASON TYREE, NEIL WHITMORE, VIVECA HANSON JOHN DRYDEN * * * * * Mr. Beebe called the meeting to order at 7:00 pm and conducted the following verbal roll call: Mr. Subrizi – present, Mr. Melvin - present, Mr. Sandridge – present, Mr. Whitmore – absent, Mr. Beebe – present. Mr. Beebe reviewed that, in addition to being physically present and participating in the meeting, citizens had the opportunity to join the meeting remotely, via Zoom or phone. The instructions for both remote options were available on the County website. Those wishing to view the meeting, live or after the fact, could do so on the Rockbridge Planning Commission YouTube channel, also linked on the County website. * * * * * The second item on the agenda was the citizen comment period. Mr. Beebe asked if there was anyone physically present that had signed up to comment. Mr. Slaydon said there was no one that had signed up. Mr. Slaydon allowed time for those participating remotely to raise their hands. There were no remote comments. * * * * * The third item on the agenda was a review of the minutes from the August 12, 2026 Planning Commission meeting. Mr. Beebe asked if the Commissioners had the opportunity to review the minutes as submitted, and if there were any questions or comments. At 7:02 pm, Mr. Sandridge made a motion to approve the minutes as submitted. Mr. Subrizi seconded the motion. The motion was approved unanimously. * * * * * 1 The fourth item on the agenda was report of the board and committee actions that had taken place since the previous Planning Commission meeting. Mr. Whitmore reported that the following had taken place: - At its meeting on August 24, 2026, the Board of Supervisors reviewed and approved the application by Castle Christian School to develop and operate a private school in the A-2 zoning district, as recommended by the Planning Commission. - Neither the TCO Board nor the Board of Zoning Appeals met during the previous month. - The Community Development Committee met on August 17th and discussed the agenda items of the past Planning Commission meeting and upcoming Board of Supervisors meeting. * * * * * The fifth item on the agenda was a discussion pertaining to potential future zoning text amendments. The first potential zoning text amendment reviewed pertained to the use of accessory dwelling units (ADUs). Mr. Whitmore briefly reviewed recent changes to the Code of Virginia, which necessitate changes to the current zoning regulations relating to ADUs. Senate Bill 531, introduced during the 2026 Legislative session and signed by the Governor on April 13, 2026, and is set to take effect on July 1, 2027. Mr. Whitmore explained that the amended law required localities to provide for the use of an ADU as an accessory to a dwelling in the Residential Zoning Districts. In review of the change to State Code, staff researched the regulations of nearby localities and how they allow for the use, and assembled the findings, the results of which were included in the Planning Commission package. Mr. Beebe said he had previously spoken with Mr. Slaydon regarding the change to State Code and noted that it pertains specifically to residential zoning districts. However, similar regulations for other zoning districts could also be reviewed. Mr. Slaydon discussed that the Residential Zoning districts make up a very small portion of the County, at only about 1.5 percent of the total area. It was reviewed that there had been previous discussions about incorporating provisions for ADUs into the County Code, and many of the inquiries that the Office of Community Development receive regarding ADUs pertain to the Agricultural zoning districts. Mr. Slaydon said that Agricultural zoning districts comprise approximately 72 percent of the County. Mr. Subrizi asked if ADUs were permitted in any district, besides garage apartments. Mr. Slaydon said that was correct. It was discussed that the potential regulations pertaining to ADUs could be placed in the section of the County Code pertaining to additional dwellings on a single lot, where the regulations for garage apartments/dwelling are currently situated in the Code. The recent amendment to the State Code pertaining to the use of accessory dwelling units, in Chapter 895 of the Acts of Assembly, was shown on the screen. Mr. Slaydon reviewed that the amendment contained regulations that localities are required to implement, regulations that localities may choose to implement, and those that a locality shall not require. Mr. Slaydon pointed out that Section 3(D) of the amendment pertained to the Regulations that a locality may choose to require. 2 Mr. Subrizi asked if the review of the amendment could begin earlier in the Section. It was noted that, although Chapter 30 of the County Code (Zoning Ordinance) contains definitions for dwelling and dwelling unit, it does not have a definition for an Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU). Mr. Subrizi pointed out that within the text of Chapter 895 of the Acts of Assembly, Accessory Dwelling Unit or ADU is defined as “an attached or detached dwelling unit on a residential dwelling lot…” Mr. Subrizi asked if the aforementioned definition would be interpreted as referring only to lots within a residential zoning district. Mr. Slaydon said that further on in the text of the amendment, it states that it pertains to “zoning ordinances for single-family residential zoning districts…” It was discussed that this language differed from that seen in the previously reviewed section of State Code pertaining to manufactured homes, which stated that it applied to any zoning district that allowed for single family dwellings. Therefore, Mr. Slaydon said Chapter 895 was interpreted as pertaining specifically to the residential zoning districts. Mr. Subrizi asked if in the current zoning ordinance, placing a garage apartment/dwelling would require a special exception permit. Mr. Slaydon said no; a garage apartment/dwelling was a by-right use. Mr. Beebe asked if that pertained only to the agricultural zoning districts. Mr. Slaydon said no; it pertained to residential and agricultural zoning districts. Mr. Subrizi asked if a second dwelling could just be placed in the backyard of a property. Mr. Slaydon discussed that he thought it was unusual that an attached dwelling unit was included in the definition of an ADU in the amended State Code, as there is little differentiation between a duplex and a single-family dwelling with an attached ADU. Mr. Subrizi said that an attached ADU would be more limited in size than a duplex. Mr. Slaydon clarified that a locality could opt to limit the size of an ADU, per State Code. Mr. Slaydon reviewed that the County Code currently allows for second dwelling on a single lot, but it has to meet the area and setback requirements and be placed such that the lot could be subdivided in the future. In the Agricultural zoning districts, for example, adding a second dwelling to a single lot would require a minimum of four acres, a minimum of 100 feet between the two dwellings to meet the internal setbacks, and meet the setbacks from the exterior property lines. Additionally, Mr. Slaydon said that the County added provisions for a garage apartment/ dwelling, which allows for decreased internal setbacks between structures. Mr. Subrizi said that as someone who lives in a residential area, he was not enthusiastic about allowing for such use. Mr. Slaydon clarified that the zoning text amendment was required due to the change in State Code. Mr. Subrizi said he could see the benefit of ADUs for those such as young professionals or elderly relatives. However, Mr. Subrizi said he was concerned about an ADU being able to be placed on the small lots of a residential zoning district, such as a half an acre property. Mr. Melvin noted that the State Code was mandating such provisions. Mr. Subrizi said that State Law gave localities some leeway in their regulations, and he was interested in determining how restrictive such an ordinance could be, in order to minimize potential problems. Mr. Slaydon reviewed the section of Chapter 895 pertaining to the requirements which localities could choose to put in place. The first of these potential requirements was a lease term 3 for the rental of the ADU of 30 consecutive days or longer. Mr. Slaydon explained that staff had previously discussed the implementation of such a regulation, prior to its inclusion in the amended State Code. It was discussed that the current Zoning Regulations for the County prohibit whole-house short-term rentals in any Residential Zoning district. However, long-term whole-house rentals, consisting of 30 days or longer, are permitted in these zoning districts. Mr. Slaydon said that there would be merits to prohibiting short-term rentals in ADUs, particularly relating to the need for affordable housing options and increased housing stock. Mr. Subrizi asked if short-term and long-term rentals were already defined in the ordinance. Mr. Slaydon said yes. Mr. Subrizi asked if the division between short- and long-term rentals was more than or less than 30 days. Mr. Slaydon said that a rental of 30 days or more is considered a long-term rental, and anything less than 30 days is considered a short-term rental. Mr. Subrizi pointed out that the State Law allowed localities to enact a requirement for renting 30 days or longer, and as such, the period associated with the regulation put in place by a locality could be greater than 30 days. Mr. Subrizi provided an example that he was aware of some residences that lease to students that require a twelve-month lease. Mr. Slaydon clarified that the lease term could be anything over 30 days. Mr. Subrizi said that if the lease term of 30 days has worked for other localities, it could work for the County. It was added that an ADU would likely only accommodate a few people because of their smaller size. Mr. Slaydon discussed that, if such a regulation pertaining to the length of rental for an ADU were implemented by the Board of Supervisors, it would not prevent a landowner from moving into the ADU and short-term renting the main dwelling. Mr. Subrizi asked if there was anything a locality could do to prevent such a situation. Mr. Slaydon said no, not under the current statute. However, that scenario would not be possible in the Residential zoning districts because whole-house short-term rentals are not allowed under the current zoning regulations. Mr. Subrizi asked if a regulation for that scenario was already in place. Mr. Slaydon said yes; there are more restrictive measures in the residential zoning district than in the agricultural zoning districts. Mr. Slaydon asked if there was a consensus of the Planning Commission pertaining to a potential restriction on the length of rental for an ADU. Mr. Beebe asked if the City of Lexington also defines long-term rentals as greater than 30 days. Mr. Whitmore said that, based on research, the City of Lexington places restrictions on the size of an ADU more than the number of days. It was noted that the City has extensive language in their Code pertaining to ADUs, particularly in the historic districts. Mr. Subrizi noted that, according to the change in State Code, any regulations pertaining to ADUs that a locality had in place prior to January 1, 2026, could remain in place. Mr. Beebe said he believed the goal of the amendment to State Code was to increase housing supply, and additional short-term rentals, if ADUs were allowed to be used for that purpose, would not help with that goal. Mr. Beebe said he was in favor of a 31-day requirement. Mr. Dryden said his original interpretation of the code section was that it was provided so that localities would have the ability to prevent short-term rentals. However, in hearing Mr. 4 Subrizi’s interpretation of the Code pertaining to the length of stay, he thought a locality may have the option to set a length of stay with a number of days greater than 30. Mr. Dryden said that upon further discussion, he believed that the intent of the provision, however, seemed to be to allow localities to prohibit short-term rentals. As such, there may be an issue with changing the number of days to anything greater than 30. Mr. Subrizi said he thought that the typical long-term rental would have a lease period of twelve months. Mr. Dryden said in some instances, particularly for students, the lease term may be nine months. Mr. Subrizi asked if a nine-month lease would be considered long-term. Mr. Slaydon said yes. Mr. Dryden confirmed that any rental term greater than 30 days would not be considered short-term, per the definitions of the Regulations. Mr. Subrizi said that he wanted to put restrictions in place on potential rental uses in Residential zoning districts, while allowing ADUs for in-law suites or for use by young professionals. Mr. Dryden reminded that localities do not have the ability to restrict who could utilize an ADU. Mr. Subrizi said he was aware, but increasing the term of rental for a short-term rental would discourage some uses of ADUs. Mr. Dryden said he would want to do research to see if it is possible to extend the use requirements of ADUs beyond 30 days. Mr. Subrizi said that a rental term of one year might be considered. Mr. Dryden said he would need to perform additional research. Mr. Subrizi said he would be fine with a 30-day period. Mr. Dryden agreed that the language of the Code was 30 days or more. Mr. Subrizi said that most apartments would not be rented for any less than one year. Mr. Dryden said he believed the provision in State Code was intended to address shortterm rental use, but he was unsure if there were merits to requiring a longer lease term than 30 days. Mr. Beebe said it seemed there was consensus amongst the Planning Commissioners to avoid the use of ADUs as short-term rentals. It was discussed that prohibiting short-term rentals of ADUs would prevent a bed and breakfast situation. Mr. Beebe said he could see extending the minimum stay requirement a bit, perhaps by a month, but did not feel any longer of a period was necessary. Mr. Sandridge pointed out that the owner of a property has discretion of how long an ADU would be leased for. Mr. Beebe said that if a longer lease period were possible, he would suggest not setting a limit of more than three to six months. Mr. Dryden said he would be happy to research the question on rental terms. Mr. Subrizi discussed that keeping the limit of 30 days would allow, for example, a visiting professional working in the area to have a place to stay during their job commitment. Mr. Slaydon gave an example of traveling nurses. Mr. Beebe said he was fine with a period of 30 days, but Mr. Dryden could still do additional research. Mr. Dryden said he will take a closer look at the provisions. 5 Mr. Beebe asked if there was a consensus for moving forward. Mr. Melvin suggested allowing time for Mr. Dryden to do additional research before deciding. The next requirements that localities could choose to require, as provided by State Code, are related to parking for an ADU. The provisions were read as follows: “Replacement of a primary dwelling’s required parking if the construction of the ADU eliminates such parking,” and “dedicated parking for ADU.” Mr. Slaydon discussed that the current regulations for oneand two-family dwellings require two parking spaces for each dwelling unit. Mr. Subrizi asked what qualifications are required for parking spaces. Mr. Slaydon said there is a square footage requirement for the size of a parking space. Mr. Subrizi gave the example of a single-family dwelling with three existing parking spaces and asked if they would be able to add an ADU without needing additional parking. Mr. Slaydon said yes. Utt Lisa Richardson Clegg Williams October 5, 2026 To: Members, Smyth County Board of Supervisors CC: Smyth County Leadership Team From: Shawn Utt, County Administrator RE: Packet summary – October 8th, 2026 Board meeting Below are summaries related to specific agenda items. Should additional information become available, we will provide as quickly as possible: 1. Call to Order, Pledge of Allegiance & Invocation: The pledge of allegiance will be led by the Emergency Services department. The invocation will be provided by a local pastor. 2. Amendments to the Agenda: if any are necessary, they will be presented at the meeting. 3. Minutes of Previous Meeting(s): draft copies of the minutes of the September 24th, 2026 meeting, September 28, 2026 reconvened meeting are enclosed (Att. 1, pg. 5-11 and Att. 2, pg. 12-14) for the Board’s review and approval. 4. Presentations: a. Smyth Strong Citizen Award – The Hurricane Helene Recovery Committee would like to recommend a citizen for the Smyth Strong Citizen Award due to his tireless efforts of helping to get a veteran the services and assistance his family desperately needed. We will have the recipient as well as the family members and committee members at the meeting for the presentation. b. Draft Ordinance Proposals – The Commonwealth Attorney (Phillip Blevins) and Sheriff (Chip Shuler) will be at the meeting to discuss proposed ordinances related to the following: i. ii. iii. iv. Custody & Visitation Violations Controlled Substances Disorderly Conduct Obstruction of Justice For your review and information, Mr. Blevins has provided the enclosed (Att. 3, pg. 15-19) drafts. Smyth County Board of Supervisors ~ 121 Bagley Circle, Suite 100 ~ Marion, VA 24354 Ph. (276) 783-3298 | Fax (276) 783-9314 | www.smythcounty.org 2 c. DSS Foster Family Presentation – Ms. Leanna Doss with the Smyth County Department of Social Service’s Foster Care program will be at the meeting to give a brief presentation on the need for additional foster care families. For your information, she has provided the enclosed (Att. 4, pg. 20) brochure. 5. Public Hearings: None. 6. Financial Status Report – The monthly revenue and expenditure reports will be presented at the board meeting due to timing of the meeting. 7. Payment of Invoices/Accounts Payable – The semi-monthly accounts payable listing is enclosed (Att. 5, pg. 21-29) for the Board’s review and acceptance. Since this set of A/P includes expenses for Fund 303 (CDBG Project), we would like to request a supplemental appropriation in the amount of $171,795.50 for Fund 303. 8. Citizen’s Time – Time has been set aside for citizens to provide comments to the Board on general items of interest or concern. 9. Old Business Items: a. Committee Reports/Recommendations i. Budget Committee – minutes of the September 29th budget committee meeting are enclosed (Att. 6, pg. 30-31) for your review and information. 10. New Business Items: a. Blue Ridge Discovery Center VDOT Permit Request: The Blue Ridge Discovery Center (BRDC) is working on the next phase of their development with the redevelopment of the former fueling stations and store at the corner of Whitetop Road and Konnarock Road. As a part of the project, they need to extend sewer service from their property to their sewer treatment plant to was built as part of the original building project. This will require a crossing of Whitetop Road and thus requires a VDOT permit. For your review and consideration, we have used a template provided by VDOT to create the enclosed (Att. 7, pg. 32) resolution. This would authorize the necessary actions to move the project forward. All costs associated by the project (including the construction and upkeep) will be borne by the BRDC. b. Budget Amendment #2 – for the Board’s review and consideration, enclosed (Att. 8, pg. 33-34) is a resolution and supporting exhibit outlining the proposed Budget Amendment #2. It has the following items included: i. TRIAD Grant for the Commonwealth’s Attorney - $2,500 ii. Junior Commonwealth Attorney Program (JCAP) grant for the Commonwealth’s Attorney, funded by Wellspring Foundation - $2,000 iii. Kinship Navigator Grant through DSS - $301,259 (fully funded program with no local match required) iv. CDBG Disaster Recovery Grant - $155,000 (fully funded program with no local match required) 3 v. Move OAA funds from General Fund to new Fund 240 (OAA Cooperative Grants and Recovery Court Grant) and Fund 241 (Direct Distribution Funds) – revenue neutral The total budget amendment is $504,191 and results in an overall budget total of $149,026,901. 11. Report from County Attorney: Time has been reserved on the agenda to allow the County Attorney to provide input and various updates as needed. 12. Report from County Administrator/Staff: Time has been reserved on the agenda to allow the County Administrator and/or staff to provide input and various updates as needed. 13. Supervisor Comment Time: Roundtable discussion for individual Board members. 14. Closed Session 4 Attachment 1 The Smyth County Board of Supervisors held its regular meeting on Thursday, September 24, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. The location of the meeting was in the Auditorium of the Marion Senior High School, 848 Stage Street, Marion, Virginia. PRESENT: Atkins District Supervisor Charles Atkins Chilhowie District Supervisor Mike Sturgill North Fork District Supervisor Rick Billings Park District Supervisor Kristopher Ratliff Royal Oak District Supervisor Courtney Widener Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris Saltville District Supervisor Roscoe Call ABSENT: None STAFF: County Administrator Shawn Utt Asst. County Administrator – Operations, Lisa Richardson Asst. County Administrator – Development, Clegg Williams Zoning Administrator Becca Creasy County Attorney Scot Farthing OTHERS: Smyth County School Board members and staff Hunter Wilson, ZMM Architects David Rose and Harrison Monette, Davenport & Company Smyth News & Messenger and approximately 45 citizens 09/24/2026 5:08 PM Chair, Atkins District Supervisor Charles Atkins called the meeting to order and welcomed everyone and noted the first part of the meeting would be a joint presentation with the Smyth County School Board regarding the Schools Facilities Study. 09/24/2026 5:08 PM County Administrator, Shawn Utt, led the pledge of allegiance. Stephanie Porter-Nichols led the invocation. 09/24/2026 5:10 PM Chair, Atkins District Supervisor Charlie Atkins moved on to presentations. 09/24/2026 5:10 PM Smyth County Schools Facilities Study Presentation - Mr. Hunter Wilson from ZMM, Architects & Engineers, presented the results of a building needs assessment conducted for Smyth County Schools. The full study consists of more than 1,300 pages and included a review of the project summary, building’s condition summary, project estimates, and enrollment analysis. He provided a focus on the Marion Senior High School since that was where the meeting was being held and noted the need for a variety of maintenance and safety repairs and upgrades. The total cost for all necessary school repairs, system wide, was in excess of $216m. 09/24/2026 5:35 PM Saltville District Supervisor Roscoe Call mentioned Oak Point Elementary School and questioned why the development did not provide the anticipated relief to the schools that had been projected when it was considered. Mr. Wilson noted his study only covered the existing conditions of the structures and not a historic look-back and it would be up to the School Board to decide on future uses of the buildings. 09/24/2026 5:40 PM 1% Sales Tax Presentation - David Rose with Davenport & Company provided both Boards with an overview of the financing options available for the necessary school 5 improvements, including revenue estimates associated with the proposed additional 1% sales tax should the public referendum be approved in the November election. Mr. Rose noted that approximately 30% of the revenue generated by the additional 1% sales tax would come from nonresidents, including visitors and travelers along I-81. It was also noted that approximately one-third of the initial project costs ($9.4m) for the proposed high school repairs/additions have already been funded through state grants, with financing needed for the remaining costs ($21.6m). If approved, the additional 1% sales tax would take effect in May 2027, with the revenue able to be held and earn interest until needed. The funds would be restricted to use on school-related projects. He projected that the 1% sales tax could result in an initial annual revenue of $2.6m, which could support $37m in debt capacity. He also noted he would continue to work with County and School staff should the referendum be successful in November. 09/24/2026 6:17 PM With no further questions or comments from either Board, School Board Chair Susan Williams adjourned the School Board meeting, while Board of Supervisors Chair Charles Atkins recessed the Board of Supervisors meeting to relocate to the library for the remainder of the meeting. 09/24/2026 6:28 PM Board of Supervisors Chairman Charles Atkins called the meeting back to order in the school’s library. 09/24/2026 6:28 PM Minutes of September 10, 2026, meeting: After further discussion, the following motion was made:  A motion was made by Saltville District Supervisor Roscoe Call to approve September 10, 2026, meeting minutes. Royal Oak District Supervisor Courtney Widener seconded this motion. After consideration, the motion PASSED by the following vote: AYES: Chair, Atkins District Supervisor Charles Atkins; North Fork District Supervisor Rick Billings; Park District Supervisor Kristopher Ratliff; Royal Oak District Supervisor Courtney Widener; Saltville District Supervisor Roscoe Call. NAYS: None. ABSTAINERS: Vice Chair, Chilhowie District Supervisor Michael Sturgill; Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris. ABSENT: None. 9/24/2026 6:29 PM Budget Reduction Update – County Administrator Shawn Utt reported that, as discussed at the September 10 meeting, a budget reduction memorandum had been issued to all County departments, agencies, and organizations receiving County funding, requesting reductions of 5–10%. The range was expanded from the originally proposed 5% after identifying areas where additional reductions may be possible. Mr. Utt further reported that he has had discussions with 27 of the 50 affected entities, with approximately 20 having presented proposed budget reductions. Discussions with the volunteer fire departments were ongoing, with additional meetings scheduled. Staff are also working on correcting revenue projections and incorporating the recommended expenditure reductions into a revised budget. Other items being reviewed include restructuring existing debt and outstanding grant reimbursements, including issues involving several constitutional offices. A revised budget incorporating the proposed changes is expected to be presented to the Board at its October meeting. Mr. Utt noted that a public hearing would not necessarily be required unless the 6 Board wished to schedule one. He further noted that the County’s financial situation would require a long-term change in approach and would not be resolved within a month or two. 09/24/2026 6:34 PM North Fork District Supervisor Rick Billings asked about the management of County grants and whether adequate oversight was in place to ensure reimbursements and required quarterly reports were submitted. County Administrator Shawn Utt confirmed that grants are assigned for management but noted the need for consistent oversight and follow-through, particularly regarding reimbursement requests and reporting requirements. Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris discussed the importance of addressing both the administrative and compliance aspects of grant management. He noted that while individual missed reimbursements may be small, they can add up and impact the County’s cash flow. He emphasized the need to identify any missed reimbursements, reduce unnecessary expenses, and remain focused on completing routine, day-to-day responsibilities in a timely manner. Mr. Utt noted that not all outstanding funds were related to past grants and that the County administers approximately $5–7 million in grants annually. Assistant County Administrator for Operations Lisa Richardson explained that many grants require the County to pay expenses upfront and seek reimbursement afterward. 09/24/2026 6:39 PM Vice-Chairman Chilhowie District Supervisor Michael Sturgill emphasized the importance of employees fulfilling their responsibilities and being accountable for their work. Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris asked about the anticipated savings from the requested 5– 10% budget reductions. County Administrator Shawn Utt stated that the goal was approximately $3 million in savings, all of which would impact the General Fund. Mr. Parris noted that allowing a range of 5–10% could provide some departments with flexibility to reduce their budgets by less than 10%. Mr. Utt stated that the County has historically been generous, and in some cases overly generous, in its funding of departments and agencies. He reported that agencies contacted regarding the reductions had generally been receptive and that 38 departments had significantly reduced spending. 09/24/2026 6:46 PM Royal Oak District Supervisor Courtney Widener emphasized the need for caution when considering reductions affecting public safety. He noted that EMS has been a significant expense and that additional discussions with other localities in the County are needed to determine how services could potentially be adjusted while continuing to meet the needs of citizens. He encouraged consideration of other ways to manage costs while maintaining necessary services. 09/24/2026 6:46 PM Davenport & Company Budget Review – County Administrator Shawn Utt reported that the County has been working with Davenport & Company to assist with analyzing the County’s budget constraints and developing recommendations to be incorporated into the revised budget. David Rose, Managing Principal with Davenport & Company, provided an overview of the firm’s review and recommendations. 09/24/2026 6:47 PM Mr. Rose discussed the importance of minimizing or avoiding additional financial pressures where possible and noted that the County should also consider the long-term implications of decisions affecting the FY 2028–2029 budget. He explained that, after several of the recommended changes have been implemented, Davenport would be able to provide additional projections within the next few months. He also noted that the potential approval of the additional 1% sales tax would be considered as part of the long-term financial analysis, while recognizing that the County’s financial needs would remain regardless of whether the referendum is approved. 7 09/24/2026 6:51 PM Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris asked about the long-term impact of the approximate $5.3 million in funding under discussion. Mr. Rose stated that the amount and its long-term implications were part of Davenport’s ongoing review and expressed hope that the 1% sales tax would be approved, noting that the decision would have financial implications for the County for many years. 09/24/2026 6:56 PM Line of Credit Discussion – County Administrator Shawn Utt reported that, following the recent decision that the School Board’s Textbook Fund is unavailable for use, the County may need to consider increasing the amount of its line of credit, at a minimum to replace the funds previously anticipated from the Textbook Fund. He reported that the County Treasurer was recommending an increase from $5 million to $10 million, while his recommendation was a minimum of $7.5 million. Mr. Utt stated that there was a slight possibility the line of credit could be needed in September, but it would almost certainly be needed in October due to large debt service payments associated with the original Courthouse project and a school debt payment. While cash flow was improving as tax bills had been mailed and revenues were coming in sooner than anticipated, he noted that the anticipated October debt payments would significantly reduce the improved cash flow. Mr. Utt also expressed concern about the spring months, when revenues typically decrease while expenditure remains high, but noted that the County's current efforts to improve cash flow and reduce expenditure should put the County in a better position to manage those periods. 09/24/2026 6:58 PM Royal District Supervisor Courtney Widener expressed concern that the County could be “kicking the can down the road” by increasing the line of credit. David Rose with Davenport & Company stated that he would be making recommendations regarding the County’s financial needs. Mr. Widener requested specific financial figures demonstrating the amount needed, and Mr. Rose noted that County staff could provide the information necessary for his review. Mr. Widener requested that the financial information be presented on a month-to-month basis to clearly show the County’s cash flow needs. 09/24/2026 7:04 PM Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris stated that he had previously voted against the line of credit as a matter of principle. He expressed concern that the County could reach the end of December still needing approximately $2 million and stated that he intended to vote against the measure again, emphasizing the need for the County to improve its financial position. 09/24/2026 7:09 PM Rye Valley District Supervisor Jason Parris stated he would like to see the County Treasurer and Commissioner of the Revenue present during future discussions. North Fork Supervisor Rick Billings agreed with Mr. Parris, given their responsibilities for the County’s financial records and funds. 09/24/2026 7:10 PM County Administrator

SMYTH COUNTY PLANNING COMMISSION Thursday, August 27, 2026 The Smyth County Planning Commission met in their regular meeting on Thursday, August 27, 2026, at 6:30 P.M. in the Smyth County Office Building. Commissioners Present: Hazel Wagoner, Chairperson, Atkins District; Graham Davidson Jr., Vice-Chairman, Chilhowie District; David C. Buchanan Jr., Saltville District; Tony Dean, Royal Oak District; Lea Meadows, Park District; and Paul Shepherd, Rye Valley District Commissioners Absent: Robert Campbell, North Fork District Staff Present: Clegg Williams and Kelsey Marchant Adoption of Agenda: Hazel Wagoner called the meeting to order. Tony Dean made a motion to adopt the agenda as presented. It was seconded by David Buchanan Jr., and the following vote was recorded. Vote: 6 yeas 0 nays 1 absent Buchanan Jr., Davidson Jr., Dean, Meadows, Shepherd, and Wagoner Campbell Minutes: Mr. Buchanan made a motion to approve the minutes as amended of the Thursday, July 23, 2026, meeting. It was seconded by Mr. Shepherd and unanimously approved. Citizens’ Time: At 6:35 PM, Dr. Charles Wassum spoke concerning the current approach to land use for data centers in Smyth County, indicating two flaws: first, it’s not legal, and second, it’s not sufficiently transparent. To correct the first flaw, he said that the Comprehensive Plan needed to be diligently updated and be transparent with the community and see if they want a data center. To correct the second flaw, he suggested making the Joint Ordinance Committee more transparent and open to the public. Old Business: Clegg Williams gave the Commissioners an update on the proposed text amendment for Data Centers from June through the present. He informed the Commissioners, based on their recommendation from their previous meeting, that the Joint Ordinance Committee met and revised the text amendment based on information collected from the jointpublic hearing in June, a public interest meeting in July, and their visits to Mecklenburg and Loudon Counties. Mr. Williams handed out drafts of the proposed ordinance. The Commissioners began reviewing and providing their comments and feedback. Most comments were concerning the maximum building height, rooftop equipment, and setback requirements. Mr. Buchanan felt that the proposed 50 feet setback requirement for rooftop equipment was excessive. He proposed either reducing it or requiring a percentage of the perimeter remain open. Recess: At 6:58 PM, Mrs. Wagoner recessed their meeting for a joint public hearing with the Board of Supervisors. SOUTHAMPTON COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS Regular Session  October 27, 2026 C. REQUEST FROM TIDEWATER EMERGENCY MEDICAL SERVICES (TEMS) Mr. David Long, Executive Director of the Tidewater EMS Council, reached out on October 13, 2026. The Council has restructured its governance and there will now be an EMS Operations Committee. The Operations Committee will be one of the two decision making committees for the region, and will be the body that carries locality input to the Board. Each of the regions 26 jurisdictions holds one seat and one alternate such that the locality will always have one vote. Southampton County currently has a TEMS representative that was appointed by the BOS. That person is Clayton Gaskins. He wishes to remain a representative under the new structure. I am told that he is currently active. If it is the desire of the BOS to reappoint Mr. Gaskins in the new capacity, that should be done tonight. We also need an alternate. I suggest that our Emergency Management Coordinator, Mr. Justin Hermann, be appointed to the alternate position. My intent is for both to attend the meetings so that they are well aware of the information presented at the meetings. Southampton County may replace its representative or alternate at any time by written notice. RECOMMENDATION: Make a motion to appoint one individual to be Southampton County’s representative on the EMS Operations Committee and to appoint one person to be the alternate.

text: SOUTHAMPTON COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS Regular Session * October 27, 2026 11C. CENERGY POWER/BAP POWER LLC — SITING AGREEMENT - The Solar Facility Siting Agreement content was approved at the June 23, 2026, Board of Supervisors’ meeting. A copy of the agreement is included for your convenience. Provided that items 11A and 11B are approved on October 27", 2026 by the BOS, the Board will need to approve the execution of the document by the County Administrator. RECOMMENDATION: Direct County Administrator to execute the Siting Agreement through a motion, second, and a board vote provided items 11A and 11B passed approval tonight. SOLAR FACILITY SITING AGREEMENT This Solar Facility Siting Agreement (the "Agreement"), dated as of , 2026 (the "Effective Date"), is made by and between Southampton County, Virginia, a political subdivision of the Commonwealth of Virginia (the "County"), and BAP Power LLC (the "Applicant"). The County and the Applicant are referred to herein each as a “Party” and collectively, the "Parties". RECITALS WHEREAS, the Applicant intends to build, operate, and decommission a commercial solar photovoltaic (electric energy) generation facility and associated electric grid interconnection facilities (collectively, the "Project") on certain real property in the County identified as Tax Map Parcel Number 92-2 (the "Property"); WHEREAS, the requirements of Virginia Code§ 15.2-2316.7 include, without limitation, the obligation of the Applicant to meet, discuss and negotiate a siting agreement with the County; WHEREAS, the Parties desire to enter into this Agreement to provide certain financial compensation to the County as authorized by Virginia Code § 15.2-2288.8(B) and pursuant to the terms and conditions hereof; WHEREAS, the Applicant has agreed to the payments and financial terms contained herein; and WHEREAS, pursuant to the requirement of Virginia Code§ 15.2-2316.8(8), the County held a public hearing in accordance with subdivision A of Virginia Code § 15.2-2204 for the purpose of considering this Agreement, after which a majority of a quorum of the members of the Southampton County Board of Supervisors approved this Agreement. AGREEMENT NOW, THEREFORE, the County and the Applicant, intending to be legally bound hereby and in consideration of the mutual covenants contained herein, the receipt and sufficiency of which are hereby acknowledged, do hereby agree as follows: Article I Conditions 1. CUP Conditions. The Applicant plans on applying for a CUP subsequent to getting siting agreement approval. The Applicant acknowledges and agrees that it is bound by all the terms and conditions of the CUP. Violation by the Applicant or by any of the Applicant's agents, assigns, or successors in interest of any terms and conditions of the approved CUP or of any other applicable zoning requirements of the County shall constitute an event of default under Article II1, Section 13 of this Agreement. Article II Payments 1. Purpose. The Parties acknowledge that the payments required hereunder shall be made to the County for use in funding substantial public improvements, and that such payments are reasonably related to the Project; in recognition thereof, the Applicant agrees to make the payments set faith on Exhibit A (in accordance with paragraph 2 of this Article), as permitted under Virginia Code § 15.2- 2288.8(B). 2. Substantial Cash Payments. a. The Applicant hereby agrees to pay the County the following payments at such times as set forth below (each a "Payment" and collectively, the "Payments"): a. The Applicant will pay the County the amount of Sixty Thousand Dollars ($60,000.00) within 365 days of the County's approval of the Conditional Use Permit (“CUP”). b. The Applicant will pay the County the amount of One Hundred and Forty Thousand Dollars ($140,000.00) immediately after the County's approval of the final building permit. c. The Applicant will pay the County the amount of Seven Hundred Twenty Thousand Dollars ($720,000.00) immediately after Commercial Operation Date, with $120,000 of such amount earmarked as $10,000 donations for each of the County’s 12 volunteer fire departments and rescue squads, as set forth in Exhibit A. As used herein, "Commercial Operation Date" means the date on which the Project commences "Commercial Operation," which means the point at which the Project becomes fully operational! and can begin selling power under the terms. of a power purchase or offtake agreement. Generation of test energy shall not be deemed Commercial Operation. d. The Applicant will pay the County the amount of Forty Thousand. Dollars ($40,000.00) annually for a period of five (5) years, for a total 2 of Two Hundred Thousand Dollars ($200,000.00). e. Annual payments as set forth in Exhibit_A attached hereto and incorporated herein (each, an "Annual Payment", and collectively, the “Annual Payments”, and together with the Initial Payment, the "Payments"). The Annual Payments shall begin no later than six (6) months following the Commercial Operation Date on a prorated basis for that year. The Annual Payments shall be due and payable on or before December Ist of each year following the Commercial Operation Date until the completion of the decommissioning of the Project by the Applicant (the “Termination Date"), as evidenced by written notice to the County from the Applicant that decommissioning of the Project is complete. The Parties acknowledge that, except as otherwise provided herein, the Applicant's obligation to make the Annual Payments shall be conditioned upon the Project commencing Commercial Operation. Each Annual Payment shall be made to the County in one lump sum payment made annually during the term of this Agreement. f. Statutory Structure of Payment; Statement of Benefit. Developer agrees that by entering into this Agreement, pursuant to Virginia Code Ann. § 58.1-2636, these payments are authorized by statute and that it acknowledges, it is bound by law to make the payment in accordance with this Agreement. The Parties acknowledge that this Agreement is fair and mutually beneficial to them both. Developer acknowledges that this Agreement is beneficial to Developer in allowing it to proceed with the installation of the Project while providing for mitigation of potential impacts. 3. Fee and Expense Reimbursement. At the time of the submission of the Final Site Plan, the Developer shall deposit an amount required by the County into escrow with the County, which shall be used to reimburse the County for the following direct fees and expenses incurred by the County: a. For a qualified consultant(s) to review and comment on the Final Site Plan, erosion and sediment control, and storm water management plans submitted to the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality, Soil and Water Conservation District, or other state or local agency; and, once such plans are approved, the compliance with such plans; b. Third-party costs directly related to the County's review and enforcement of erosion and sediment control, decommissioning cost estimates, and semi-annual inspections during operations to verify compliance with the CUP; c. Attorney's fees, third party consultant's fees and other operational expenses encountered by the County during the term of this Agreement. In the event the actual fees and expenses set forth in this Section 3 to be reimbursed by the Developer do not exceed the Deposit Amount and/or funds remain in the Escrow Account as of the Termination Date, the County will send notice to the Developer and the remaining funds will be disbursed to the Developer. For all reimbursable fees and expenses, the County will provide the Developer with a reasonable estimate prior to the fee or expense being incurred. Upon the 3 request from the Developer no more than twice per year, the County will provide a statement of disbursements from the Escrow Account and remaining funds. 4, The Applicant will pay the County for the building permit per the County requirement. Article IT Miscellaneous Terms 1. Term; Termination; Automatic Renewal. This Agreement shall commence on the Effective Date and shall continue until the Termination Date. The Applicant shall have no obligation to make any Payments after the Project is decommissioned. The Annual Payment due for the year in which the Project is decommissioned shall be prorated as of the Termination Date. Written notice of termination shall be given by Applicant (a "Notice of Termination"), and such Notice of Termination shall provide an anticipated termination date that is at least three (3) months from the date the Notice of Termination is given. The termination of this Agreement shall not limit the Applicant's legal obligation to pay local taxes in accordance with applicable law at such time and for such period as the Project remains in operation. Notwithstanding anything contained herein to the contrary, the Applicant may, in its sole discretion, terminate this Agreement at any time prior to Commercial Operation by delivery of written notice thereof to the County. 2. Mutual Covenants. The Applicant covenants to the County that it will pay the County the amounts due hereunder when due in accordance with the terms of this Agreement, and will not seek to invalidate this Agreement, or otherwise take a position adverse to the purpose or validity of this Agreement. The County covenants to the Applicant that it will not seek to invalidate this Agreement or otherwise take a position adverse to the purpose or validity of this Agreement. 3. No Obligation to Develop. The Applicant has no obligation to develop or construct the Project, and this Agreement does not require any Payments until after the Commercial Operation Date. Any test energy or other energy produced prior to the Commercial Operation Date shall not trigger any Payments under this Agreement. It is understood that development of the Project by the Applicant is contingent upon several factors including, but not limited to, regulatory approvals, availability and cost of equipment and financing, and market demand for the Project's energy. No election by the Applicant to terminate, defer, suspend, or modify plans to develop the Project shall be deemed a default of the Applicant under this Agreement. 4. Successors and Assigns. This Agreement shall be binding upon the successors or assigns of the Applicant, and the obligations created hereunder shall be covenants running with the Property. If Applicant sells, transfers, leases, or assigns all or substantially all of its interests in the Project or the ownership of the Applicant, this Agreement will automatically be assumed by and be binding on the purchaser or transferee. Upon such assumption, the sale, transfer, lease, or assignment shall relieve the Applicant of all obligations and liabilities under this Agreement accruing from and after the date of sale or transfer, and the purchaser or transferee shall automatically become responsible under this Agreement. The Applicant shall execute such documentation as reasonably requested by the County to memorialize the assignment and assumption by the purchaser or transferee. 5. Execution of Agreement Deems Project "Substantially In Accord" with County's Comprehensive Plan. Pursuant to Virginia Code§ 15.2- 2316.9(C), execution of this Agreement deems the Project to be substantially in accord with the County's Comprehensive Plan in satisfaction of the requirements of Virginia Code§ 15.2-2232. 6. Memorandum of Agreement. A memorandum of this Agreement, in a form substantially similar to that attached as Exhibit B hereto (the "Memorandum"), shall be recorded in the land records of the Clerk's Office of the Circuit Court of the County (the "Clerks Office"). Such recordation shall be at the Applicant's sole cost and expense and shall occur as soon as reasonably practicable after the Effective Date. Upon the termination of this Agreement, the Parties shall execute and record a release of the Memorandum in the Clerk's Office. uv. Notices. Except as otherwise provided herein, all notices required to be given or authorized to be given pursuant to this Agreement shall be in writing and shall be delivered or sent by registered or certified mail, postage prepaid, by recognized overnight courier, or by commercial messenger to: If to the County: Southampton County 26022 Administration Center Drive Courtland, Virginia 23837 Attn: Lynette C. Lowe, Acting County Administrator If to the Applicant: BAP Power LLC 26880 Aliso Viejo Parkway, Suite 100 Aliso Viejo, CA 92656 Attention: Bill Pham, Manager The County and the Applicant, by notice given hereunder, may designate any further or different persons or addresses to which subsequent notices shall be sent. 8. Governing Law; Jurisdiction; Venue. THIS AGREEMENT SHALL BE GOVERNED BY AND CONSTRUED IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE LAWS OF THE COMMONWEALTH OF VIRGINIA, WITHOUT REGARD TO ANY OF ITS PRINCIPLES OF CONFLICTS OF LAWS OR OTHER LAWS WHICH WOULD RESULT IN THE APPLICATION OF THE LAWS OF ANOTHER JURISDICTION. THE PARTIES HERETO (A) AGREE THAT ANY SUIT, ACTION OR OTHER LEGAL PROCEEDING, AS BETWEEN THE PARTIES HERETO, ARISING OUT OF OR RELATING TO THIS AGREEMENT SHALL BE BROUGHT AND TRIED ONLY IN THE CIRCUIT COURT OF SOUTHAMPTON COUNTY, VIRGINIA, (B) CONSENT TO THE JURISDICTION OF SUCH COURT IN ANY 5

text: SOUTHAMPTON COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS Regular Session * October 27, 2026 12 B. PUBLIC HEARING — Rezoning — REZ 2026- 01 — Applicant — Brian Layne Rezoning Classification —to request a change in zoning from A-1 Agricultural to B-2 Mixed Use of approximately 19.4 acres. The property is identified as Tax Parcel 76-36 and is located on the North corner of Story Station Road (Route 611) and Southampton Parkway (Route 58). It is located in the Jerusalem Magisterial District and the Fairgrounds Voting District. The initial Planning Commission public hearing was held on February 12, 2026. The Commission voted 7-0 in favor of allowing a change to the zoning classification. The Traffic Impact Analysis has been favorably updated and the applicant is now ready to move forward with his submission of the application and facts to the Board of Supervisors. Regan Prince, Director of Community Development, is here to present the details of the application and other relevant information. Attached Packet: Letter from Community Development to Board of Supervisors List of Adjacent Property Owners Notice of Public Hearing Application Letter from VDOT Traffic Impact Study RECOMMENDATION: Planning Commission requests that you approve the Rezoning as evidenced by the favorable 7-0 vote from the February 12, 2026, Planning Commission meeting. Randall (owners). The owners withdrew both applications from the March 24" 2026 Board of Supervisor meeting to correct and resubmit the Traffic Impact Analysis to VDOT. Site plan and proffers revisions were required by VDOT as part of the rezoning application. The first hearing is to consider a request to amend the future land use map of the Comprehensive Plan from Low Density Residential to Mixed Use of approximately 19.4 acres. The property is identified as ‘Tax Parcels 76-36 and is located on the north corner of Story Station Road (Route 611) and Southampton Parkway (Route 58) and located in the Jerusalem Magisterial District and Fairgrounds Voting District. The second hearing is to consider a request a change in zoning classification from A-1 Agricultural to B-2 Mixed Use of approximately 19.4 acres. The purpose of the application is to develop a mixed use development. The property is identified as Tax Parcel 76-36 and is located on the north corner of Story Station Road (Route 611) and Southampton Parkway (Route 58) and is in the Jerusalem Magisterial District and Fairgrounds Voting District. The first application is to consider an amendment to the Comprehensive Plan was the subject of a public hearing by the Planning Commission on February 12, 2026. After considerable discussion, a motion was adopted 7-0 to recommend approval of CPA 2026-01, a change of the future land map from Commercial to Mixed Use. The amendment being requested is to allow the entire parcel to be consistent with the Comprehensive Plan. The second application requesting a change in zoning classification was the subject of public hearing by the Planning Commission on February 12, 2026. After considerable discussion, a motion was adopted 7-0 to recommend approval of zoning classification for REZ 2026-01. Staff reviewed the revised VDOT supported Traffic Impact Analysis, site plan and proffers with no comments. Therefore, staff recommends the Board consider approval for both applications as the development satisfies VDOT Traffic Impact Analysis and site design requirements. We are committed to working alongside families, early childhood educators in centers and homes, Head Start, and VPI Pre-K programs to strengthen the quality of instruction, enhance interactions with children, and improve outcomes for the children and families we serve. In partnership with Ready Regions Southeastern, we are strengthening early childhood systems, elevating family voice, and expanding access to high quality childcare that supports healthy child development, school readiness, and lifelong learning. Through partnerships with the Western Tidewater Early Childhood Collaboration & Franklin Southampton Wellness Coalition, we are expanding our reach and making a meaningful difference in our community. We visit schools and under-resourced neighborhoods alongside our partners (such as Family 4 Eternity, Western Tidewater Community Services Board, Franklin City Parks and Recreation, Girl Scouts of the Colonial Coast, & Blackwater Regional Library) to distribute locality specific resource guides and educational materials to connect families with essential resources. We,also support families with cribs and safe-sleep resources, winter essential clothing, backpacks and school supplies. We’re also working with our partners to develop and expand extracurricular opportunities based on needs identified by parents. These activities include Family Reading Night, After-School Connections, and Girl Scouts Community Troops. One of our newest and most exciting initiatives is Dolly Parton’s imagination Library, which promotes early literacy by providing books to young children from the time they are born until their fifth birthday. We are thrilled to share that 448 children in Franklin & Southampton County are actively enrolled! This milestone reflects our commitment to nurturing a love of reading, supporting early learning, and helping every child build a strong foundation for lifelong success. We are excited about the progress we are making in reaching families and communities with these and many other vital services and opportunities. Through these efforts, we strive to create brighter possibilities for our children and positively shape their futures. Your generosity helps make this work possible, and we are deeply grateful for your investment in our children, families, and community. “Raising our children out of poverty.” Thank you, And may the Force be with you! Background: Funding Source(s): Attachments: (click item to open) attachment. Altavista Planning Commission - Meeting Minutes 03AUG26.pdf 2 Altavista Planning Commission: Meeting Minutes - August 3rd, 2026 The Altavista Planning Commission held a regular scheduled meeting on Monday, August 3, 2026, at 5:00pm, in the Council Chambers of Town Hall, 510 7th Street, Altavista, Virginia. Members present: Reggie Bennett, Town Council Liaison Meghan Bolling John Jordan, Chairman Marie Mitchell, Vice Chair Absent: Ashby Robinson Town Staff: Jamie Gillespie, Director of Planning and Community Development Gary Shanaberger, Town Manager John Eller, Town Attorney CALL TO ORDER Chairman John Jordan confirmed a quorum, and called this meeting to order at 5:00pm. PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE & INVOCATION Chairman Jordan delivered an Invocation; and led everyone in reciting the Pledge of Allegiance. APPROVAL OF AGENDA Without any amendments made to this agenda, the Planning Commission voted in favor, 4-0, and approved the August 3rd meeting agenda as presented. APPROVAL OF MINUTES Upon review, the Commission expressed no revisions needed to the minutes of their June 2026 meeting. With a motion by Vice Chair Marie Mitchell, seconded by Mayor Bennett, the Planning Commission voted in favor, 4-0, and approved the June meeting minutes as presented. PUBLIC EXPRESSION There were no public comments given on this date. PUBLIC HEARING No public hearings were scheduled for this meeting date. NEW BUSINESS Presentation: Altavista Small Area (Downtown) Master Plan Altavista On Track (AOT) Executive Director David Green shared a brief overview of AOT’s grant awards over the past couple of years, including a $40,000 grant to create a Downtown Altavista Master Plan. Mr. Green introduced David Hill and Jonah Collins, Hill Studio, to deliver the presentation. Mr. Collins noted demographics used while creating the master plan; and shared some of the ideas they believed would be quickly attainable; such as exterior art murals and decorative lighting installations. He also stated that the Town’s wayfinding signs were too small for adequate visibility by motorists, and shared potential improvements. Mr. Collins referenced Dalton’s Landing and said the Town was underutilizing the Staunton River as a dependable revenue source. He suggested having boat/kayak and tubing activities; and introducing an Outfitters Store to Downtown Altavista. P a g e 1|3 3 Altavista Planning Commission: Meeting Minutes - August 3rd, 2026 Mr. Collins concluded the presentation by emphasizing the importance of creating spaces that generate interest and support economic growth. Mr. Hill shared some of the plan’s more extensive projects, which may qualify for federal and state tax credits or grants; noting the potential to add store frontage to vacant lots, or to revitalize existing properties into vibrant, relevant spaces. Chairman Jordan and Commissioners thanked Mr. Hill and Mr. Collins for their presentation; and Mr. Green and Mrs. Gillespie for their work efforts on this project. UNFINISHED BUSINESS There was no unfinished business to discuss at this time. ITEMS FROM THE COMMISSION - Chairman Jordan asked for an update on the Vista/Leggett Restoration Project. Director of Planning and Community Development Jamie Gillespie said new roofs had been installed on both the Vista Theatre and Leggett building; and noted that, through a Virginia Brown Fields Grant, lead and asbestos remediation had also been conducted on both buildings. She said the project was currently at a pause while Staff reviewed potential plans of operation. Chairman Jordan asked if the Town would continue to own the two properties. Town Manager Gary Shanaberger answered that the Altavista EDA (owner) was keeping an open mind to selling the properties to a developer, but there were no prospects at that time; therefore, the current path was for the AEDA to control operations, which could utilize grants and historic tax credits to help cover the cost of additional renovations. - Vice Chair Mitchell referenced the presented Master Plan for Downtown Altavista, specifically renderings of ideas for some of the vacant buildings and properties in the downtown area, and asked if there were policies in place where Altavista could control what an owner or buyer could do with said properties. Director of Planning and Community Development Jamie Gillespie answered there was not. She said AOT could utilize the plan to influence property owners with renderings of what their property could look like; and also use the plan as a tool to acquire grant funding, enabling them to partner with property owners to help accomplish desired goals for their property. ADDITIONAL MATTERS FROM STAFF 2026 Business Report: Mid-year Update Director of Planning and Community Development Jamie Gillespie presented this report, noting Commission and Staff activities from January 1st through June 30th. She informed the Commission that the new enforcement approach for grass violations, involving posting notices on properties, had shown to have positive results. Mrs. Gillespie also noted that the Altavista Board of Zoning Appeals held a special-called meeting in May 2026, that resulted in denying a various request, VAR-26-01. P a g e 2|3 4 Altavista Planning Commission: Meeting Minutes - August 3rd, 2026 Mrs. Gillespie shared an update on the Town’s Mosley Heights Community Revitalization Project; noting the $828,000 DHCD Grant awarded for housing rehabilitation. She said that Town Council would be adopting the required documents at their August 11th meeting, meeting the deadline of September 9th for submission to the DHCD; after which construction projects could begin. Mrs. Gillespie referenced the new legislation that impacts zoning, planning, and land use, and stated that Staff would collaborate with Town Attorney John Eller to bring these items to the Commission for the process of updating Altavista’s Town Code for state compliance. Mrs. Gillespie also referenced the Town’s Frazier Property Redevelopment Project, and noted that Expressions of Interest were due July 1st, and the Altavista EDA was currently working through submissions, and looking to move this well-anticipated project forward. There were no comments or questions from the Commission. Chairman Jordan thanked Mrs. Gillespie for the updates; and for the work that she does for the Planning Commission and the Town of Altavista. ADJOURNMENT With no further business to discuss, Chairman Jordan adjourned this meeting at 5:55pm. ___ John Jordan, Chairman Altavista Planning Commission ___ Jamie Gillepie, Director of Planning and Community Development, Altavista P a g e 3|3 5 TOWN OF ALTAVISTA PLANNING COMMISSION October 5, 2026 AGENDA COVER SHEET AGENDA ITEM #: 7.1 Unfinished Business Title: Review of upcoming Chapter 86 - Zoning Text Amendments Staff Resource: Matt Perkins, Zoning Administrator Action(s): Prepare for review of Staff recommendations at the December 7th meeting of the Planning Commission. Make a motion for Staff to bring proposed text amendments to Planning Commission. Explanation: The Virginia General Assembly in their 2026 legislative session passed several bills that affect both community development and land use planning and development. Staff believes that certain actions need to be initiated now to align our local Town code to State Code. Town Code 86-781 states, that, "Whenever the public necessity, convenience, general welfare, or good zoning practice requires, the council may by ordinance amend, supplement, or change the text of this chapter including the regulations, district boundaries, or classifications of real property. Any such amendment may be initiated by resolution of the council, [or] by motion of the planning commission..." Background: Funding Source(s): Attachments: (click item to open) attachment. Zoning Action Summary Discussion PC Meeting OCT05.pdf 6 Legislative Summary: Community Development and Land Use HB 802 Vacant buildings; registration by registered agents, etc., annually. Description: Permits any locality to require, by ordinance, the owner, or his registered agent, of any building that has been continuously vacant for at least three years to register such building with the locality annually. SB 531 Zoning; development and use of accessory dwelling units, delayed effective date. Description: Requires a locality to include in its zoning ordinances for single-family residential zoning districts accessory dwelling units, or ADUs, as defined in the HB 655 / SB 346 Zoning; manufactured housing. Description: Amends existing provisions that require localities to permit manufactured homes in areas zoned for agriculture by expanding such requirement to all zoning districts where site-built housing is allowed, with certain conditions Recreational substances (Regulations found at 3 VAC 10-10 et seq.) Specifically any raw material or processed product made from or containing any part of the Cannabis sativa plant intended to be consumed by inhalation. Retail marijuana sales begin July 1, 2027. The Cannabis Control Authority is tasked with developing the regulatory framework for a sale and legal retail market. However, under the legislation localities will not be able to ban retail cannabis operations but localities do retain land use authority over cannabis retailers and retailers must demonstrate that their premises are in accordance with local land use requirements. 7 10/1/2026 Code of Virginia Title 15.2. Counties, Cities and Towns Chapter 11. Powers of Cities and Towns § 15.2-1127. Vacant building registration; civil penalty. A. Any locality may by ordinance require an owner, or his registered agent, of buildings that have been vacant for a continuous period of 12 months or more and (i) that meet the definition of "derelict building" under § 15.2-907.1, (ii) that meet the definition of "criminal blight" under § 15.2-907, or (iii) in which a locality has determined a person is living without the authority of an owner to register such buildings on an annual basis. B. Any locality may by ordinance require an owner, or his registered agent, of buildings that have been vacant for a continuous period of three years or more to register such buildings on an annual basis. C. Any locality that adopts a vacant building registration ordinance pursuant to this section may impose an annual registration fee not to exceed $100 to defray the cost of processing such registration. D. The registration of buildings shall be on forms designated by the locality and filed with the agency designated by the locality. Such forms shall include a requirement to provide the name and contact information, including telephone number, for the owner, or the registered agent of an owner, required to register pursuant to this section. Failure to register shall be a $200 civil penalty; however, failure to register in conservation and rehabilitation districts designated by the governing body, or in other areas designated as blighted pursuant to § 36-49.1:1, shall be punishable by a civil penalty not exceeding $400. Notice shall be mailed to the owner, at the address to which property tax notices are sent, at least 30 days prior to the assessment of the civil penalty. 1993, c. 829, § 15.1-29.24; 1997, c. 587; 1999, c. 250; 2006, c. 299; 2013, cc. 253, 355, 405; 2020, c. 145; 2024, cc. 613, 616; 2026, c. 427. 8 10/1/2026 Code of Virginia Title 15.2. Counties, Cities and Towns Chapter 22. Planning, Subdivision of Land and Zoning § 15.2-2292.4. (Effective July 1, 2027) Development and use of accessory dwelling units. A. As used in this section, "accessory dwelling unit" or "ADU" means an attached or detached dwelling unit on a residential dwelling lot that: 1. Provides complete independent living facilities for one or more individuals; 2. Is located on the same lot as a proposed or existing primary residence; and 3. Includes facilities for living, sleeping, eating, cooking, and sanitation. B. Zoning ordinances for single-family residential zoning districts shall be deemed to include accessory dwelling units as a permitted accessory use, and no locality shall require compliance with any other requirements except as provided in this section. C. Any person proposing an ADU shall first obtain an ADU permit from the locality, for which the locality may charge a fee of no more than $500. Such fee shall be in addition to any other applicable fees, including inspection, site, or building permit fees, that may be required in connection with the ADU. A locality shall issue the permit if the applicant demonstrates that the ADU complies with the requirements of this section and the local codes and ordinances referenced herein. D. Localities may require the following: 1. A lease term for the rental of an ADU of 30 consecutive days or longer; 2. Replacement of a primary dwelling's required parking if the construction of the ADU eliminates such parking; 3. Dedicated parking for the ADU; 4. Limits on floor area, lot coverage, and impervious area of an ADU of no less than (i) 350 square feet on lots less than 2,500 square feet and (ii) 500 square feet on lots 2,500 square feet or greater; 5. Compliance with (i) building codes, including the requirements of the Uniform Statewide Building Code (§ 36-97 et seq.), for an accessory dwelling unit if the ADU is attached or for a dwelling unit if the ADU is detached; (ii) water, sewer, septic, emergency access, flood zone, and stormwater requirements; (iii) historic and architectural districts and corridor protection restrictions; and (iv) Air Installations Compatible Use Zone restrictions; 6. Owner occupancy of the ADU or the primary dwelling, but not both, only at the time an application is submitted to construct or convert an accessory dwelling unit; 7. That the ADU shall be no more than 500 feet from the primary dwelling; 8. No ADUs on a residential lot that has more than one dwelling unit; and 9. No ADUs sold separately or subdivided from the primary dwelling. E. Localities shall not require the following: 1. Rear or side setbacks for the ADU that are greater than the setback required for the primary dwelling or the setback required for accessory structures on the residential lot, whichever is less; 2. Restrictions for ADUs that are more restrictive than those for single-family dwellings within the same zoning area with regard to height, rear or side setbacks, lot size or coverage, or building frontage; 3. A restrictive covenant concerning an ADU on a lot or parcel zoned for residential use by a single-family dwelling; 4. Improvements to public streets as a condition of allowing an ADU, except as necessary to reconstruct or repair a public street that is disturbed as a result of the construction of the ADU; or 5. Consanguinity or affinity between the occupants of an ADU and the primary dwelling. F. Nothing in this section shall be construed to supersede or limit contracts or agreements between or among individuals or private entities related to the use of real property, including recorded declarations and covenants, the provisions of condominium instruments of a condominium created pursuant to the Virginia Condominium Act (§ 55.1-1900 et seq.), the declaration of a common interest community as defined in § 54.1-2345, the cooperative instruments of a cooperative created pursuant to the Virginia Real Estate Cooperative Act (§ 55.1-2100 et seq.), or any declaration of a property owners' association created pursuant to the Property Owners' Association Act (§ 55.1-1800 et seq.). 9 G. Nothing in this section shall apply to any existing permits for an ADU approved by the locality prior to July 1, 2027. H. Nothing in this section shall be construed to restrict a locality's passage prior to July 1, 2027, of an ADU ordinance, or a subsequent amendment thereof, that substantially complies with the requirements of this section. I. Nothing in this section shall apply to a locality that adopted an ADU ordinance prior to January 1, 2026. 2026, c. 895. 10 10/1/2026 Code of Virginia Title 15.2. Counties, Cities and Towns Chapter 22. Planning, Subdivision of Land and Zoning § 15.2-2290. Uniform regulations for manufactured housing. A. Localities adopting and enforcing zoning ordinances under the provisions of this article shall provide that in all agricultural zoning districts, or districts having similar classifications regardless of name or designation, where agricultural, horticultural, or forest uses such as those described in § 58.1-3230 are the dominant use and where site-built housing is allowed, the placement of manufactured homes shall be permitted. B. Localities adopting and enforcing zoning ordinances under the provisions of this article shall provide that, in all zoning districts, other than zoning districts listed in subsection A, where site-built housing is allowed, the placement of manufactured homes shall be permitted for manufactured homes that are (i) converted to real property in accordance with § 46.2-653.1, (ii) constructed so that the certificate of occupancy is issued within five years following the date of manufacture listed on the home's data plate, and (iii) placed on individual lots. Localities shall not adopt or enforce any zoning, land-use, or development regulation that treats manufactured homes differently or more restrictively than a singlefamily site-built dwelling allowed in the same zoning district. Nothing in this subsection shall be construed as limiting the authority of localities to adopt ordinances pursuant to §§ 10.1-2206.1 and 15.2-2306 designed to protect existing or future areas of historical or archaeological significance, historical sites, historical landmarks, and historical buildings and structures, or to establish local historical districts. C. Localities adopting and enforcing zoning regulations under the provisions of this article may, to provide for the general purposes of zoning ordinances, adopt uniform standards, so long as they apply to all residential structures erected within the zoning district. The standards shall not have the effect of excluding manufactured housing built in compliance with the Virginia Manufactured Housing Construction and Safety Standards Law (§ 36-85.2 et seq.). D. Local zoning ordinances adopting provisions consistent with this section shall not relieve lots or parcels from the obligations relating to manufactured housing units imposed by the terms of a restrictive covenant. 1990, c. 840, § 15.1-486.4; 1991, c. 198; 1995, cc. 540, 583;
