Board Action APPROVAL OF MINUTES August 20, 2026 OTHER BUSINESS ADJOURNMENT Staff Memorandum – Variance Request Board of Zoning Appeals – October 22, 2026 Applicant / Property Owner: Ryan Stanley Address of Subject Property: 1179 Ruff Drive, Bedford VA Tax Map Number: 170-A-16T Variance Sections: Sections 608.08.a. and 701.03.a. Zoning District: Manufacturing – M-1 Variance Requests: The applicant is requesting a variance from two Town Code sections in the zoning ordinance to add a 16-foot by 22-foot addition to the existing house for an office and storage. Section 608.08.a. in the Manufacturing (M-1) zoning district text requires minimum building setbacks to be 25 feet in all yards. Section 701.03.a. prohibits enlargement or area increase of a nonconforming use. Facts: On July 26, 2016, a deed was recorded for applicant Ryan Stanley to purchase the subject 6.14 acre parcel at the end of Ruff Drive, which has a zoning designation of Manufacturing M-1. In April 2018, the applicant’s father-in-law, Scott Bonheim, spoke with then zoning administrator Bart Warner about permitting construction of a new single-family dwelling on the parcel with an existing house in the M-1 zoning district. Since a single-family dwelling is not a permitted use in the M-1 district, the zoning administrator requested that Mr. Bonheim provide his request in writing in order to make a zoning determination or ruling. In an email from Mr. Bonheim to Mr. Warner dated April 11, 2018 (attached), Mr. Bonheim stated his intent was to build a new single-family home for his daughter and her family. He stated the existing 1930s home would be dismantled and some of the construction material would be repurposed into the new house. He also stated the existing dwelling would be converted to a detached garage. On April 13, 2018, the zoning administrator provided a written ruling that the zoning permit application could be approved with a finding of several facts and application of conditions (attached). That ruling allowed the replacement of the old dwelling with a new one to maintain the nonconforming use of a residence in the M-1 district with substantially similar “area of use”. The determination did not grant approval for further or future expansions of the nonconforming residential use, whether to the dwelling or by adding accessory residential structures. The zoning administrator advised that Mr. Bonheim may consider an appeal of his ruling to the Board of Zoning Appeals or request a change in the zoning designation to a residential district. A zoning permit was issued on April 13, 2018 for a 28-foot by 26-foot, two-story dwelling and no other structures. That application requested a structure with 728 square feet per floor for 1,456 square feet of finished living area. The setbacks from property lines were shown on the application drawing as being 60 feet from the northwestern property line in the area where the addition is proposed now. The house received a certificate of occupancy on October 3, 2018 from Bedford County. 1 Land Uses and Zoning: The property is at the end of Ruff Drive, a private street. The zoning designations on adjoining parcels are M-1 and Low Density Residential (R-1) (formerly Planned Residential, PRD). Surrounding uses are single-family residential houses, a cemetery (owned by the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks), vacant land proposed for residential development (former Elks Home property), and agricultural pasture. The recent zoning ordinance update adopted by Town Council in March 2024 affirmed the M1 zoning of the Ruff Drive area. No citizens from the area spoke about changing the zoning from M-1 to another district during the process that included two public hearings. The zoning Intent of the Manufacturing District M-1 is as follows: 608.01. Intent of Manufacturing District M-1. It is the intent of this district to accommodate industrial uses that provide desirable employment, consistent with the goal of maintaining the town's high environmental quality. To this end, high performance requirements are established and additional protection from adverse environmental effects is provided for residential districts bordering the district. The district is protected against encroachment from commercial or residential uses. The Future Land Use Map of the Comprehensive Plan designates the parcel as “Industrial / Manufacturing” use. There are two variances to be heard. The first addressed here is the nonconforming use of land. If this variance is not granted to expand the nonconforming use, there is not a need to act on the second request for a variance from the minimum setback. Variance Request 1: Section 701.03.a. – Nonconforming Uses of Land A single-family residential use is not permitted in the M-1 district, which makes the house and any other residential use or structure a nonconforming use of land. Section 701.03.a. states: “No such nonconforming use shall be enlarged or increased, nor extended to occupy a greater area of land than was occupied at time of enactment or amendment of this Land Development Ordinance.” The zoning ruling issued in 2018 allowed the expansion of the nonconforming use of land to build a single-family dwelling based on the existence of an old house. The constructed house has a finished footprint of 728 square feet on the ground. There are also porches and decks that add 264 square feet per the County GIS system. The total current residential area use of the house is 1,720 square feet, excluding any other residential use of the parcel. The requested addition of 16 feet by 22 feet would increase the nonconforming use by 352 square feet for a total structural area of 2,072 square feet. Variance Request 2: Section 608.08.a. – Setbacks in the Manufacturing M-1 District Minimum yard setback requirements for all property lines, front, rear and side, are 25 feet in the M-1 District currently. The ordinance in effect at the time of construction would have been dated 2017, which also set minimum setbacks in M-1 of 25 feet on the sides and rear. The house that was permitted to be constructed in 2018 was allowed to be in a different location than the old house and maintain the nonconforming status with a condition that stated: “2. The area of use may be defined as the building envelope (i.e. the area defined by the applicable setbacks for the district). So long as the new residential structure is placed on the lot to meet the applicable setbacks, the non-conforming use shall not be defined as having been ‘moved’ per se.” All property in the Town is subject to setbacks. The sketch on the zoning permit application showed the setback being 60 feet from the northwestern property line. No determination was made whether 2 this property line was a side or rear so 25 feet applied to either. For this report, a rough measurement of distance from the aerial photo in the County GIS system indicates the house was constructed a distance of approximately 36 feet from that property line, not 60 feet as permitted (map attached). The requested addition is shown on the application sketch to be 16 feet from the northwestern property line within the 6.14 acre parcel. This would be an encroachment of nine feet into the minimum 25-foot required setback. Findings to be made by the Board The applicant will need to address questions related to their request in the public hearing. The application provides answers to those questions in the attached document. The board of zoning appeals shall have the following duties and powers: 1103.01. To hear and decide appeals from any order, requirement, decision, or determination made by an administrative officer in the administration or enforcement of this Land Development Ordinance. The decision on such appeal shall be based on the board's judgment of whether the administrative officer was correct. The determination of the administrative officer shall be presumed to be correct. At a hearing on an appeal, the administrative officer shall explain the basis for his or her determination, after which the appellant has the burden of proof to rebut such presumption of correctness by a preponderance of the evidence. The board shall consider any applicable ordinances, laws, and regulations in making its decision. For the purposes of this subsection, determination means any order, requirement, decision, or determination made by an administrative officer. 1103.02. To authorize upon appeal in specific cases a variance from the terms of the provisions of this Land Development Ordinance relating to zoning as will not be contrary to the public interest, when owing to special conditions provisions will result in unnecessary hardship; provided that the spirit of the ordinance shall be observed and substantial justice done as follows: a. No such variance shall be authorized by the board unless it finds: (1) that the property interest for which the variance is being requested was acquired in good faith and the hardship was not created by the applicant for the variance; (2) the granting of the variance will not be of substantial detriment to adjacent property and nearby properties in proximity to its geographical area; (3) the condition or situation of the property concerned is not of so general or recurring a nature as to make reasonably practicable the formulation of a general regulation to be adopted as an amendment to this Land Development Ordinance; (4) the granting of the variance does not result in a use that is not otherwise permitted on such property or a change in the zoning classification of the property; and (5) the relief or remedy sought by the variance application is not available through a conditional use permit. c. No such variance shall be authorized except after notice and hearing as required by Code of Virginia, § 15.2-2204. d. In authorizing a variance the board may impose such conditions regarding the location, character, and other features of the proposed structure for use as it may deem necessary to the public interest, and may require a guarantee or bond to insure that the conditions imposed are being and will continue to be complied with. e. Once a variance has been authorized for a change in lot dimension, location and size of proposed structures or yard dimensions, the lot, and any existing or proposed structures shall be considered in conformance with zoning requirements. Subsequent improvements to such lot or property that are in conformance with the zoning requirements of the area, and the minimum requirements of the Town of Bedford shall not require an additional variance. f. A request may be made by or on behalf of a disabled person for a variance in order to alleviate a hardship by granting a reasonable modification to a property or the improvements thereon. If so provided in the variance, such variance may expire when the person benefited by it is no longer in need of the modification to such property or improvements provided by the variance, subject to the provisions of state and federal fair housing laws, or the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (42 U.S.C. § 12131 et seq.). g. To hear and decide appeals from the decision of the zoning administrator in the application of the zoning provisions of this Land Development Ordinance after notice and hearing as provided by Code of Virginia, § 15.2-2204. However, when giving any required notice to the owners, their agents, or the occupants of abutting property and property immediately across the street or road from the property affected, the board may give such notice by first-class mail rather than by registered or certified mail. 1103.04. To hear and decide applications for interpretation of the zoning map where there is any uncertainty as to the location of a district boundary. After notice to the owners of the property affected by the question, and after public hearing with notice as required by Code of Virginia, § 15.22204, the board may interpret the map in accordance with the principles set forth in Article IV of this Land Development Ordinance. Ms. Saxton seconded the motion. The motion carried by a vote of 4-0. Additional Comments The Commission thanked Mayor Michael for his assistance during the transition period. title: Packet
text: TOWN OF SOUTH BOSTON REGULAR MEETING MINUTES MONDAY SEPTEMBER 14, 2026 COUNCIL CHAMBERS 420 MAIN STREET SOUTH BOSTON, VA 24592 CALL TO ORDER AND INVOCATION Mayor Edward Owens called to order a regular South Boston Town Council meeting at 7:00 pm on August 10, 2026. ROLL CALL Present: Mayor Edward Owens, Vice-Mayor Sharon Harris, Councilman Joe Chandler, Councilman Tommy Elliott, Councilwoman Barbara Speece, Councilman Brian Burton Absent: Councilwoman Tina Younger Also Present: Town Manager Matthew Candland, Assistant Town Manager Patrick Elwell, Town Clerk Sarah Lowe, Finance Director Danyell Duncan, Public Works Director John Hatcher, Police Chief Ronnie Edmonds, Fire Chief Ray Conner, Recreation Director Matthew McCargo APPROVAL OF MINUTES On motion of Councilman Burton, seconded by Councilman Chandler the meeting minutes from the Town Council’s regular meeting on August 10, 2026, were approved. APPROVAL OF THE CONSENT AGENDA On motion of Councilman Elliott, seconded by Vice-Mayor Harris, the agenda for September 14, 2026 was approved. AGENDA 57|Page 1, PUBLIC HEARING FOR A REZONING REQUEST FROM MCAP HALIFAX LLC, KEVIN WILLIS TO REZONE THE REAR 0.35 ACRES OF TAX PARCEL 5302 Mayor Owens opened the duly advertised public hearing on a rezoning request from MCAP Halifax, LLC to rezone the rear 0.35 acres of Tax Parcel 5302. The Mayor called for anyone wishing to speak in favor of the request to come forward. No one came forward, and that portion of the hearing was closed. The Mayor then called for anyone wishing to speak in opposition to come forward. No one came forward, and the public hearing was closed. There being no further discussion, on motion of Councilman Chandler, seconded by Vice Mayor Harris, the rezoning request was approved. 2. PUBLIC HEARING FOR PROPOSED YARD WASTE ORDINANCE AMENDMENT Mayor Owens opened the duly advertised public hearing on the proposed amendment to the Yard Waste Ordinance adopted in February. Staff reported that the amendment reflects public comments received this spring. It removes the requirement that yard waste be bundled or tied, increases the allowable length from four feet to eight feet, sets a limit of three bundles per set-out, and clarifies that hazardous waste and construction debris may not be set out. A resident from 1021 Washington Avenue, spoke in favor of the amendment. The speaker thanked the Council for removing the bundling requirement, citing physical difficulty for older residents and the added cost of materials amid rising prices. Another resident from Marshall Avenue noted that the ordinance text was not included in the agenda packet. The speaker asked whether a resident could be charged with a misdemeanor under the penalty section, which allows either a criminal or civil penalty. Staff stated that all ordinances require a penalty, that the language is standard, and that the Town has not imposed such a penalty in recent memory. The speaker cautioned that leaving the penalty type unspecified could create problems in the future. Barbara Owen, 1102 Marshall Avenue, stated that she preferred the amended version to the February ordinance. Staff confirmed that bundling is no longer required and that small piles allow faster collection by hand. Ms. Owen objected to the criminal penalty in Section 44-2, stating that it could apply to individual homeowners rather than only contractors. She also opposed the $200 fine for subsequent violations and suggested $50. There being no further speakers, the public hearing was closed. A motion was made by Councilman Elliott and seconded by Councilwoman Speece to approve the amendment as presented. During discussion, a Council member asked whether the criminal penalty could be removed, and staff agreed to consult the Town Attorney. Staff stated that collection is intended to occur weekly and confirmed that the Council may set a lower fine for subsequent violations. Members expressed a preference to resolve these questions before acting. The motion to approve the amendment failed. The Council agreed to bring the matter back at the October meeting following the Town Attorney's review of the penalty provisions and consideration of a reduced fine. 58|Page 3. DOG PARK PRESENTATION — RYLAND CLARK Ryland Clark presented a proposal, developed with community members, for a public dog park in the Riverdale Green Space. The proposed site is adjacent to an existing park, with a tree buffer and room for separate areas for small and large dogs. The layout includes fencing, activity equipment, a central seating area with shade, water, and landscaping. The contractor’s estimate is approximately $150,000, with a project budget of up to $200,000 to allow for contingencies. The proposal was prepared by a state- contract vendor, the same contractor that prepared the Harris Park proposal and built the South Hill dog park, so no competitive bid would be required. The presenter reported that $30,000 has been committed to date and that two large companies have pledged significant contributions but require a 501(c)(3) recipient. The goal is to raise at least $100,000 privately. Mr. Clark asked the Town to consider a matching commitment of $100,000 or another amount, and to assist with approvals, ownership, maintenance, and implementation. A QR code and survey are available for residents wishing to volunteer or donate. In response to Council questions, the presenter confirmed the total cost range of $150,000 to $200,000 and the fundraising goal of $100,000. No action was taken. 4. RESOLUTION REQUESTING THE HALIFAX COUNTY SERVICE AUTHORITY TO REOPEN ITS CUSTOMER SERVICE OFFICE TO THE PUBLIC FOR REGULAR BUSINESS HOURS The Council considered a resolution requesting that the Halifax County Service Authority reopen its customer service office to the public during business hours. Mark Estes, with Halifax County Service Authority, addressed the Council. He stated that the Authority changed its operations during COVID to protect its water and wastewater plant operators from exposure. He said the Authority modeled its approach on the Western Virginia Water Authority and on other utilities and agencies that moved to online and appointment-only service. The Authority replaced its solid front door with an accessible door so staff can see arriving customers and assist them at the door or at their vehicles. It also provides a drop box, a lobby for completing applications, and 24-hour call service. Administrative staff were reduced from seven to five during this period. He stated that customer service has not declined and that online options have expanded. He noted that the Authority receives no tax revenue and is funded entirely through rates and fees, which must meet debt coverage requirements. The Authority has funded over $30 million in water and sewer projects and plans a $26 to $30 million water plant upgrade to remove PFAS and other contaminants. He stated that the Authority is developing a mobile app, newsletters, and an improved website to enhance customer service and transparency. A motion was made by Councilman Chandler and seconded by Vice Mayor Harris to adopt the resolution. 59|Page 5. INTRODUCTION OF NEW SOUTH BOSTON POLICE DEPARTMENT OFFICERS —- JAYDE HANNELL AND JONATHAN GEE Ronnie Edmonds, Chief of Police, introduced the South Boston Police Department's two newest officers, Jayde Hannell and Jonathan Gee. Both have completed the police academy and are now serving their probationary period. Hannell stated that he served eight years in the Army Reserves and was born and raised in Colorado. He has lived in South Boston for nearly eight years and joined law enforcement out of a sense of calling and a family history in the profession. Gee stated that he is from Charlotte County and served about ten years with the Department of Corrections before becoming a police officer closer to home. 6. RESOLUTION TO ADOPT A POLICY TO PROMOTE TOBACCO FREE PARKS AND OPEN PUBLIC SPACES WITHIN THE TOWN OF SOUTH BOSTON, VIRGINIA The Council considered a resolution adopting a policy to promote tobacco-free parks and open spaces in the Town of South Boston. Matthew Candland explained that the resolution follows a presentation made by local high school students in June. The policy is voluntary and educational, with signs to be posted in Town parks discouraging tobacco use. It carries no fines or enforcement provisions. A motion was made by Councilwoman Speece and seconded by Councilman Burton to adopt the resolution. 7. FINANCE REPORT Finance Director Danyell Duncan presented the July 2026 financial report, covering the first month of FY 2026-2027. Against an annual budget of $17,914,675.59, the Town has received $535,059.91 in revenue and spent $936,211.20, leaving expenditures over revenue by $401,151.36 year to date. Real estate tax bills have been mailed. Personal property tax bills are waiting on the billing from the Commissioner of the Revenue. July spending included first-quarter payments to outside organizations, a Fire Department purchase and Town Hall renovation costs. Public Works and Police vehicle purchases are planned later in the year. General Fund spending is at 5% of budget, with 8.3% of the year elapsed. Revenue is 2% because major tax revenues, grants, transfers and loan proceeds have not yet been received. Mrs. Duncan noted that the shortfall reflects the timing of collections and payments, not an operating deficit, and that revenue and spending will continue to be monitored. 8. TOWN MANAGER UPDATES 60|Page Patrick Elwell, Assistant Town Manager, reported that the tree resting on lines along Main Street has been removed; the lines were communication lines, not power lines, and the owner was contacted to remove the tree. The Harris Park ribbon cutting is sched uled for Saturday, November 14, with details to follow at the next meeting. Matthew Candland, Town Manager, reported that Lieutenant Mitch Bowen retired from the Police Department after more than 18 years of service and was recognized at an event at the police station; the Department will seek to fill the vacancy in the near future. Firefighter Caleb Wade resigned from the Fire Department to become the County Public Safety Coordinator. The historic district expansion, an approximately two-year process funded by a grant, is about halfway complete; the first public hearing has been held, and the consultant will prepare the next report for submission to the U.S. Department of the Interior. Expansion would allow property owners to qualify for federal and state historic tax credits, and target properties include the Button Factory and the Prizary building next to Ace Hardware. At the Council's request, staff will bring a map of the current and proposed district boundaries to the next meeting. The Town Hall renovation is progressing well, with demolition largely complete and completion expected in late spring or early summer 2027, and the hotel renovation is expected to be complete around February. The Town has hired Asmita Poudel as Community Standards Specialist, formerly the Code Enforcement Officer position; she will begin work this Friday and will be introduced at the October meeting. . CITIZEN COMMENTS Talley Roberts, speaking on behalf of her father, Christian Roberts expressed support for the proposed dog park and its benefits to the community. Another resident requested that the sidewalk be extended from Hamilton Boulevard to the Centerville area on at least one side, noting that pedestrians walk in the ditch and that the area is inaccessible on foot, and asked that the Town begin the project in phases. Town Manager Matthew Candland responded that the project faces two primary challenges: acquiring right-of-way from property owners, who opposed the idea when approached years ago, and cost, noting that a comparable VDOT sidewalk application for Sinai Road was estimated at approximately $7 million. The speaker suggested extending the existing sidewalk on the school side and adding a crosswalk. Staff noted that some properties have changed ownership since the owners were last approached about 10 to 12 years ago and stated that the Town will look into the matter, including surveying property owners and considering a phased approach. Mark Estes, of South Boston, asked whether marijuana could be added to the tobacco- free parks policy, citing secondhand marijuana smoke in Town parks. Ryland Clark commended Town Manager Matthew Candland for his assistance with the dog park project, his work on the IDA infrastructure committee and the high school track effort, and his support of Feed Halifax. Finance Director Danyell Duncan reminded citizens that tax payments are being accepted at 1927 Jeffress Boulevard, at the Washington-Coleman Community Center, and that online payment portals are available. Payments by mail 61|Page should continue to be sent to 455 Ferry Street, as the post office will forward mail without an address change. 10.CLOSED SESSION On the motion of Councilman Chandler, seconded by Vice Mayor Harris, the Council voted unanimously to convene in closed session under the Virginia Freedom of Information Act to discuss the acquisition of real property for a public purpose, as allowed under Virginia Code §2.2-3711(A)(3). Voting Aye: Chandler, Harris, Speece, Burton and Elliott. Absent and Not Voting: Younger On the motion of Councilman Chandler, seconded by Councilman Burton, the Council voted unanimously to return to open session. Voting Aye: Chandler, Harris, Speece, Burton and Elliott, Absent and Not Voting: Younger On a motion of Councilman Chandler, seconded by Vice Mayor Harris, Council certified by the following vote: Chandler, Harris, Speece, Burton and Elliott. Opposed: None; Absent/Not Voting: Younger; that to the best of each Council member’s knowledge, only public business matters lawfully exempted from the open meeting requirements of the Virginia Freedom of Information Act and identified in the Motion convening the closed session were heard, discussed or considered in the closed session. There being no further business, the meeting was adjourned. Mayor Edward Owens Attest: Sarah Lowe, Clerk of Council 62|Page

title: NOTICE: Ward 1 Vacancy on South Hill Town Council
text: NOTICE OF WARD 1 VACANCY ON SOUTH HILL TOWN COUNCIL The South Hill Town Council is seeking an individual to fill the Ward 1 Council vacancy created by the passing of Councilor Lillie Feggins-Boone on October 10, 2026. The appointment will be for the remainder of the current term, through December 31, 2026. Interested candidates must be registered voters residing in Ward 1 of South Hill, Virginia. Resumes must be submitted by 5:00 p.m. on Friday, October 30, 2026, and can be either mailed or hand-delivered. Mailing Address: Town of South Hill Attn: Mayor Mike Moody 211 S. Mecklenburg Avenue South Hill, VA 23970 Delivery Address: Town of South Hill Attn: Mayor Mike Moody 111 E. Danville Street South Hill, VA 23970 The South Hill Town Council will hold its regular meeting on Monday, November 9, 2026, at 7:00 p.m. Interested candidates for the Ward 1 vacancy are invited to attend the meeting and address Council. In accordance with § 24.2-228 of the Code of Virginia, Council will reconvene on Monday, November 23, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. to make the interim appointment, allowing for the required minimum seven-day period between the public announcement of proposed appointees and the appointment.

title: PDF Agenda for Town Council Regular Meeting - 10/13/2026 - 9:00am
text: TOWN COUNCIL REGULAR MEETING 21 Main Street Tuesday, October 13, 2026 at 9:00 AM AGENDA Possible additions to the agenda and related materials are not set forth herein. Times set forth are approximate and may be adjusted as necessary. I. WORKSESSION - 9:00 AM A. Parks and Recreation Master Plan: Vision, Priorities, and Strategic Direction Staff and the Town’s consultant, Kimley-Horn, will provide an update on the Parks and Recreation Master Plan with a focus on the emerging priorities and strategic direction for the Town’s parks, recreation facilities, programs, and services. Town Council will be asked to provide feedback to guide development of the draft Master Plan; no formal action or approval of individual projects is requested. Presenter: Kelly Koernig, Director of Parks and Recreation, and Kimley-Horn B. Fall Leaf Collection Program Overview Staff will provide an overview of the Town’s fall leaf collection program, including the collection schedule and service areas, how residents should prepare leaves for collection, and what residents can expect during the program. The presentation is intended to prepare Town Council and the community for the upcoming collection season and answer common questions about the service. No Council action is requested. Presenter: John Ward, Director of Public Works C. Capital Improvement Program Quarterly Update Staff will introduce a new quarterly work session presentation for the Town’s Capital Improvement Program and provide an overview of what Town Council can expect from future updates. The presentation will also highlight the status of selected capital projects, including projects under construction, recently completed, in design or approaching construction, and on the horizon. No Council action is requested. Presenter: Judson Rex, Town Manager, and Michael Wharton, Director of Capital Asset Management D. Town Council Ward System Review Discussion. Mayor Nevill will lead a discussion regarding the Town’s current ward system and whether Town Council is interested in establishing a citizenbased committee to review the existing system and potential alternatives. Presenter: Mayor Carter Nevill E. Finance Committee Update Committee Chair, Bill Semple, Ward 2 will provide an update on recent Finance Committee Meetings, information presented and items discussed. Committee Members: Bill Semple, Ward 2 (Chair) and Paul Mooney, At-large. Staff Liaison: Stephanie Miller, Director of Finance Capital Improvement Project Contingency Policy Presenter: Judson Rex F. Public Safety Committee Update Committee Chair, Michele O'Halloran, Ward 4 will provide an update on recent Public Safety Committee Meetings, information presented and items discussed. Committee Members: Michelle O'Halloran, Ward 4 (Chair) and David McGuire, At-large. Staff Liaison: Tim Carter, Police Chief. G. Planning Commission Update The Planning Commission has not met or taken action since the last Town Council meeting; therefore, there are no projects or other matters to update at this time. H. Town/County Liaison Committee Meeting Update Staff will provide an update on the September 28, 2026, Town/County Liaison Committee meeting. In addition, Town Council is requested to provide input on potential topics for future Liaison Committee meetings. No formal Council action is requested. Presenter: Judson Rex, Town Manager. I. Agenda Review Staff will provide an overview of the 6:30 p.m. Regular Meeting agenda and provide Town Council an opportunity to raise questions, comments, or requested changes. Presenter: Judson Rex, Town Manager J. Closed Session The Town Council will meet in Closed Session to discuss topics allowed under the Virginia Freedom of Information Act. II. REGULAR MEETING - 6:30 PM A. INVOCATION. B. PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE. C. PROCLAMATIONS AND RECOGNITIONS. a. A Proclamation Recognizing and Celebrating the 100th Anniversary of The Rotary Club of Warrenton, Virginia. b. ExcellenceinAction! D. CITIZEN'S TIME. E. APPROVAL OF THE AGENDA. F. PUBLIC HEARINGS. a. Ordinance 2026-14: Town Code Amendment Regarding Commercial Refuse Collection Outside the Historic District. Town Council will consider an amendment to Section 8-21 of the Town Code that would discontinue Town-provided refuse collection for commercial properties outside the Historic District and require affected businesses to arrange for private collection beginning January 1, 2027. Presenter: Judson Rex, Town Manager, on behalf of Lauren Kruck, Project Manager. b. Ordinance 2026-15: Town Code Amendment Regarding Noise Regulations for Building Operations and Animals. Town Council will consider amendments to Section 11-19 of the Town Code related to permitted building operations on weekends, holidays, and outside normal construction hours, as well as regulations addressing continuous animal noise. Presenter: Rob Walton, Director of Community Development. c. Ordinance 2026-16: Town Code Amendment Regarding Expanded Polystyrene (Styrofoam) Food Service Containers. Town Council will consider amendments to the Town Code implementing state requirements prohibiting food vendors from dispensing prepared food in expanded polystyrene food service containers and establishing procedures for exemptions and enforcement. Presenter: Rob Walton, Director of Community Development. G. CONSENT AGENDA. a. Approval of Town Council Minutes The Town Council will consider approval of prepared minutes for the Novem0ber 11th, 2025, Regular Town Council Meeting & November 24th, 2025, Special Town Council Meeting. Presenter: Stephen Clough, Town Clerk b. Resolution for FY 2027 Budget Amendment: VDOT State of Good Repair Funding for Street Resurfacing. Town Council will consider a resolution amending the FY 2027 Adopted Budget to appropriate $29,405 in Virginia Department of Transportation State of Good Repair funding for resurfacing portions of Broadview Avenue, Falmouth Street, Main Street, and Alexandria Pike. The projects are fully funded by VDOT with no Town funding required. Presenter: Michael Wharton, Director of Capital Asset Management. H. NEW BUSINESS. I. UNFINISHED BUSINESS. a. Main Street Improvement Project After-Action Review and Next Steps. The Town Manager will present an after-action review of the Main Street Improvement Project focused on lessons learned and organizational improvements resulting from the project. The discussion will address changes underway to strengthen communication, stakeholder engagement, and capital project delivery, as well as next steps for developing a more intentional Town-wide approach to economic development. No formal Council action is requested. Presenter: Judson Rex, Town Manager. J. TOWN ATTORNEY'S REPORT. K. TOWN MANAGER'S REPORT. L. COUNCILMEMBERS TIME. M. ADJOURNMENT.

Council Meeting Date: October 13, 2026 Agenda Title: Parks and Recreation Master Plan Update Requested Action: Receive Visioning and Implementation and provide feedback on emerging trends, priorities, and strategic direction in the development of the Master Plan Department / Agency Lead: Parks and Recreation Staff Lead: Kelly Koernig, Director of Parks and Recreation EXECUTIVE SUMMARY The Town is continuing development of the Parks and Recreation Master Plan to establish a long-term framework for maintaining, improving, and investing in the Town's parks, recreation facilities, programs, and services. This work session builds upon the Phase 1 Needs Assessment presented to Town Council in January 2026 and provides Council an opportunity to review and provide feedback on the emerging vision and strategic direction before development of the draft Master Plan. As part of Phase 2, Kimley-Horn facilitated a Visioning and Implementation Workshop on August 19, 2026. The workshop built upon the findings of the previously completed Needs Assessment and brought together Town staff, as well as Fauquier County Parks and Recreation representatives to identify desired outcomes, priorities, implementation considerations, partnerships, and potential near- and long-term opportunities. Kimley-Horn will present the results of the workshop and the emerging strategic direction for the Master Plan. Council feedback from the work session will help guide development of the Plan's vision, guiding principles, goals, actions, and phased implementation framework. BACKGROUND Plan Warrenton 2040 identifies the development of a Parks, Recreation, and Open Space Master Plan as an implementation action to guide long-term investment in the Town's parks and recreation system. The Comprehensive Plan calls for a master plan that builds upon existing park infrastructure and addresses physical and programming improvements, implementation, operations, and maintenance costs. The Town initiated the Parks and Recreation Master Plan process with Kimley-Horn to evaluate the existing system, identify community needs, and guide future investment and service delivery. 21 Main Street Warrenton, Virginia 20186 • 540-347-1101| www.warrentonva.gov 5 Item A. Page 2 Phase 1 of the planning process focused on understanding the current condition and performance of the Town's parks, facilities, programs, and services. The Needs Assessment included park and facility evaluations, level-of-service and peer benchmarking, demographic and recreation trend analysis, stakeholder and focus group engagement, a community-wide survey, and a focused evaluation of the Warrenton Aquatic and Recreation Facility (WARF). The Needs Assessment found that Warrenton's parks and recreation system is starting from a position of relative strength. Parks perform well overall, community satisfaction with maintenance is high, parkland exceeds the peer average, and the WARF continues to serve as a highly valued recreation asset. The assessment also identified areas requiring continued attention, including reinvestment in aging facilities and assets, connectivity and access, park amenities, changing recreation needs, and long-term asset protection. Phase 1 findings were presented to Town Council in January 2026. The presentation provided Council with an overview of the Needs Assessment findings, including stakeholder and community input, demographic analysis, park and system evaluations, level of service, and WARF-specific findings. Following completion of the Needs Assessment, the project moved from understanding the existing system to establishing future vision and priorities for implementation. On August 19, 2026, Kimley-Horn facilitated a workshop with Town staff and representatives from Fauquier County. Participants were asked to consider what the Parks and Recreation system could deliver over the next 10–15 years and then evaluate those ideas that could realitiscally move forward within the next five year years based on funding, staffing and operating capacity, partnerships, sustainability, timing, and implementation readiness. The workshop identified five overarching themes that provide an emerging framework for the Master Plan: Protect – Maintain, reinvest in, and sustain existing parks, the WARF, and recreation assets. Connect – Improve trails, sidewalks, access, wayfinding, and connections between parks and the community. Activate – Expand programs, events, and recreation opportunities for all ages and abilities. Enhance – Make targeted improvements and add amenities where they provide the greatest value. Evolve Strategically – Over the longer term, evaluate opportunities to expand parks, facilities, recreation amenities, and open space across the system based on changing community needs, available resources, partnerships, and the Town's ability to sustainably operate and maintain those investments. Respond to changing needs and opportunities by adapting the parks and recreation system over time. Future investments should be guided by demonstrated need, available resources, partnerships, and the Town’s ability to sustainably operate and maintain them. The strongest and most consistent theme was taking care of the Town's existing parks and facilities. Maintenance, safety, cleanliness, staffing, replacement of aging assets, and sustainable funding were repeatedly identified as core priorities, with maintenance and reinvestment generally taking precedence over significant expansion. 6 Item A. Page 3 The workshop also identified opportunities to improve connectivity, expand recreation programming, and provide additional comfort amenities (i.e. shade, seating, restrooms), strengthen park identity and wayfinding, advance park-specific improvements, and evaluate longer-term opportunities such as expanded indoor recreation, aquatics, and other facility needs. One of the exercises specifically asked participants to distinguish between long-term priorities and initiatives that are currently well positioned to move forward. Funding availability and staffing/operating capacity were recurring constraints, reinforcing that while community interest is an important consideration, available resources and capacity also influence when projects can move forward. STAFF RECOMMENDATION Staff recommends that Town Council receive the presentation from Kimley-Horn and provide feedback on the emerging vision, priorities, and strategic direction for the Parks and Recreation Master Plan. No formal action or approval of individual projects is requested at this work session. Council's feedback will be used to inform development of the draft Master Plan and its recommendations and implementation framework. Service Level/Collaborative Impact The Master Plan will provide a framework for future Parks and Recreation service delivery, asset management, capital investment, programming, accessibility, and community partnerships. Implementation will require continued coordination across Town departments, including Public Works, Community Development, Capital Asset Management, Finance, Communications, and other departments as appropriate. The planning process has also identified opportunities for collaboration with Fauquier County, schools, community and nonprofit organizations, local sports organizations, businesses, sponsors, foundations, and other community partners. Policy Direction/Warrenton Plan 2040 The Parks and Recreation Master Plan directly supports several goals and policies established in Plan Warrenton 2040. P-3 calls for all Town residents to have opportunities to access recreational assets and natural resources, while P-3.1 and P-3.2 focus on improving access to parks, trails, green space, and other recreational resources, including a goal of access within a 10-minute walk. P-4 establishes a long-term approach to preserving the Town's parks, open spaces, and natural resources, and P-4.3 specifically calls for development of a system-wide Parks Master Plan to guide long-term investment. The Plan also identifies ADA access, trails, sidewalks, and other park improvements as measures of progress The emerging Master Plan themes of Protect, Connect, Activate, Enhance, and Expand Strategically build upon these Comprehensive Plan goals and provide a more detailed framework for Parks and Recreation investment, operations, programming, partnerships, and implementation over the next 10 years. Fiscal Considerations 7 Item A. Page 4 There is no additional fiscal impact associated with receiving the presentation or providing direction at this work session. Future recommendations contained in the Master Plan may have operating or capital budget impacts. As recommendations are developed, implementation considerations will include estimated costs, funding availability, staffing and operating impacts, partnerships, and long-term sustainability. The workshop specifically identified funding readiness and staffing/operating capacity as important considerations when determining when projects should advance. Any future funding requests would be considered through the Town's annual operating budget, CARP/CIP, or other applicable approval processes. Legal Considerations There is no anticipated legal impact associated with the presentation or Council discussion at this work session. Any future Master Plan recommendations requiring contracts, agreements or other legal action would be reviewed separately as appropriate. ATTACHMENTS 1. RE: CITIZENS' PERIOD Mayor Taylor advised that the next agenda item is Citizens' Period. She stated that there was one citizen listed on the sign in sheet who wished to address the Council during Citizens' Period. Mayor Taylor inquired if Mr. Bob McWhirter would come to the podium to address the Council. Mr. Bob McWhirter was recognized and addressed the Council regarding his appreciation for the removal of the Flock cameras, his concerns about the recent styrofoam exemption, his concerns with narrow lane widths in town and his concerns regarding excessive noise from music at St. John's Episcopalian Church and on Main Street. He stated that, recently, Councilman Hand made a noise complaint against him. Mr. McWhirter explained that Councilman Hand raised concerns that their music was too loud, and that a neighbor had just passed away and that the family had to deal with the sound coming from his home. He commented that he was not aware of the neighbor's passing, and that Councilman Hand's 911 call included him saying that it was not fair to everyone else. Mr. McWhirter noted that he also believes that it is not fair for everyone to listen to all the sounds that are being produced in town, whether it comes from Main Street, a church, commercial mowing, etc., when it is substantially loud. He continued to address his concerns regarding excessive noise with the Town Council. Councilwoman Atkins stated the following: "Excuse me. May I ask a question? Can you give me those two addresses again, please? I know you said Cassell Road." Mr. McWhirter stated Cassell Road right at Papa John's. Councilwoman Atkins stated the following: "Yes. Okay. Then Old Stage Mall?" Mr. McWhirter stated that is correct, the little road across from Petals Florist/Wine Bar. Councilwoman Atkins stated the following: "Thank you so much." 6 Section 7, ItemA. Mayor Taylor advised that there were no other citizens listed on the sign-in sheet who wished to address the Council during Citizens' Period, therefore, she would proceed with the agenda. 9. RE: PRESENTATIONS TO TOWN COUNCIL A. RE: AUGUST 2026 FINANCIAL STATEMENT Mayor Taylor advised that the next agenda item is the presentation of the August 2026 Financial Statement by Town Treasurer Angela Pennington. Town Treasurer Pennington stated that the Town finished August 2026 in the negative by $3.6 Million, which is $2.3 Million more than last year. She noted that she has received the books from the Commissioner of the Revenue's Office for real estate and personal property taxes, and she advised that she hopes to send out tax tickets in October so that the Town can begin receiving that revenue. Town Treasurer Pennington then presented the annual comparison of meals tax, lodging tax and sales tax from the same time in 2025. She inquired if any of the Council members had any questions regarding the August 2026 Financial Statement. There being none, Mayor Taylor proceeded with the agenda. B. RE: PLANS FOR USE OF HARRAH-MCDONALD FOUNDATION DONATED FUNDS Mayor Taylor advised that the next agenda item is a presentation by Director of Parks and Recreation Josh Sharitz regarding the plans for the use of the donation funds received by the Harrah-McDonald Foundation. Director of Parks and Recreation Sharitz stated that the Town Council recently approved the acceptance of $250,000 from the Harrah-McDonald Foundation in memory of Larry Harrah. He noted that the types of projects proposed by the donor were intended to keep children active, either through active play or with upgrades to the Town's ball field facilities. Director Sharitz explained that Staff has identified three (3) projects that they would like to put the donated money towards. He stated that the first project would be upgrading the dugouts at the Wytheville Community College (WCC) ball fields, due to drainage issues within the space. Director Sharitz advised that these upgrades would include covered dugouts and the addition of steps from the WCC track to the ball field. He stated that the anticipated cost of this project is $46,000, however, there will be little to no ongoing upkeep cost associated with it. Director Sharitz commented that he anticipates the project will begin around the middle of October and expects it to be completed by the end of the year. He advised that the second project would be the installation of a playground at the Wytheville T-Ball Park. He stated that, currently, there is only one playground in Withers Park, and it is primarily aimed at children ages five (5) to twelve (12). He explained that this playground project would be primarily aimed at children aged two (2) to five (5) years old, as they are the heavier users of the T-Ball Park. Director Sharitz remarked that this project would focus on the installation of low climbing structures and swings, and that he anticipates the cost of this project to be around $50,000. He noted that he expects this project to begin and to be completed by the end of the current budget year. Director Sharitz stated that the third project would be upgrading the playground structure at Withers Park. He commented that this is the only playground structure in Town and it is nearly 20 years old. Director Sharitz advised that this project will most likely take place later 7 Section 7, ItemA. than the first two projects, because Staff is awaiting the final design and layout of the proposed splashpad in that area. He noted that the anticipated cost for this project is around $150,000, however, Staff are seeking additional grants to help offset the cost of installations for more playground equipment in that space. Director Sharitz inquired if there were any questions. There being none, Mayor Taylor proceeded with agenda. 10. RE: NEW BUSINESS A. RE: WYTHE BLAND FOUNDATION GRANT - HOMESTEAD SMOKEHOUSE RESTORATION PROJECT Mayor Taylor advised that the next agenda item is a Staff Report by Director of Museums Grant Gerlich regarding the Wythe Bland Foundation grant for the Homestead Smokehouse Restoration Project. Director of Museums Gerlich stated that the Museums Department has been fortunate enough to receive a grant from the Wythe Bland Foundation for the Smokehouse Restoration Project. He noted that he is asking for the Council's approval to accept this grant and to work on a mid-year budget line item for this project. Director Gerlich explained that when they applied for the grant, they asked for $16,500, and that the grant was approved for $15,000. He advised that he is requesting an extra $2,000, in case there are any extra expenses. Director Gerlich stated that the smokehouse is the only outbuilding that is original to the site, and he noted that the contractor completing the restoration work calls it a treasure. He inquired if the Council had any questions. Mayor Taylor inquired if the smokehouse has been operational at all. Director Gerlich stated that people are able to look inside of it, however, they cannot go in it. He noted that the smokehouse was built by John Huffard in the 1840s. Director Gerlich explained that the chinking is all original, that there is some rotting logs and that the porcelain cement foundation needs to be replaced with a stone foundation. Vice-Mayor Johnson thanked Director of Museums Gerlich for all he does for the Town's Department of Museums. Mayor Taylor inquired if there was a motion to accept a $15,000 grant from the Wythe Bland Foundation for the Town of Wytheville Department of Museums' Homestead Smokehouse Restoration Project; approve a $2,000 mid-year budget amendment for project costs exceeding the grant award, establishing a total project budget of $17,000; and, to authorize Town staff to execute all necessary grant and contract documents. Motion made by Vice-Mayor Johnson, Seconded by Councilwoman Atkins. Mayor Taylor inquired if there was any discussion on the motion. There being none, the motion was approved with the following voting results, by roll call vote: Voting Yea: Councilman Hand, Jr., Councilwoman Pattison, Mayor Taylor, Councilwoman Atkins, Vice-Mayor Johnson. RE: EAST MAIN STREET PAVEMENT RESURFACING AND SIDEWALK PROJECT Mayor Taylor advised that the next agenda item is a Staff Report by Landscape Architect/Grants Administrator John Woods regarding the East Main Street Pavement Resurfacing and Sidewalk Project. Street, between 5th Street, all the way out just short of Liberty Street. He noted that Staff was also pleased, this year, that VDOT has expanded the type of work that can be completed through this program including the upgrading of existing non-compliant Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) ramps. Landscape Architect/Grants Administrator Woods explained that in looking at the existing curb and gutter throughout the project area, there are various areas where work needs to be improved or replacements need to be made before the paving is completed. He advised that the State of Good Repair Program reimbursement rate is 100 percent of the cost of the eligible work. He stated that an extra $40,000 is what is estimated to cover the cost of the additional crosswalk associated with the ramps, a portion of the cost overrun and some contingency. Schoolcraft/ Vice-Chairman Honorable Fred Luntsford Honorable Randy Carter Honorable Robert R, Adkins Honorable Steve Bates Honorable Tim Boardwine Honorable Clarence S. The motion was unanimously approved. AGENDA A motion was made by Bob Adkins/ seconded by Randy Carter/ to approve the agenda as presented to include items in red and to add an item to "Oppose AEPs Proposed Rate Increase" to the Consent Agenda. The motion was unanimously approved. PUBLIC HEARING ~ PROPOSED 1% INCREASE IN WISE COUNTY'S FY26/27 BUDGET A public hearing was duly advertised for this date to receive citizens' comments regarding a proposed 1% increase in Wise County's FY26/27 Budget. There being no comments/ the public hearing was closed. PRESENTATION - MECC UPDATE - DR. KRISTEN WESTOVER. PRESIDENT Dr. Kristen Westover/ President of Mountain Empire Community College appeared and offered a brief update about the college/ citing its enrollment numbers and highlighting the Promise Program which has a retention rate of 93%. She explained the decline in college enrollment is mostly due to high school enrollments shrinking. Currently, there are just over 2,000 students enrolled/ which includes high school students eligible for dual enrollment. Students can get an associate's degree for about $2/700. 1 PRESENTATION - CASH AND INVESTMENTS - DELORES SMITH, TREASURER Wise County Treasurer Delores W. Smith presented the Cash and Investment Report for the period ending August 31, 2026. The report included a monthiy summary of General Fund cash and investments, budget-to-actual information, General Fund transactions/ and a comparison of cash and investments across various governmental funds for flsca! years 2023 through 2026. As of August 31, 2026, the General Fund had total cash and investments of $14,262/155, compared to $16,628,619 at July 31, 2026. The report noted a month-to-month decrease of approximately $2.37 million. After accounting for the fund balance restriction under County policy, the remaining unrestricted fund balance was approximately $4.38 million. For the first two months of FY 2026-2027, Genera! Fund revenues totaled approximately $29.95 million, while expenditures totaled approximately $33.63 million, resulting En a net cash flow decrease of approximately $3.68 miilion. The Treasurer aiso reviewed historical cash and investment balances. As of June 30, 2026, total governmental funds held approximately $34.83 million, compared with $33.13 miillon at June 30,2025, $37.27 million at June 30, 2024, and $39.15 miliion at June 30, 2023. PRESENTATION - ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT UPDATE - BRIAN FAUN. EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, IDA Brian D. Falin/ Director of Economic Development and Executive Director of the Wise County Industrial Development Authority/ provided an update on "Project Recover/' a proposed municipal waste processing and recovery facility. Mr. Falin reviewed the current status of the Blackwood Landfill/ noting that the existing landfill footprint is anticipated to reach capacity within 18 to 24 months and that a final expansion would cost an estimated $6 million to $8 million and provide an additional three to five years of capacity. Mr. Falin outlined Project Recover's goals of increasing recycling and material recovery/ reducing landfill use/ extending landfill capacity/ and lowering long-term waste management costs. He reported that the IDA purchased a 23.714-acre site in the Blackwood Industrial Park in March 2026 for the proposed project. The site is zoned M-2 Heavy Industrial/ has utilities available/ and is adjacent to the existing landfill. The proposed facility is expected to recover approximately 95% to 99% of Incoming waste and is designed to process between 175/000 and 250/000 tons annually. The project represents an estimated $170 million capita! investment and is projected to create approximately 80 full-time Jobs. Mr. Falin stated that the developer is proceeding with permitting and financing, while the IDA and developer are negotiating a lease-purchase option for the site. The anticipated project 2 timellne is 18 to 24 months. Staff will continue to evaluate short-term landfill expansion and transfer options while development of Project Recover continues. ADJOURNMENT/RECESS September 1, 2026 The Wythe County Planning Commission held its regular monthly meeting on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, in the Board Room located at 340 South Sixth Street, Wytheville, Virginia beginning at 6:00 p.m. MEMBERS PRESENT David P. Midkiff Christopher C. King Susan M. Branscome Rodney S. Dunford Garry Rusty Beamer Heidi D. Lyall MEMBERS ABSENT Robert A. Epperson OTHERS PRESENT Matt Hankins, Deputy County Administrator Johnny Kincer, County Engineer Carol Jean Bryant Duncan Jimmy Scott Horne Lisa Shelton, County Planner William Barham Bryant Compton Jerri Webb DETERMINATION OF QUORUM AND CALL TO ORDER Chair Midkiff determined that a quorum was present and called the meeting to order. The Commission said the pledge of allegiance. DUNCAN/COMPTON REQUEST FOR VARIANCE Chair Midkiff asked to hear from staff. Mrs. Shelton stated that Bryant Compton wishes to subdivide approximately 4.5 acres off his property located along Beecher Lane, in the Fort Chiswell Magisterial District, and give it to Carol Jean Bryant (Duncan). Simultaneously, Mrs. Duncan wishes to subdivide approximately 11.3 acres off her property located along Beecher Lane and give it to Mr. Compton. Because both parcels do not have the 100’ state-maintained road frontage, the proposed division of this property would leave two non-conforming lots. They are requesting a variance to Section 5.3.1(8) of the ordinance in order to proceed with this proposed division. Mrs. Shelton pulled up the map that shows what they are requesting and showed the Commission that the subdivision would straighten up the boundary lines of parcels and clean them up some. Chair Midkiff asked if there was anyone that would like to address the Planning Commission regarding this variance, please state your name and address. William Barham, 362 Beecher Lane, Draper, VA, “I am an owner on top of the hill on Beecher Lane, I just want to make sure this is not interfering with any right-of-way through Beecher Lane. This division of property adding to or taking from, whatever, it’s not September 1, 2026 Unapproved Minutes interfering with anything. There are several people that have a right-of-way on Beecher Lane and as long as everything stays the same everything should be fine. I think the land should be divided up however they want it to be divided. I don’t think anybody has a problem with that as long as the right-of-way is the same.” Mr. Hankins stated that this shouldn’t change the right of way. Chair Midkiff asked if there is anyone else that would like to address the Planning Commission regarding this variance. Hearing none, he closed the Public Hearing and proceeded with the variance. Chair Midkiff asked if Beecher Lane was a private right-of-way. Mrs. Shelton stated that it is not a state-maintained road. After some discussion, it was deemed that it never had road frontage and never will and at least they are cleaning the lots up some. Chair Midkiff entertained a motion. Mrs. Lyall made a motion to approve the variance as requested. Mr. Dunford seconded it, and it passed unanimously. CITIZENS’ TIME Chair Midkiff asked if anyone wished to address the Commission during Citizens’ Time. Hearing none, Chair Midkiff closed Citizens’ Time and proceeded with the agenda. APPROVAL OF MINUTES A motion was made by Mr. King to approve the August 3, 2026, minutes. The motion was seconded by Ms. Branscome and passed unanimously. SUBDIVISION ORDINANCE A. Adjoining Owner/Lot Line Revision – The Commission reviewed three subdivision plats showing an adjoining owner/lot line revision approved by Mrs. Shelton for Robert & Jeanne Lance/Mary & William Krouskop, Speedwell; Roger & Beverly Wynn/Michael Jones, Black Lick, and Groseclose Brothers, LLC/Buford Sawyers, Speedwell. B. Lot Line Revision – The Commission reviewed a subdivision plat showing a lot line revision approved by Mrs. Shelton for Paul Goad & Paul Dewayne Goad, Fort Chiswell. COMING EVENTS The Board reviewed upcoming holidays and meetings for the month of September. MANUFACTURED HOME ORDINANCE – REQUEST FOR REVISION OF A SPECIAL USE PERMIT – HORNE September 1, 2026 Unapproved Minutes Mr. Jimmy Scott Horne of 6332 Stoney Fork Road, Wytheville, Virginia is applying for a revision to an existing Special Use Permit for an already established campground located at 5965 Stoney Fork Road, U.S. Route 52, in the Black Lick Magisterial District. The Special Use Permit was granted on November 27, 2018, by the Planning Commission and December 11, 2028, by the Board of Supervisors. Mr. Horne is proposing to take out Camp Site 10, 11 & 12 and the storage building that is on the property. Mr. Horne would like to leave 9 campsites and add 1 two-bedroom mobile home site. The Commissioners reviewed maps of the current RV Campground and the proposed changes. Mrs. Shelton spoke with Stacy (Tuck) Holiday in the Wythe County Health Department concerning the septic. He stated the requirements for a septic is 150 gallons per day per bedroom and 100 gallons per day per camper. There are two septic systems on the property and since this septic system was approved for 8 campers, if Mr. Horne takes out 3 camper sites, it should be good for a two-bedroom mobile home. Chair Midkiff entertained a motion. Mr. King made a motion to recommend this to the Board of Supervisors to approve the request, as presented. Mr. Dunford seconded it, and it passed unanimously. APPLICATION FOR CREATION OF AG AND FORESTAL DISTRICT Mrs. Shelton presented an application to the Planning Commission for informational purposes. She stated that she changed # 2 from “Each copy of this form shall be accompanied by United States Geological Survey 7.5 minute topographic map of the area that clearly shows the boundaries of the proposed district and boundaries of properties within the proposed district owned by each applicant. A general County highway map showing the general locations of the proposed district shall also accompany each copy of this form.” To now say “Each copy of this form shall be accompanied by maps and/or arial imagery or photographs that clearly show the boundaries of the proposed district as well as each addition and boundaries of properties within the proposed district owned by each applicant.” COUNTY ENGINEER REPORT Mr. Kincer showed pictures and gave an update on Progress Park Lot 35 and on the railroad repairs. EX OFICIO REPORT Mr. Burnett stated that the Board of Supervisors has approved the 1% sales tax to be voted on this fall. Dr. Street gave a presentation at all the schools about the 1% sales tax increase. Mr. Burnett gave a brief explanation about it. Mr. Burnett reported about some of the board and county staff going to visit data centers in Henrico County and that Sherriff Cline just announced that he is cancelling the contract with the flock cameras. DEPUTY COUNTY ADMINISTRATOR REPORT September 1, 2026 Unapproved Minutes Mr. Hankins took a tour with Citizens last week to see the progress on the broadband project. They have completed Miller’s Creek, Connors Valley Road and Stillwell. There are a lot of areas in the Eastern end of the county that Citizens is still working on. Most of them will have access to fiber by the end of September. LAND USE ORDINANCE REVIEW Mr. Hankins reminded everyone that the community input session for the Planning Commission and the Board of Supervisors is set for Thursday of this week at Scott Memorial Middle School at 6 p.m. It will be set up so that each district has a table. Folks can go to their district and talk to their representatives. The folks who come are welcome to talk to any of the Supervisors and Planning Commissioners. Mr. Hankins stated that he has made some changes to the ordinance, per the joint work session, and is making map changes. There are still a few changes that may need to be look at again. COMMISSION CONCERNS Mr. Dunford asked how far along the AI data center was in the Eastern part of the county. Mr. Burnett stated that right now they do not own any property, and they have no permits. Mr. Hankins stated that they have done their Geotech and have submitted a 288-page set of plans to the county engineer and DEQ for review. They have submitted for their storm water plans and their erosion and sediment plans will follow that. Mr. Dunford asked if it would be grandfathered in if the zoning was passed. Mr. Hankins stated that if there is affirmative government act between now and the time that the zoning is implemented, then yes, they would be grandfathered. Ms. Branscome asked if the County knew who the consumer is going to be for the data center in Progress Park. Mr. Hankins stated that they have not publicly indicated anything yet. Mr. Midkiff asked Mr. Burnett if any of the 14 data centers they went and visited was a Google data center or Alphabet. Mr. Burnett said the only one he remembers specifically was the Meta. Mr. Dunford asked how much water was BlueStar going to use? Mr. Hankins stated much more that any data center would use. Mr. Hankins stated that our water maximum licensure at the New River water treatment plant is 6 million gallons a day. It only took about 16 minutes today with a lower water level for it to flow by the Ivanhoe River gauge. We don’t take all that in at one time but that gives some perspective to how much capacity we have here. Ms. Branscome asked about training and equipment to fight a fire at a data center or solar farm. Mr. Hankins stated that with the solar farm there shouldn’t be anything to worry about there but if the Battery Energy Storage comes in or anything special in the data centers then yes there should be some concern, but that cost should be up to the developers not the county. September 1, 2026 Unapproved Minutes Chair Midkiff talked about the phone calls he has been receiving about the 1% sales tax increase. He has tried to explain that if we don’t increase it there and let travelers help pay for the school repairs, then it could possibly increase the Real Estate or Personal Property Taxes and we would much rather them increase the sales tax. Mr. King asked about the 1% sales tax increase. If it passes, when will it expire? Mr. Hankins said it would expire in 20 years. Mr. Hankins also stated that this increase is just for school construction and rehabilitation. It is not for teacher salaries, buses or anything else. Mr. King said he got an email from the Town of Wytheville talking about their Comprehensive Plan and he is wondering if they want people in the County to answer those questions. Mr. Hankins stated he is not sure. He would tend to think that it’s more for the folks in Wytheville to help make those determinations. ADJOURNMENT With no further business to transact, the Planning Commission adjourned at 7:36 p.m. until the next meeting on Monday, October 5, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. ___ David Midkiff, Chair September 28, 2026 The Wythe County Planning Commission held a special called joint meeting with the Board of Supervisors on Monday, September 28, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. in the Emergency Operations Conference (EOC) Room of the County Administration Building, 290 South Sixth Street, Wytheville, Virginia. Lyall BOARD MEMBERS PRESENT James D. “Jamie” Smith Bradley D. Martin J.W. “Dicky” Morgan BOARD MEMBERS ABSENT Sarah P. Crockett Rolland R. Cook Jesse Burnett Stacy A. Terry OTHERS PRESENT Stephen D. Bear, County Administrator Matt Hankins, Deputy County Administrator Martha Collins, Clerk/Administrative Assistant Lisa Shelton, County Planner DETERMINATION OF QUORUM AND CALL TO ORDER Chair Midkiff determined that a quorum was present and called the meeting to order. LAND USE ORDINANCE Mr. Hankins reviewed the current survey results and requested mapping changes. He presented a proposed schedule moving forward and discussed the logistics and procedures for the public hearings. The suggested schedule is as follows: Planning Commission: - October 5 – Set Public Hearing - October 26 – Hold Public Hearing - November 2 – Consideration and Vote Board of Supervisors: - November 12 – Review Planning Commission Recommendation, Set Public Hearing - December 3 – Hold Public Hearing - December 8 – Consideration and Vote September 28, 2026 Unapproved Minutes Mr. Hankins requested that the boards consider an effective date for the ordinance should it be adopted, noting that staff will need time to put procedures in place. ADJOURNMENT With no further business to transact, the Planning Commission adjourned at 7:37 p.m. until the next meeting on Monday, October 5, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. ___ David P. The hearing will be conducted in the auditorium of George Wythe High School, 1 Maroon Way, Wytheville, VA. Citizens will be heard in the order they are received. Alternatively, written comments for the record may be received via electronic mail to Lisa Shelton, County Planner, at ldshelton@wytheco.org or by mail at 290 South Sixth Street, Suite 350, Wytheville, VA 24382.
